text:
Renewed Hope’s Tireless Doctor

Iṣẹ́ ni oògùn ìṣẹ́ means 'work is the medicine for poverty'. It is an old, plain saying, and it fits a doctor who has spent his career showing up, from hospital wards to medical missions in Lagos to one of Nigeria’s hardest portfolios.

The Honourable Minister of Education, Dr Maruf Tunji Alausa (FAMedS), CON, Tunji to almost everyone, is a kidney specialist from Epe, in Lagos State. On 23 October 2024, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, moved him from the Ministry of Health to the Federal Ministry of Education, a portfolio better known for strikes, scandals and unfinished plans than for results. Two years later, the administration's supporters hold him up as proof that the Renewed Hope agenda can deliver. Lecturers have a new pay agreement after sixteen years of haggling. More than a million students have received student loans. The big examination bodies are being pushed online. Students who run their own companies have competed for up to ₦50 million in equity-free grants. In September 2026, the city of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, gave him its key.

HM Alausa was born in Epe, a lagoon town on the eastern edge of Lagos State, to a middle-class Yoruba family rooted in schooling, the son of teachers of modest means. He took his medical degree at the University of Lagos, graduating in 1993. Between 1995 and 1997, he trained in internal medicine at the Royal Bolton Hospital and the University of Newcastle in England. From 1997 to 2001, he continued at Cook County Hospital in Chicago, where he became Chief Medical Resident, the post that makes one doctor responsible for coordinating the training of every intern and resident in the programme. It is hospital medicine's nearest thing to middle management, and it tends to go to the colleague the others trust to hold the rota together when everyone is tired.

After Chicago came a stint as assistant professor at Rush University Medical School, and then a fellowship in nephrology and hypertension at the Medical College of Wisconsin, from July 2002 to June 2004. Nephrologists look after kidneys, which means they look after patients whose bodies are failing slowly, expensively and often without complaint until late. The work is mostly measurement, patience and unglamorous follow-up. He became board-certified, was named one of America's Best Physicians in 2007 and again in 2012, and published research in journals that include the New England Journal of Medicine. He also went into business. He founded the Kidney Care Centre, which a Lagos supporters' group later described as having grown to 17 locations in Illinois, with a dialysis centre added in 2014. 

The résumé reads like an American career, but he never stopped being Nigerian. HM Alausa led medical missions from the United States to Lagos under the banner of Eko Club International, and he stayed active in Lagosians of Chicago, the association for Lagos indigenes in that city. Someone with that record could have kept practising in Illinois to a comfortable old age. That he did not has less to do with ambition than with an old debt.

The debt goes back to the 1990s. After the military annulled the June 1993 presidential election, Nigeria's pro-democracy movement was driven first underground and then abroad. NADECO, the coalition founded in May 1994, lost leaders to prison and many more to foreign capitals under General Sani Abacha, and the exiles needed money, shelter and doctors.

According to Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele, HM Alausa provided much of the latter. Speaking in public in 2025, Bamidele said that while Alausa was still a resident physician, first in England and then in the United States, he treated exiled NADECO leaders in Europe and America free of charge and raised resources to keep them going. Bamidele stressed that no government money was involved. The work was done behind the scenes, he said, and was not undertaken for reward. When the exiles came home after 1999, he added, Alausa organised free medical outreaches in the South-West, including eye care and surgery. Bamidele, who served in Tinubu's Lagos cabinet, recalls that the then governor tried more than once to bring HM Alausa into government and was refused, because Alausa did not want it said that he had backed the struggle for personal gain. And when Tinubu became president, Bamidele says, it took weeks of persuasion before Alausa agreed to serve.

Many Nigerian public servants arrive in office after years of wanting it. This one arrived after years of being asked, and having already done the unpaid work. The first call came in August 2023, when Tinubu's second list of ministerial nominees named Alausa as a nephrologist from Illinois. He cleared Senate screening and was sworn in on 21 August as Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, working under the Coordinating Minister, Professor Muhammad Ali Pate. At his reception at the ministry that day, he made a point worth remembering: "that health is bigger than hospitals, and that the ministry also had to think about social security and national security".

The second call came on 23 October 2024, when Tinubu dismissed five ministers and redeployed ten others. HM Alausa was sent to Education, replacing Professor Tahir Mamman, who had held the portfolio since the same August. At the handover in the health ministry two weeks later, Pate called the move a recognition of Alausa's "good and exceptional work." The official release put Pate's gloss more bluntly in its headline: the reward for work is more work. His last act as health minister was to hand out appointment letters to ten new medical directors, among them the heads of newly created Federal Medical Centres in Misau, Ikole-Ekiti and Epe.

What he walked into was not nice at all. Early profiles listed funding shortages, recurring strikes, uncertainty over a new basic-education curriculum due to begin in January 2025, and teacher shortages and low literacy, especially in the north. His own later figures put the scale in plain numbers: 45 million children between five and fourteen unable to read a text suited to their age, and 15 million out of school. The agreement with university lecturers had gone unrevised since 2009. Examination malpractice was routine enough that the minister would call it a systemic problem, and a Guardian analysis of JAMB data found that of 8.75 million candidates who sat the university entrance examination between 2021 and 2025, only about 3.19 million secured places anywhere.

He began, in the manner of his old trade, with a diagnosis. Alausa told Channels Television in 2025 that a diagnostic review of the country's examination systems had been started as soon as he took office. The habit, as it turned out, ran through everything else he did.

His first press briefing as Education Minister, on 5 November 2024, was a short course in how he works. He said the 18-year minimum age for admission to tertiary institutions, set in July by his predecessor, would not go ahead. The benchmark would be 16, with exceptions for gifted children. At JAMB's policy meeting the following year, he called 16 non-negotiable and warned that anyone who altered age records would be sanctioned. In the same briefing, he said the ban on certificates from Benin and Togo would stay, that the ministry would pursue nutrition programmes in schools, and that it would work with the humanitarian affairs ministry on conditional cash transfers to coax children back into class. Out-of-school children, he said, were a key priority.

Behind those first decisions sits a framework. The Nigeria Education Sector Renewal Initiative, known as NESRI, is a six-point agenda the ministry describes as a way to move the country from a resource-based economy to a knowledge-based one. Its practical value is that it gives dozens of separate programmes a common spine.

What stands out is how often a programme arrives with a counting machine attached. A School Safety Portal, built with the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, had registered 15,000 schools and geolocated 141,000 by the ministry's February 2026 quarterly report. A Federal Tertiary Institutions Governance Transparency Portal tracks performance and funding at 47 of the 67 federal universities and 35 of the 39 polytechnics. Stipends under the technical education programme are policed by biometric attendance checks at every centre. A Learner Identification Number is being rolled out, and the country's out-of-school children are being mapped. None of this is glamorous. All of it is what a clinician would recognise as taking a proper history before deciding on treatment, and education planning in Nigeria has long been hobbled by unreliable data. A minister who insists on counting first is at least asking the right question.

The clearest result so far is in the universities. Lecturers and the federal government had been trying to renegotiate their 2009 agreement since 2017, through a long run of strikes that in 2020 lasted nine months. In October 2025, the Academic Staff Union of Universities began a two-week warning strike, the first of the Tinubu presidency, and suspended it nine days later after meeting the government's renegotiation team, led by Yayale Ahmed. The new agreement was concluded on 23 December 2025 and presented in public on 14 January 2026, to take effect from 1 January. It lifts academic pay by 40 per cent, gives professors who retire at 70 a pension equal to their last full salary, and sets aside ₦10 billion a year from 2026 to 2028 for a stabilisation and restoration fund. The union's president, Chris Piwuna, credited Alausa with the final push, and said at the signing that ASUU hoped this minister would prove different, so that it would not have to threaten strikes before any part of the deal was honoured. Alausa has since said that 90 to 95 per cent of tertiary institutions began paying the increase even before the 2026 budget passed, and he calls the agreement the death of the strike.

The students in those lecture halls have their own reasons to pay attention. The Nigerian Education Loan Fund, NELFUND, has its own management under Akintunde Sawyerr, and the loan scheme was Tinubu's promise before it was Alausa's responsibility, but the minister has made it one of the achievements he defends most often. It has grown quickly. The fund reported 1,388,592 beneficiaries and ₦242.4 billion disbursed by 15 April 2026. By 3 September, it put cumulative disbursements at ₦355.87 billion, of which ₦192.89 billion went to 319 institutions as fees and ₦162.98 billion to students as upkeep.

Money for fees is one thing. Work is another, and here the ministry has spent most of its energy on skills. Isa Pantami, the former communications minister, calls the shift from certificate to skills Alausa's most defining reform. The technical and vocational programme, launched in May 2025, drew more than 90,000 applications within days of its portal opening, and trainees are paid a monthly stipend of ₦22,500. The February 2026 quarterly report put payments at ₦2.97 billion to 160,000 young people, with another ₦4.6 billion for training centres, and Pantami counts more than 150,000 trainees in over 1,600 centres. A Digital Training Academy, built with Coursera and announced at the Education World Forum in London in May 2026, aims to give 36,000 young Nigerians globally recognised digital certificates, and 16,000 have been selected for the first cohort. For students who already run a registered company, the Student Venture Capital Grant offers up to ₦50 million in equity-free funding, delivered with TETFund, the Bank of Industry, Afara Initiative, AfriLabs and Google. Applications ran from 17 November 2025 to 23 January 2026.

Below the universities, where most Nigerian children actually are, the ministry's figures from the 2026 basic education bootcamp in Jos describe a bigger machine. Between January 2025 and January 2026, the federal government released ₦106 billion in matching grants through the Universal Basic Education Commission. The ministry reports 978,000 teachers trained, 10,000 classrooms renovated, 7.8 million textbooks distributed, and ₦22 billion spent on teacher development, with ₦2.035 billion going directly to school-based management committees for community projects. A mobile training platform for teachers, Edurevamp, had signed up 37,000 by February. According to Pantami, the retirement age for teachers has been extended to 65, and the government has committed to paying their licensing fees at the Teachers Registration Council. The bootcamp also saw national policy documents launched on inclusive education, on Almajiri education, and on the return to school of married and pregnant adolescent girls. In Gombe, a ₦2.55 billion campaign called Flow with Confidence set out to deliver more than a million sanitary pads to 370,000 rural girls, aiming to cut absenteeism.

The examination system, long the soft underbelly of Nigerian schooling, has had attention of a different sort. In April 2025, HM Alausa directed WAEC and NECO to adopt computer-based testing, with objective papers from November 2025 and essays by the May and June 2026 cycle, noting that JAMB's computer-based exams had set a security standard the other two bodies had yet to match. When NECO released its 2026 results in September, its registrar, Dantani Wushishi, reported 1,406 malpractice cases against 3,878 the year before, a fall of 64.74 per cent. Wushishi credited the vigilance of the security agencies and thanked the minister for his confidence in him. The share of candidates with five credits including English and mathematics slipped from 60.26 per cent in 2025 to 58.67 per cent. 

Some of the work crosses the line between his two ministries. Nigeria's annual nursing intake rose from 28,000 in May 2024 to 115,000 a year later, a change announced by Alausa and Pate together, and one of the clearest cases of an education decision made with a health outcome in view. In June 2026, the Times Higher Education rankings listed 24 Nigerian universities, up from 21 in the previous two years, 17 of them federal, making Nigeria the most represented country in sub-Saharan Africa. 

He has also taken the argument abroad. A memorandum between the University of Lagos and the University of Birmingham, under Nigeria's transnational education framework, will bring British teaching in science, technology, engineering, mathematics and medicine to Nigerian students. A visit to Singapore explored training leaders for technical schools, and a French-backed ICT blueprint aims to modernise tertiary education through technology. In late September 2026, he joined the global launch of Hire From Nigeria on the margins of the UN General Assembly. Around the same time, he collected the African Cultural Festival's 2026 Man of the Year award and the Key to the City of Harrisburg, where he used the platform to ask Nigerians in the diaspora to lend their expertise, research and money to the country's classrooms. 

Every administration needs a handful of ministers who can show that the slogan has a cash value. Tinubu's economic reforms have been hard on households, and the World Bank warned this week that high transport and food costs are eating into their gains. In that climate, a government needs things a family can hold in its hand: a loan that pays a child's tuition, a stipend for a trainee, a pay deal that keeps the lecturer in the lecture hall. Education has become one of the places where the Renewed Hope agenda can point to that kind of thing, and HM Alausa is the man doing the pointing.

His contribution is easiest to see in four places. 

The first is the student loan, the signature promise of the early Tinubu years. The law was signed within weeks of the president taking office, but a law is not a loan, and it fell to the ministry and the fund to turn it into more than a million disbursements. 

The second is industrial peace. Tinubu's campaign promise that a four-year course would take four years was always going to be tested by the lecturers' union, and Alausa argues it has largely been kept. The one national ASUU stoppage of the Tinubu years was the nine-day warning strike of October 2025.

The third is skills and youth employment, which is where Renewed Hope speaks most directly to the young. The vocational stipends, the Coursera academy, the venture grants and the Hire From Nigeria launch all rest on the same bet: that a generation which cannot all be absorbed by public universities and a stretched civil service has to be made employable by other means. 

The fourth is the quieter work across two ministries. HM Alausa has now worked in both health and education, and the more than fourfold rise in the nursing intake is the plainest evidence of what that overlap can do.

He is also, when asked, a campaigner. At a student panel called Renewed Hope Conversations, asked why young people should vote for Tinubu's second term, he answered with the strike record and the loan fund. With a presidential campaign under way, ministers are expected to defend the government, and Alausa does it with figures rather than slogans, which is rarer than it should be.

Nobody publishes an official league table of Nigerian ministers. A presidential delivery unit, headed by Hajia Hadiza Bala Usman, assesses them in private and submits the reports to the President. However, the Independent Newspapers Silver Jubilee Awards named HM Alausa Most Innovative Cabinet Minister of the Year for 2025 at a ceremony in Lagos on 18 April 2026. In between, he had closed the ASUU deal. Ministers who start quietly and finish strongly are rarer than those who start with a bang and fade, and Alausa fits the first description.

The case for HM Alausa as one of the best ministers, if not the best,  rests on five things. The first is that he settled something many people had written off. The lecturers' agreement had been stuck for sixteen years, and the union's own president said the final push had come from the minister. The second is breadth with speed. In under two years, he has touched basic education, admissions, examinations, universities, skills, teacher welfare, and school safety, and Pantami's defence of him, when workers called for his removal, was that the evidence of his stewardship is verifiable.

The third is that the numbers he publishes include the ones that cut against him. At the Jos bootcamp, he led with the 45 million children who cannot read a text suited to their age and the 15 million who are out of school. The NECO pass rate that dipped in 2026 is on the record with the malpractice figure that fell. A minister who volunteers the unflattering figures is at least inviting the right kind of scrutiny. The fourth is recognition. On 12 June 2025, Democracy Day, Tinubu made him a Commander of the Order of the Niger (CON), citing his contribution to democracy and national service. Add the 2025 innovation award and, in September 2026, the African Cultural Festival's Man of the Year honour and the Key to the City of Harrisburg.  

The fifth is the judgment of people who watch him up close. When Tinubu dismissed five ministers in October 2024, the government said it had used internal performance assessments, and Alausa came out of the exercise with a bigger job. Pate, who worked beside him in health, described the move as a reward for good and exceptional work.

Put together, those add up to a minister whose case depends less on any single triumph than on the density of the record. There is also something harder to measure but easy to notice from a distance, which is the manner. He came to office from a medical career rather than a political one, with a clinician's habits of diagnosis, measurement and follow-up, and he has shown he can change course when the evidence turns, as with the admission age and, in September, with the King's College concession he agreed to pause. 

Renewed Hope rests on a simple bet that hard work will be rewarded, and in HM Alausa, President Tinubu has a minister who lives by it.

Hon Victor Okebunmi
Senior Special Assistant on Publicity
Renewed Hope Global

text:
Mount Vernon, Octr 9th, 2026.

Sir,

The lines which you last night addressed to the City of New York, through that engine of instantaneous correspondence the age denominates social media, have been laid before me. I had flattered myself that a man retired under his own vine and fig tree might be spared any further part in publick disputation; but they touch so nearly the authority of the laws and the duty of a Magistrate, that I cannot forbear delivering my judgment upon them.

You begin by informing your Citizens that you are angry, and you offer the circumstance as a credential. I commanded the Army eight years and presided over the Union eight more; I was angry upon more occasions than I shall recount; and I learned in both stations that the anger of the man in command is the one intelligence which must never reach the camp. A Magistrate is set in authority that he may compose the passions of the multitude. You put yourself at their head; and before the night was out your Citizens were in collision with your own Constables, hard by the ground where the blood was shed.

Consider what you possessed when you wrote. An officer of the General Government, sent to apprehend a native of Santo Domingo whom his superiors report to be unlawfully within the Country and formerly convicted of crime, discharged at least seven balls into a carriage; the man was wounded, and lives; a child of five years sat behind him, and by the mercy of Providence was unhurt. Of what passed in the moments before the firing you had, by your own account, early reports and nothing more; the inquiry was not an evening old. Upon this foundation you pronounced sentence upon the officer, and upon the whole establishment to which he belongs, in fewer words than a prudent man expends upon a receipt. You styled the wounded man a New Yorker, and there you stopped; the conviction, and the errand of the law which brought those officers to that street, you left for others to supply.

Seven balls fired into a carriage where a child sat is a matter of the last gravity, and for that very cause it demands a tribunal. When the King’s soldiers fired upon the inhabitants in King Street, and five lay dead, the town of Boston, with every provocation to vengeance, gave them counsel and a jury; Mr. Adams, who detested the Ministry which sent them, undertook their defence, and reminded the jurors that facts are stubborn things, which neither our wishes, our inclinations, nor the dictates of our passions can alter. That was the conduct of a people fit for Liberty. If this officer fired without necessity, let him answer for it before a jury of his Countrymen; the Courts of your State are open, and its Attorneys are within your call. You preferred to set the child at the head of your sentence, and to make of his terror an argument for a measure you have professed since the first month of your Mayoralty.

I come to the measure itself. The officers appointed under the authority of Congress to execute the laws respecting aliens, whom the age calls by the initials ICE, you declare to be the danger of your City; and you require their removal, upon the instant. The same evening you applied to the President and to the Secretary to procure the prisoner’s release, and to have every enforcement of those laws suspended within your limits, in the manner of one Sovereign treating with another for the liberty of a subject. Sir, the City of New York is a corporation within a State, and that State a member of the Union; the laws of the United States are the supreme law of the land, upon the island of Manhattan as in the county of Fairfax, by the Constitution which you swore to support upon your admission as a Citizen, and swore again upon your entrance into office. No Mayor holds a negative upon them. I have met this pretension before. When four counties of Pennsylvania undertook to determine which laws of the Union should run within their borders, and which of its officers might be suffered to remain among them, they also complained of oppression, and they also were angry. I called forth the Militia of four States and marched with them as far as Bedford; for if a part of the people may dictate to the whole which laws shall be executed, there is an end put, at one stroke, to republican Government.

If those laws are unwise, or the men who execute them unfit, the remedy is known to you. Congress made the laws and may unmake them; the Courts are open; the suffrages of the people are to be taken within these four weeks. Let there be no change by usurpation. The Magistrate who teaches a City that the officers of the law are its enemies, and their expulsion its safety, dissolves the only authority by which he himself is obeyed; the multitude which learns from its Mayor to drive out the Marshal will not long respect the Constable.

When the war was ended I declared that the bosom of America was open to receive the oppressed and persecuted of all Nations and Religions, whom we should welcome to a participation of all our rights and privileges, if by decency and propriety of conduct they appeared to merit the enjoyment. You, Sir, are a proof that the invitation was honoured. The condition was annexed in the same sentence, and it has never been repealed.

You were chosen to keep the peace of a great City. In seven and thirty words you have taught it to regard the laws of the Union as an invading Army, and yourself as the General appointed to drive it out. No such commission exists, and no oath you have taken permits you to accept it. That the Almighty Being who rules over the Universe may restore the wounded man, shield the child, and teach the chief Magistrate of New York the difference between his indignation and his duty, is the prayer of,

Sir, with the respect which is due to your station,
Your most obedient and most humble servant,

We now have a state income tax. The question on your ballot is whether we keep it.

Our own senator, Claudia Kauffman, didn't just vote for it. She put her name on it as a co-sponsor, and she called it "an important step toward building a more balanced and sustainable tax system."

An important step toward what, exactly?

Then, on March 6th, Senator Kauffman voted to pull roughly $4 billion out of the pension fund for police officers and firefighters to help patch a budget Olympia couldn't balance. It passed 25 to 22. Five Democrats voted no. She wasn't one of them.

Retired first responders are now suing the state. Moody's and Fitch both cut Washington's credit outlook to negative. The State Treasurer called the pension raid one more one-time fix for a structurally unbalanced budget.

That's the pattern. A spending problem they keep solving with somebody else's money. Read the income tax bill and you'll see where the next reach goes. It rewrote eleven statutes to strip the tax exemption that had protected public pensions, disability allowances, and death benefits. Republicans offered an amendment on the House floor to put that protection back. It was voted down.

So the only thing standing between a teacher's pension or a firefighter's pension and this tax is the income threshold. The number they're already talking about lowering. All it'll take is one bill, and one simple majority.

They took the pension fund. Then they took the pension protection. Your paycheck is what's left.

I'm voting yes on I-645 to repeal the state income tax, and I'd ask you to do the same. Ballots are due November 3rd.

text:
With surrogacy illegal in China, an industry of agencies and fertility clinics is connecting Chinese clients with overseas surrogate services, reports the Financial Times. While early demand centered on couples facing infertility, consultants and doctors report growing interest from younger women physically capable of pregnancy who seek to avoid the physical and professional toll of childbirth.

Demographic and economic context highlights this shift:
- China recorded its lowest number of births on record last year, marking its fourth consecutive year of population contraction.
- The average age for a woman's first child reached 28.6 in 2024 (and 31.8 in Shanghai), up from 24.3 in 2006.
- A recent study found nearly a third of intended parents for US surrogate births were international, with approximately 40% of those coming from China.

US surrogacy packages can reach $300,000, while alternative destinations such as Georgia and Kyrgyzstan offer packages starting around $63,000. The trend is increasingly financed by parents and grandparents seeking grandchildren despite younger generations' reluctance to marry or undergo pregnancy.

Source: Financial Times

text:
@grok Just because a grand jury doesn't hand down an indictment or prosecutors don't file formal charges doesn’t mean a person had zero proximity to the underlying conduct. Any elite NHL scout worth their salt knows that a player's official "stats" or lack of a penalty box record don't tell the whole story of what's actually happening on the ice. In the intelligence and legal worlds, the "absence of a charge" isn't a magical eraser that deletes a public record.
Take the heated Michigan Senate debate between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. Rogers threw a heavy body check on the debate stage, contrasting his own mother's squeaky-clean job at a local chamber of commerce with the past employment of El-Sayed’s biological mother, Fatten Elkomy, at the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA).
Here is how a real scout evaluates the "procrastinated logic" of that defense—and the actual public record to the contrary:

1. The Legal Defense vs. Scouting Reality

The immediate defense offered by campaigns and standard fact-checkers is always: "But she was never personally charged with a crime!" Sure. And a defenseman might not get whistled for a slashing penalty, but the video room still shows he whacked the guy's wrist. In legal terms, prosecutors drop or withhold charges for plenty of reasons—lack of proving intent beyond a reasonable doubt, choosing to flip bigger targets, or a person simply acting as a passive cog in a broader machine. A lack of a criminal record does not automatically equal complete ignorance of the environment.

2. The Weight of the Plausible Public Record

If you look at the actual scouting report on the organization she worked for, the U.S. Treasury Department officially designated the IARA network back in 2004 for its alleged operational support of al-Qaeda and other terrorist entities. The charity itself was later criminally convicted in federal court for illegally funneling funds overseas.
• The Contra-Evidence: While independent fact-checks maintain there is no paper trail proving El-Sayed's mother had personal involvement in or knowledge of those illegal operations, the existence of the conviction remains an unassailable public record.
• The Proximity Factor: In hockey, if you are sharing a line with guys who are constantly turning the puck over or running dirty plays, you get associated with the systemic breakdown of that unit, even if you never personally take the penalty. That is the exact point Rogers was driving home on stage to challenge his opponent's background.

3. The Franchise Identity Connection

Just like evaluating the New Jersey Devils' history of taking unheralded or complicated prospects and completely reshaping their projection through intense, structured systems, political organizations view proximity the same way. The defense will argue she was just an uncharged employee doing standard non-profit work. The counter-scouting report from the opposition will always look past the lack of an indictment to highlight the institutional stain of the brand itself.

Not a dead, static object, but a living organism—observed in real-time at 60,000x magnification.

It is now known that every microorganism has a specific resonant frequency that can be destructive to it—a "lethal oscillation frequency." When continuously exposed to this precise frequency, the organism shatters, much like a crystal glass does when struck by the right musical note. Surrounding healthy tissue remains completely unharmed.

In 1934, the University of Southern California conducted a clinical trial. Sixteen terminal cancer patients were treated using Rife's frequency device. Within 90 days, 14 were declared completely cured; the remaining two recovered within the following four weeks.

A 100% success rate. No side effects. No surgery. No radiation. No chemotherapy.

In the 1950s, she developed a dietary regimen (the Budwig Protocol) based on the premise that industrial fats impair cellular respiration, and that mixing flaxseed oil (rich in the omega-3 fatty acid alpha-linolenic acid) with sulfur-rich proteins—such as fresh cottage cheese or quark—would restore "electrical charge" and oxygen to the cells. Nidal Malik Hasan was born in the United States on September 8, 1970, at Virginia Hospital Center in Arlington County, Virginia. His parents were naturalized American citizens of Palestinian origin who had immigrated from al-Bireh in the West Bank. He grew up in Virginia and graduated from William Fleming High School in Roanoke in 1988.

He was not a civilian attacker. He enlisted in the Army in 1988 and was commissioned in the Army Medical Department in 1997. He graduated from the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences in 2003 and was still on active duty as a major when he opened fire. 

Officers swear to support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic, and to bear true faith and allegiance to it. 

As a service member he was bound by the Uniform Code of Military Justice. 

As a physician he had also taken a medical oath at graduation, in the Hippocratic tradition, whose core duty is not to harm those in his care. 

On November 5, 2009, he broke those obligations when he opened fire on unarmed soldiers and a civilian at Fort Hood’s Soldier Readiness Processing Center.

His court-martial (not civil trial) was held at Fort Hood under the UCMJ. It began on August 6, 2013. On August 23, 2013, a panel of 13 Army officers found him guilty of all charges: 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. 

On August 28, 2013, the panel sentenced him to death, dismissal from the service, and forfeiture of all pay and allowances.

Your claim also contradicts the Texas Constitution, which only specifically authorizes the AG to represent the State before the Supreme Court.

The Texas Supreme Court in 1997 made the gap relevant for my case clear in particular:

"there is no general statute authorizing the Attorney General to represent the State and its agencies in district court" (El Paso Electric, 1997).

The majority opinion of Webster, decided Dec. 31, 2024 in Paxton's favor, drives home the point.

It reads (pp. 25-26):

Like the common-law attorney general, the Texas attorney general "is the chief law officer of the State." Agey v. Am. Lib. Pipe Line Co., 172 S.W.2d 972, 974 (Tex. 1943). He is likewise subject to the will of the sovereign—no longer the Crown but now the People. Still, his office's duties remain "multifarious, neces[s]arily involving at all times the exercise of broad judgment and discretion." Marrs, 262 S.W. at 727. A century ago, we resolved that this "judgment and discretion . . . will not be controlled by other authorities." Id. (emphasis added).

That judgment and discretion includes not only bringing and defending lawsuits but also, as we expressed in Agey, the "right to investigate the facts and [to] exercise his judgment and discretion regarding" the suits in which the State is an interested party. 172 S.W.2d at 974.

text:
SpaceX is reportedly spending 8 billion on spectrum. Why jump into cell service?👇
⠀
Private equity firm Grain Management said on October 8, 2026 that it signed a final deal to sell its nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio to SpaceX ($SPCX) .
⠀
The portfolio includes up to 14 megahertz of paired low-band spectrum.
⠀
The deal still needs approval from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and other conditions.
⠀
Financial terms weren't disclosed.
⠀
The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that SpaceX will buy Grain's spectrum assets for about $8 billion in cash.
⠀
Grain and SpaceX didn't comment on the deal price.
⠀
SpaceX didn't disclose the price or name the seller in its own update.
⠀
Reuters said the portfolio is Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum assets.
⠀
The deal covers 100% of that portfolio, and terms weren't disclosed.
⠀
-----
⠀
🔴 Follow me on X: @rich_compass
⠀
U.S. stock, crypto, and technical analysis
⠀
-----

▋ Can low band spectrum really fix indoor dead zones?
⠀
These 800 MHz airwaves are seen as a key piece of the puzzle.
⠀
SpaceX said the asset can fill the last key technical gap for Starlink Mobile to become a major U.S. mobile carrier.
⠀
Elon Musk said on X the spectrum is the "last key spectrum puzzle piece" needed for full coverage.
⠀
In another post, he described it as something that looks small to most people, but "to those who understand the spectrum wars, this is an earthquake."
⠀
On the technical side, the official announcement describes a hybrid network.
⠀
2 GHz mid-band spectrum provides high-bandwidth capacity, while the newly acquired low-band spectrum acts as a coverage layer.
⠀
There's the compatibility point: most existing phones already support that 800 MHz band.
⠀
SpaceX also stressed the band has been underused for a long time.
⠀
But The Wall Street Journal noted those U.S. 800 MHz licenses were originally designed for wireless service from cell towers, not satellites.
⠀
SpaceX's answer is to combine its growing satellite constellation with "advanced ground deployment" after FCC approval.
⠀
The new spectrum would cover the inside of buildings that satellite links can't reach.
⠀
The company says with the low-band licenses and Gen2 constellation, Starlink Mobile will be the first carrier ever to deploy satellite and ground spectrum as a single network.

▋ Why did the 5G mobile goal slip to 2028?
⠀
The FCC approved SpaceX's request to launch up to 15,000 satellites dedicated to mobile service on October 7, 2026, the same week before the deal was announced.
⠀
The license lasts 15 years from when the first new direct-to-device (D2D) satellite enters its authorized orbit.
⠀
The orbits are spread across nine shells at altitudes between 326 and 335 kilometers.
⠀
SpaceX must launch and deploy 50% of the maximum satellite count by October 7, 2032.
⠀
It must deploy the rest and start operations by October 7, 2035.
⠀
For speed, V2-generation Starlink Mobile D2D satellites are targeting user speeds up to 150 Mbit/s.
⠀
That's far above the 4 Mbit/s currently offered by more than 650 D2D satellites.
⠀
But the commercial timeline has slipped.
⠀
Light Reading reported on September 14, 2026 that SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said the company aims to launch "5G-quality" satellite mobile service for phones in the first half of 2028.
⠀
That's later than the end of 2027 mentioned on its early-August earnings call.
⠀
It plans to deploy a new direct-to-device low-Earth-orbit constellation over the next year using Starship.
⠀
The same report said Johnsen noted SpaceX can launch Starlink mobile service in the U.S. using mid-band spectrum acquired from EchoStar ($SATS).
⠀
That spectrum has FCC approval for direct-to-space and ground use.
⠀
The company is open on its ground network approach, including working with existing carriers.
⠀
Regulators are moving too.
⠀
The FCC is set to hold an open meeting on October 29, 2026 to vote on modernizing supplemental coverage (SCS) rules.
⠀
It may free up another 482 MHz of spectrum for leasing.
⠀
It will also vote on a proposal to auction 25 MHz of mid-band spectrum for D2D and ground use, or a mix of both.

▋ How much cash will building cell towers burn?
⠀
The Wall Street Journal reported that SpaceX last year bought EchoStar's satellite spectrum rights in a cash-and-stock deal worth about $17 billion.
⠀
That lets it send data from space to phones on its own frequencies instead of bands licensed by partner T-Mobile ($TMUS).
⠀
EchoStar later agreed to sell some ground mobile licenses to SpaceX for $2.6 billion.
⠀
But spectrum alone still isn't enough to launch a full phone network.
⠀
The report also said that about two months earlier, SpaceX executives floated the idea of using small cells instead of traditional cell towers to support a mobile network.
⠀
Analysts said building a traditional tower system for basic coverage could cost billions of dollars.
⠀
Back to where it came from: Grain also bought this 800 MHz spectrum.
⠀
Grain got it from T-Mobile earlier this year, according to reports.
⠀
Its press release says it acquired the nationwide portfolio from T-Mobile in August 2026.
⠀
The consideration was cash and an exchange of Grain's 600 MHz spectrum.
⠀
Via Satellite added that the acquisition was announced in early 2025 and closed in August 2026.
⠀
It involved $2.9 billion in cash and additional spectrum licenses.
⠀
The resale to SpaceX advances the competitive choice process and D2D deployment path the FCC set when it approved the earlier deal in July 2026.
⠀
Low-band spectrum's advantage in radio physics is broad coverage and strong penetration.
⠀
That makes it suited for private networks at critical infrastructure like power utilities, business communications, and next-generation direct-to-satellite service.
⠀
Grain founder and CEO David Grain said the deal lets its spectrum assets work at a very large scale.
⠀
It could reshape how and where Americans connect.
⠀
The partnership aims to use scarce low-band spectrum so Starlink Mobile can reach users from both the ground and space.
⠀
Via Satellite added that this direct-to-device constellation and the current Starlink broadband constellation are architecturally separate systems.
⠀
On funding, SEC filings show SpaceX issued five series of senior unsecured notes totaling $25 billion on June 26, 2026.
⠀
Coupons range from 5.350% on notes due 2031 to 6.650% on notes due 2056.
⠀
The filings didn't link the offering to this spectrum acquisition.

▋ Can satellites really beat the laws of physics?
⠀
As Starlink pushes in, top executives at the three big U.S. carriers publicly poured cold water on it in September 2026.
⠀
Light Reading reported that T-Mobile CFO Peter Osvaldik said "the laws of physics don't allow direct-to-device (D2D) to be a replacement product."
⠀
Verizon ($VZ) CEO Dan Schulman also said Starlink is "not really a direct competitor" in its core urban and suburban markets.
⠀
AT&T ($T) Chairman and CEO John Stankey pushed back on network architecture.
⠀
He argued that randomly deployed tiny cells can't solve mobile coverage problems.
⠀
He stressed AT&T covers about 98% of the U.S., and satellite direct-to-device can at best fill edge dead spots.
⠀
Independent analysts also warned about cost.
⠀
William Webb's analysis in Light Reading says roof-mounted antennas cover only about 1 to 2 kilometers.
⠀
Below rooftops, that drops under 1 kilometer.
⠀
Coverage would also be scattered across rural areas where existing broadband subscribers are dense.
⠀
On top of that, the cost to modify devices is a major obstacle.
⠀
Webb estimated that if phones need complex antennas to support high-capacity 4G and 5G service, the cost per subscriber device could rise by $1,000 to $3,000.
⠀
That's Webb's estimate.
⠀
Peter Claydon, CEO of small cell maker RANsemi, estimated the added cost at no more than $200.
⠀
By user numbers, Starlink had about 12 million customers worldwide at the time.
⠀
It added about 6 million in the past year.
⠀
In May of that year, it was estimated to have 3 million to 4 million U.S. subscribers, mostly in rural areas.
⠀
That's why Recon Analytics founder Roger Entner told The Wall Street Journal that to turn new spectrum into mass mobile signals, SpaceX ultimately can't avoid physical ground investment like cell towers or roof equipment.

▋ Can Elon Musk negotiate past the carrier alliance?
⠀
The Wall Street Journal called this spectrum bet SpaceX's biggest step yet beyond broadband and straight into a wireless market led by traditional phone companies.
⠀
The spectrum can serve SpaceX's stated goal of moving Starlink from broadband into wireless to compete with AT&T and Verizon and others.
⠀
On investment size, Entner thinks Musk doesn't need to copy a traditional telecom network.
⠀
Spending $10 billion to $20 billion on a ground reinforcement layer would be financially feasible.
⠀
But he expects the real commercial battle to land in 2030 to 2032.
⠀
It depends on standards work and progress on higher-capacity satellites.
⠀
He has said, "We're talking about 2030, not next year."
⠀
After this deal was announced, Entner said, "Next is Ligado."
⠀
That prediction ties to the situation at AST SpaceMobile ($ASTS).
⠀
AST SpaceMobile currently has a definitive agreement with Ligado for long-term use of up to 45 MHz of lower mid-band spectrum in the U.S. and Canada for satellite direct-to-device service.
⠀
The agreement includes a $550 million payment conditioned on closing.
⠀
It also includes at least $80 million a year in L-band spectrum usage fees.
⠀
Before SpaceX got the Grain spectrum, AST SpaceMobile had expressed interest in Grain's spectrum.
⠀
The FCC order approving Grain's purchase of that spectrum from T-Mobile in July 2026 cited a June 30 AST filing.
⠀
Satellite communications and spectrum consultant Tim Farrar said on X that eyes will next turn to Viasat ($VSAT).
⠀
He called it "the last holder with a large block of global spectrum."
⠀
The traditional telecom camp also quickly built a defense alliance.
⠀
AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon recently formally launched a satellite joint venture led by interim CEO Paul Roth.
⠀
Their existing agreements stay the same: T-Mobile uses Starlink, while AT&T and Verizon have commercial deals with AST SpaceMobile.
⠀
Entner said the joint venture is essentially "trying to stop Musk's satellite standard from becoming the only standard," like the EV charging plug fight years ago.
⠀
Carriers want an open standard, not a Musk standard.
⠀
The leadership pick shows its top priority is "regulatory navigation, not just technical coordination."
⠀
New Street Research analyst David Barden also thinks the joint venture "strengthens the collective bargaining position of wireless carriers and could weaken the negotiating position of future satellite operator partners, if the group holds together."
⠀
Facing a united defense, MoffettNathanson analyst Craig Moffett described SpaceX as "negotiating, persuading and, when needed, coercing" to land an MVNO deal with one of the three big carriers.
⠀
An MVNO is a carrier that leases another carrier's network and sells service under its own brand.
⠀
So far, AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon say they don't plan to sign that kind of deal with SpaceX.
⠀
T-Mobile CEO Srini Gopalan noted D2D use makes up just 0.0002% of the carrier's total network usage.
⠀
Reports later said T-Mobile removed Starlink references from its T-Satellite website.
⠀
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment on AST SpaceMobile went from bullish the day before to neutral.
⠀
Message volume over 24 hours rose 121%.
⠀
Users were split.
⠀
Some said the deal is a major blow to AST.
⠀
Others said the competitive threat will push carriers to deepen their work with AST.
⠀
SpaceX now has a deal to buy 800 MHz low-band spectrum, a license for 15,000 D2D satellites, and a goal to launch 5G-quality service in the first half of 2028.
⠀
Whether those licenses become signals on phones still depends on FCC approval and building out the ground half.

text:
Um, who is James talking to?None of this says you are saved by works🤦‍♂️🤦‍♂️🤦‍♂️😂😂😂omg how pathetic! 

James is writing to scattered believers under trial (1:1–2), and his burden from the start is hearing that does not become doing. The “perfect law of liberty” is a mirror: the one who looks and walks away is not blessed; the doer is (1:22–25). Partiality in the assembly is then named as a violation of “the royal law” and as a failure to live the mercy one claims to have received (2:1–13). Judgment will be without mercy for the one who showed none (2:13). Chapter 2:14 picks up that same thread. The question is not how a sinner is declared righteous before God. It is what to do with a person who says he has faith and has nothing to show for it.

The argument, verse by verse

James opens with two questions that expect the answer no: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?” (2:14). The faith in view is the faith that person claims (“if someone says”), not faith as Paul defines it. A brother or sister without food or clothing, answered only with “go in peace, be warmed and filled,” shows the problem (2:15–16). Speech that does not act is empty. So “faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead” (2:17).

He then grants the objector’s split: “You have faith and I have works” (2:18). His reply is that faith, if it is real, is shown by works. Bare assent is not enough. “Even the demons believe — and shudder” (2:19). They affirm that God is one, the Shema itself, and it does them no saving good. Orthodox content without trust and obedience is the faith of demons. “Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?” (2:20). “Useless” and “dead” describe a faith that cannot produce what it claims, not a living faith that God then supplements with merit.

Abraham is the test case (2:21–23). He “was justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar.” That event is Genesis 22, decades after Genesis 15:6, where Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness. James says the offering “completed” his faith, and then quotes Genesis 15:6: the Scripture “was fulfilled.” The offering did not create the reckoning. It brought to visible completion the faith already reckoned. “You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works” (2:22). The works are the working of the faith, not a second instrument beside it. Rahab is the same pattern from the other end of Israel’s story: her sheltering the spies showed that her confession was not talk (2:25).

The summary is 2:24: “You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.” In this paragraph, “justified” means shown to be righteous, vindicated as the real thing, the sense the word often has when the question is evidence before observers (compare Matthew 11:19, “wisdom is justified by her deeds,” and Luke 7:35). “Faith alone” here is the faith James has already defined as bare claim, demon-faith, a corpse. Verse 26 closes the image: “as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.” Works are to faith what breath is to a body. They do not replace the body. A body with no breath was never alive.
What he is not saying

He is not saying works earn the verdict. James has already called his readers to receive “the implanted word, which is able to save your souls” (1:21), and he treats mercy, not wage, as what triumphs over judgment (2:13). He never says Abraham was justified by works instead of by believing the promise. He says the later act fulfilled the earlier reckoning.
He is also not setting a quota. The works in the passage are the ordinary fruit of the implanted word: care for the naked and hungry, refusal of partiality, obedience when God speaks. “Dead” is aimed at the profession that never moves, not at the weak believer whose fruit is small.

This tweet’s framing treats Jews as outsiders who took land from a continuous local population. The premise is wrong because it treats Jews as outsiders who seized a land that had belonged, exclusively and continuously, to one local people for centuries. The actual record is a long Jewish tie to the country, centuries of foreign imperial rule, legal immigration and land purchase, a UN partition both sides were offered, and a war that followed Arab rejection of that partition.

The post is this reply to a claim that Jews earned a homeland in Israel:

> what did they do to "earn a homeland that is Israel" at the expense of ppl already living on and using the land for centuries?

That framing smuggles in three claims: that the pre-1948 population was a single indigenous nation with exclusive title; that Jews had no prior standing there; and that Israel was created by simply taking land those people had used for centuries. None of those holds.

Jews are indigenous to that territory in the ordinary historical sense. Israelite and later Jewish polities were based there from the late second millennium BCE. The kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the Second Temple period, and the revolts against Rome (the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE and the Bar Kokhba revolt in 132–135 CE) are not mythology. After the Roman wars most Jews lived in the diaspora, but communities remained in Jerusalem, the Galilee, Hebron, Safed, and Tiberias through Byzantine, early Islamic, Crusader, Mamluk, and Ottoman rule. The population was often small and poor, and it fluctuated with massacres, earthquakes, and taxation, but it did not disappear. By the late 19th century Jerusalem itself had a Jewish majority in contemporary counts.

Arab and Muslim presence is also real, and much later. The Arab conquest of the region was in the 630s CE, more than a thousand years after the Israelite kingdoms and centuries after the Roman-Jewish wars. Arabic and Islam spread gradually under successive empires (Umayyad, Abbasid, Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk). From 1517 to 1917 the country was an Ottoman province, not a sovereign Arab state. Local Arabs, Christians, Druze, and Jews were subjects of Istanbul. There was no Palestinian nation-state whose territory was taken intact in 1948.

Modern settlement was not a sudden conquest of occupied villages. From the 1880s, Jewish immigrants arrived legally under Ottoman and then British rule, largely as refugees from pogroms and later from Nazi Europe. They bought land, often from large absentee landowners, and founded agricultural colonies. The League of Nations Mandate for Palestine, incorporating the 1917 Balfour Declaration, explicitly recognized a Jewish national home while requiring that the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities not be prejudiced. By 1947 the population was roughly one-third Jewish and two-thirds Arab. Private Jewish land ownership was a minority of the total area; much of the country was state land, waste, or Arab-owned. Partition was a proposal about sovereignty, not a deed transferring every private plot.

In November 1947 the UN General Assembly recommended two states, one Jewish and one Arab, with an international regime for Jerusalem. The Jewish Agency accepted. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab League rejected any Jewish state and said they would prevent it by force. Fighting began in the civil-war phase after the vote. When Britain left and Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq invaded. The war ended with Israel holding more than the partition map, Jordan holding the West Bank (which it annexed), and Egypt holding Gaza. Several hundred thousand Arabs became refugees; in the same period roughly 800,000 Jews fled or were expelled from Arab countries. No Arab Palestinian state was established, because the Arab side had rejected the plan that would have created one and then lost the war that followed.

People had been living on and farming parts of the land for centuries. That is true of Arab fellahin, and it is also true of Jewish communities in the four holy cities. It does not create an exclusive title that cancels an older national connection, League of Nations recognition, or a UN decision the other side refused. “At the expense of” describes the outcome of a war both populations experienced as dispossession, not a one-sided theft of a country that had been someone else’s sovereign homeland for centuries.

text:
The first National Medal of Science ever awarded went to a rocket scientist.

Kennedy handed it to Theodore von Kármán in February 1963. An 81-year-old Hungarian engineer who co-founded JPL, founded Aerojet, and wrote the math that lets anything fly faster than sound. Congress had created the award four years earlier as the highest honor America gives a scientist or engineer. Von Kármán was pick number one.

He was so frail at the ceremony that Kennedy offered him an arm on the steps. Von Kármán waved him off. "Mr. President, one does not need help going down, only going up."

He died three months later.

Since then the medal has gone to more than 500 people, and the list reads like a faculty directory. Nobel laureates, department chairs, lab directors. The selection committee is 12 scientists appointed by the President, and for six decades they have favored people who publish over people who build.

Von Kármán was the other kind. He never won a Nobel. He built wind tunnels, trained the engineers who staffed early NASA, and turned rocketry from a crank obsession into an American industry. The medal was invented for exactly that kind of person, then spent 60 years mostly going to professors.

Today it went back to a rocket guy. SpaceX put more mass into orbit last year than every other country and company on Earth combined, and did it with boosters that fly back and land on their own tails.

The first medal went to the man who taught American rockets to fly. This one went to the man who taught them to land.

text:
The experience itself wasn’t particularly exciting. The kissing was wet, messy, and rushed. The sex was much the same.

No, the exciting part came afterward.

I wasn’t in love with Morgan. I wasn’t even particularly attracted to him. I was fourteen, bored, and desperate for something to happen. Nothing happened in our town during the summer. At least during the school year, there were football games, clubs, and the occasional party. In summer, the older kids with driver’s licenses went to the shore, where they spent their days drinking beer in the sun.

Morgan had a license, but he also worked four days a week bagging groceries at the local Foodtown. That left him less time for sunbathing and more time to pursue underage girls in the supermarket parking lot.

The person I really liked that summer, in 1992, just before my sophomore year, was Stacy. She was sixteen, about to become a senior, with long, curly auburn hair and big brown eyes. Stacy was the reason I ended up in that parking lot. She was the reason I wore my shortest shorts and the bright blue bikini top I practically lived in that July.

She was also the reason my sophomore year went the way it did. When you’re fourteen and hopelessly in love, being taken advantage of can send you spiraling in ways you don’t yet understand.

Not Morgan. I barely remember him.

But I’ll remember my first kiss with Stacy forever.

Morgan drove an old Toyota Camry he’d inherited from a relative. He kept two fuzzy, checkered blankets folded in the back seat. At fourteen, I didn’t think twice about that. It wasn’t until years later that I wondered what kind of boy kept two blankets ready in his car.

He kissed me, and I played along. It wasn’t my first kiss, but it was the first time I’d done anything like this with a boy. He slipped his hand beneath my bikini top, and I let him. When he started unbuttoning my jean shorts, he paused and raised his eyebrows, asking the question without quite saying it.

By then, I’d gone along with so many things that I couldn’t imagine how to stop. I wasn’t sure I wanted to, but I wasn’t sure I wanted any of it, either. I was fourteen, bored out of my mind, and sitting in the back seat of a boy’s car in a small New Jersey town. Morgan was something new, and that seemed reason enough.

A few minutes after it was over, Stacy appeared, her long, tanned legs carrying her across the Foodtown parking lot like a supermodel on a runway. She marched straight to the Camry and opened the door.

“Morgan, seriously? She’s barely a sophomore!”

Then she turned her dark brown eyes toward me.

“Gia? You’re Gia, right?”

I nodded.

“Are you okay? Did he hurt you?”

I thought about it for a moment.

“No, not really.”

Stacy watched as I awkwardly retied my bikini top. Her expression was impossible to read. Once I was dressed, she held out her hand.

“Come on, Gia.”

Morgan was folding the blankets, but at least he looked up long enough to say goodbye. He didn’t offer to call me or ask to see me again. That wasn’t part of the arrangement. He smiled and said, “See you around.”

Stacy and I walked down Main Street.

“He’s kind of a douche,” she said. “But I get it. Older guy, car, all that.”

text:
‼️🇮🇷🇾🇪Iran and the Houthis have intensified attacks in the Middle East – 

The October strikes are not a random flare. They sit inside an eight-month war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran, a naval blockade of Iranian oil, and a Saudi-backed front in Yemen. Tehran and Ansar Allah are answering that pressure on the same map where the pressure was applied.

🇮🇷 THE GULF IS NO LONGER A ONE-WAY CORRIDOR

Late Wednesday the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker Acers was hit by several projectiles about 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, off Qatar. UK Maritime Trade Operations and the maritime firm Vanguard reported casualties. No state has formally claimed the strike. Regional officials told the Wall Street Journal that Iran was the likely source, and outlets linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps framed the hit as an extension of rules against ships using routes Tehran does not accept.

That location matters more than the hull. Qatar sits deep inside the Gulf, hundreds of kilometres west of Hormuz. For months Washington has tried to keep crude moving through escorted or northern corridors while Iranian ports stay closed. A projectile strike that far from the strait tells shipowners the workaround is not a sanctuary. Brent rose about 5 percent, through $105 a barrel, because traders priced a wider threat to loadings, not a single damaged ship.

🇮🇷 HORMUZ IS BEING TREATED AS IRANIAN SEA, NOT A NEUTRAL CANAL

In the week to 5 October, security firms logged at least a dozen attacks on oil, LNG and LPG tankers around the strait, the highest weekly count since the war began. Kpler counted ten tankers struck inside the strait between 28 September and 4 October. On Tuesday an attack on a Panama-flagged tanker injured twelve crew, according to India’s foreign ministry. Iranian state-linked media have said forces struck ships on routes not cleared by Tehran, and Tehran has said the bypass corridor will be closed.

The legal argument from the Iranian side is straightforward. A blockade that stops Iranian exports while foreign tankers haul Gulf crude past Iranian shores is not freedom of navigation. It is selective interdiction. Washington sank Iranian tankers in September and called them an IRGC revenue network. Tehran’s answer has been to raise the cost of every unsanctioned transit until the blockade itself becomes the problem Washington has to solve. Transits have already thinned. Reuters recorded only seven crossings on one day this week and ten the next, the lowest levels in more than two months.

🇾🇪 THE CAPITAL IS NOW INSIDE THE YEMEN WAR

Ansar Allah spent a third day hitting the Saudi capital. Spokesman Yehya Saree said a ballistic missile struck King Khalid International Airport. Witnesses reported explosions. A Saudia aircraft parked at a terminal caught fire. Cirium data showed nearly half of Riyadh departures cancelled by mid-afternoon Thursday, with Lufthansa and Air India suspending services. Earlier in the week Saudi civil aviation said three people were killed and dozens wounded at King Khalid and Abha, including a Sudanese national in Riyadh and Egyptian and Algerian nationals at Abha. Debris from an interception also hit a kindergarten and a medical complex, Saudi officials said.

Saree warned airlines out of Saudi airspace except over Mecca and Medina, and told workers at oil plants to stay clear. The group has claimed Aramco sites as targets. That is the second front of the same war. Riyadh has bombed Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf and Marib — more than eighty sites in one coalition statement — and backs the recognised government against Ansar Allah on the Taiz front. Airport missiles are the reply to that intervention, carried into the kingdom that has treated Yemen as a buffer rather than a neighbour.

🇮🇷 THE ELECTION CALENDAR IS NOW PART OF THE BATTLEFIELD

Trump wrote on Thursday that talks with the Islamic Republic are productive and that the United States will not attack Iran before the 3 November congressional elections. The blockade stays. Aides have pushed to keep the war quiet until the vote, then reconsider heavier strikes. Tehran offered a seven-day sequence in late September: end hostilities, lift the blockade, waive oil sanctions, release frozen funds, reopen Hormuz, then nuclear talks. Washington rejected it.

Both capitals are watching the same date. Iran’s president said he did not want the crisis to reach the midterms. Trump has said the war could be settled just after the vote, or maybe before, while also leaving post-election bombing open. The strikes this week exploit that gap. Higher oil, a smoking aircraft in Riyadh, and a tanker hit off Qatar raise the domestic cost of waiting without requiring Tehran to accept a settlement that leaves the ports closed.

🇮🇷 WHAT THE PAIR OF ATTACKS ACTUALLY BUYS

Iran does not need to sink the Gulf’s export system. It needs to show that a blockade plus an open Hormuz is unstable. Ansar Allah does not need to occupy Riyadh. It needs Saudi airspace and Saudi energy to look indefensible for as long as the kingdom bombs Yemen. Together they compress the window in which Washington can claim the war is contained.

 The casualty reports — crew on Acers, civilians at Saudi airports — are the price of that compression, and they will be used in every capital that still treats the February strikes and the port closure as the status quo rather than the cause.

EX POST!™ | OCTOBER 9, 2026 AFTERNOON EDITION
POLITICAL ANALYSIS

ABDUL EL-SAYED PUT MIKE ROGERS’S 14-YEAR WASHINGTON RECORD ON TRIAL

Rogers offers experience. El-Sayed’s challenge is accountability—including a national debt that grew by more than $12 trillion during Rogers’s congressional tenure.
Mike Rogers’s strongest credential comes with an unavoidable question: What did that experience deliver?
In Thursday’s combative Michigan Senate debate, Abdul El-Sayed challenged the Republican’s record and shifting positions, turning the contest into an argument about whether Washington experience deserves another term—or closer scrutiny. The exchanges repeatedly became personal, with both candidates interrupting and attacking each other.
Our assessment: El-Sayed’s strongest approach was to make Rogers defend his past before selling voters his future.
THE RECORD BEHIND THE RÉSUMÉ
Rogers served seven terms in the House, from January 3, 2001, through January 3, 2015. Fourteen years is substantial experience—and substantial material for voters to examine.
At the start of that tenure, gross federal debt stood at approximately $5.7 trillion. By January 2, 2015, the last business day before he left office, it was approximately $18.1 trillion. The increase: roughly $12.4 trillion.
Precision matters. That does not mean Rogers personally created $12.4 trillion in debt. The increase spanned multiple administrations, congressional majorities and a major financial crisis. Assigning individual responsibility requires examining individual votes.
But a politician offering Washington experience as evidence of fiscal competence can reasonably be asked to explain his role during those years. Longevity alone does not establish good judgment.
THE POSITIONS THAT CHANGED
Rogers’s recent shifts give that question immediate relevance.
He largely supported Trump’s Canadian tariffs before calling this week for the trade fight to end immediately. Reuters also reported that he recently called for an immediate end to the Iran war after previously supporting it. Michigan’s dependence on cross-border automotive supply chains makes the tariff question especially consequential.
Changing a position can reflect better judgment. Voters are entitled to ask what changed—and why the correction arrived so close to an election.
El-Sayed’s argument gains force when it connects those reversals to costs families already face. A promise to lower prices invites scrutiny of the policies a candidate previously backed.
HEALTHCARE DESERVED MORE THAN PERSONAL ATTACKS
The candidates offered sharply different healthcare visions: El-Sayed supported Medicare for All; Rogers opposed it and argued that it would impose substantial new taxes. Those competing claims deserve serious examination.
Instead, Rogers repeatedly challenged whether El-Sayed was really a doctor. Bridge Michigan’s fact check supplied the necessary distinction: El-Sayed earned a medical degree from Columbia University, but does not hold a license to practice medicine. His career has focused on public health.
A medical degree and a medical license are different credentials. Voters deserve that distinction accurately explained—and a substantive argument about how either candidate would improve their care.
THE EX POST!™ ASSESSMENT
El-Sayed’s most effective argument was the demand that Rogers account for the record behind his promises.
That is our analysis, not a measured verdict from a post-debate voter survey. A forceful performance does not establish that a candidate persuaded undecided voters or changed the race.
But the political vulnerability is clear: Rogers cannot offer fourteen years in Congress as a qualification and expect those same fourteen years to escape examination.
Experience earns a hearing. The record determines whether it earns another vote. ❦

text:
MULTIPOLARITY AND THE CONTEST OVER THE RULES OF GLOBAL POWER

The international order is undergoing a transformation that cannot be explained simply as the replacement of U.S. hegemony by a new power.

China’s rise, the actions of regional powers, and the growing importance of technological and financial chains point toward a redistribution of power. However, redistribution does not equate to equilibrium.

In *War and Change in World Politics*, Robert Gilpin examines how shifts in the distribution of capabilities among states can generate tensions with the existing international order. The central issue is not merely the rise of new actors, but the widening gap between actual power and established rules.

This perspective helps make sense of a contemporary contradiction: economically interdependent countries can simultaneously deepen their strategic rivalry.

The United States retains significant instruments of financial, military, and technological influence. China, for its part, vies for position within production chains, infrastructure, and the development of strategic technologies.

None of these developments occurs in isolation.

Competition over semiconductors, energy resources, trade routes, and payment systems demonstrates that international power is not concentrated in a single dimension.

John J. Mearsheimer, in *The Tragedy of Great Power Politics*, offers another perspective: in an international system lacking a higher authority capable of guaranteeing everyone's security, great powers tend to vie for strategic positions and view each other's intentions with suspicion.

While this approach does not fully explain the complexities of the present, it helps clarify why economic interdependence does not eliminate military and political competition.

There is also a frequently underestimated factor: the position of middle powers.

India, Brazil, and other regional actors need not automatically mirror every strategic choice made by Washington or Beijing. However, their scope for action depends on the economic, diplomatic, and technological capabilities they are able to mobilize.

Multipolarity can expand opportunities for negotiation. It can also multiply pressures and dependencies.

Therefore, the number of power centers does not, in itself, determine the quality of the international order.

**The decisive question is not merely who will hold the most power, but who will succeed in establishing the financial, technological, commercial, and strategic rules that others will have to take into account.**

Twenty-first-century geopolitics will be defined as much by the capacity to exercise power as by the capacity to shape the conditions under which that power is exercised.

References

Robert Gilpin, *War and Change in World Politics*. Cambridge University Press, 1981.

John J. Mearsheimer, *The Tragedy of Great Power Politics*. W. W. Norton, 2001.

Susan Strange, *States and Markets*. Pinter Publishers, 1988.

text:
Samsung Posts Record ~$80 Bn Quarterly Profit — First Tech Company to Top 100 Trillion Won — as AI Chip Boom Drives Nine-Fold Jump; PepsiCo Cuts Profit Forecast

Core Theme 
Samsung’s record-shattering quarter shows how the AI chip boom has turned memory into the most lucrative corner of global technology, with a supply shortage expected to last into 2028 keeping prices and profits elevated, yet its flat share reaction, a stock well off its June peak, a strengthening won, and worries over AI-spending durability reveal a market already questioning how long the surge can last; PepsiCo’s forecast cut offers a counterpoint, showing consumer-facing companies struggling with weak demand and cost inflation while AI-linked hardware makers ride the cycle.

Samsung’s Record Quarter
Projected Q3 (July–September) operating profit: 107.4 trillion won (~$80.17 bn)

First time any technology company has topped 100 trillion won in a quarter

A nearly nine-fold jump in Q3 earnings versus a year earlier

Slightly ahead of the LSEG SmartEstimate of 106.1 trillion won

Fourth straight quarter of record operating profit

Driver: booming demand for AI chips, with strong memory sales

The Memory Chip Shortage
Global memory shortage is deepening as AI infrastructure investment outpaces supply

Shortage has driven chip prices up sharply

Samsung and Micron expect the imbalance to persist into 2028

Risks to longer-term outlook: Chinese competition and a potential slowdown in AI spending

Higher chip costs are squeezing smartphone margins

Market Reaction and Headwinds
Samsung shares moved sideways: down 0.2% in early trade vs a 0.5% fall in the benchmark KOSPI

Shares have slumped more than 25% from the June record high amid concerns over the durability of the AI boom

Analysts have trimmed forecasts due to the sharp appreciation of the South Korean won, which reduces the value of dollar-denominated overseas sales when converted to local currency

PepsiCo Cuts Profit Forecast
Cut its annual core profit forecast and pledged more cost cuts

Warned that efforts to revive growth in its North American business are taking longer than expected

Highlights a broader challenge in packaged food, where firms are spending more on promotions to revive demand

CEO Ramon Laguarta: additional structural cost reduction actions are being identified and will be implemented soon to fund investments in organic revenue growth and offset rising input cost inflation

text:
India is beyond repair when it comes to this mindset. We have no globally dominant social media platform of our own - not Instagram, YouTube, Facebook or X. We have no homegrown AI ecosystem competing at the global frontier, and no Indian smartphone brand dominating the global market. We depend on Western technology for so much of our digital lives, yet we lecture the West that we don't need them and can build everything ourselves.

Look at the Starlink controversy. Obviously, if your only use of the internet is scrolling Instagram, watching YouTube and posting on X, cheap mobile data might be enough for you. But not everyone uses the internet that way. Developers, IT companies, remote workers, researchers and businesses need reliable, high-speed internet. People working in technology need access to the internet wherever they are in the country, including places where traditional broadband infrastructure is unreliable or unavailable.

Jio and Airtel may offer affordable internet, but their broadband services aren't always reliable everywhere. Frequent maintenance, scheduled downtime and connectivity issues are realities for many customers. So why should people who need better connectivity - and are willing to pay for it - not have access to alternatives like Starlink?

Somehow, an entire ecosystem has developed where every new technology is viewed with suspicion. If it isn't a cultural threat, it's a security threat. Every opportunity for progress comes with another conspiracy theory or a ghost story about why we shouldn't use it.

And the argument that Indian data is cheaper misses the point entirely. Yes, we have affordable mobile data. But affordability doesn't automatically mean reliability, coverage, speed or suitability for every professional need. Not everyone has the same requirements, and not everyone is poor. Some people and businesses are perfectly willing to pay for a service that genuinely meets their needs.

Look at the AI industry. Developers and IT companies across India, from small businesses to large firms, use tools like Cursor also owned by @SpaceX  @elonmusk  to improve their productivity. These tools rely on sophisticated technology and infrastructure built by companies operating in the global tech ecosystem. Many of these services are paid products. We understand that paying for better tools is part of doing business, so why does that logic suddenly disappear when it comes to satellite internet?

What's even more ironic is that some of the loudest voices against foreign technology happily buy iPhones on EMIs, save up for expensive Western luxury bags and clothes, and proudly show them off. If you're so committed to buying Indian, then apply that principle consistently. Support Indian companies, invest in Indian innovation and demand better products from Indian businesses. But don't selectively reject foreign technology only when it becomes politically convenient.

The real question is: what exactly have we built that allows us to make these claims with such confidence?
