text:
STATE HOUSE PRESS RELEASE 

FG, States Push Nutrition 774 To Grassroots, Draw Lessons From Ethiopia 

** Governors, ministers back stronger local action on child nutrition 

** Pate says Nigeria, Ethiopia to develop roadmap for accelerated gains

The Federal Government @NigeriaGov and states have pledged to deepen collaboration at the grassroots as Nigeria moves to translate its nutrition policies into measurable improvements in communities and households. 

The renewed push is aimed at strengthening nutrition delivery through coordinated action across health, education, agriculture, water, sanitation and social protection, with states and local governments expected to play a central role in implementation. 

Speaking on the sidelines of the Nigeria–Ethiopia Nutrition Leadership Exchange in Addis Ababa, where the Nigerian delegation is led by Vice President Kashim Shettima, governors and federal ministers said Ethiopia’s experience offers useful lessons for Nigeria’s efforts to tackle malnutrition and child stunting through stronger national and subnational coordination. 

Governor Ademola Adeleke of Osun State @AAdeleke_01;  said interventions must pay particular attention to children under five and pregnant women, noting that while Nigeria has recorded some progress, there is room for improvement. 

“Especially for the young ones under five and, of course, pregnant women, it is very, very important. 

“We have some success, but we can improve on it. That is why I am here, to learn from our counterparts in Ethiopia,” Governor Adeleke said. 

His Abia State counterpart, Dr. Alex Otti @alexottiofr, said Nigeria must be willing to learn from countries that have achieved progress rather than attempt to reinvent the wheel. 

“There’s nothing wrong with saying that we have not done as well. And there’s also nothing wrong in learning from those who have done it, so that you don’t go reinventing the wheel,” Governor Otti said. 

He stressed that nutrition goes beyond food security, saying progress requires coordinated interventions in healthcare, education, agriculture, climate action and poverty reduction. 

“Today, we have learned that it’s not just about food security. It’s also about health. It’s about education. It’s about climate change. It’s about agriculture. So, a whole lot of things are intertwined,” he said. 

Governor Otti said Abia State had recruited 9,469 teachers, was developing 20 smart schools and rehabilitating more than 200 primary and secondary schools, while committing about 20 per cent of its annual budget to education. 

For Zamfara State Governor Dauda Lawal @daudalawal_, insecurity has worsened nutrition challenges in a state traditionally known for substantial food production. 

“In the past, when you spoke about nutrition, we didn’t even have anything like that in the state because we produced enough to feed our people. However, because of those challenges now, it has become difficult,” he said. 

Governor Lawal, however, said insecurity must not define the state, stressing the need to align with Federal Government programmes while adapting interventions to local circumstances. 

“Should we be defined by the insecurity? The question is no. What else can we do?” he asked. 

Jigawa State Governor Umar Namadi @uanamadi said Ethiopia’s experience under the Seqota Declaration offers useful lessons for Nigeria’s Nutrition 774 Initiative, particularly in taking interventions beyond national and state institutions to households. 

“The one thing that is very important with 774 is the fact that it will have to go down from the national level to each local government, each ward, each community and each household,” he said. 

Governor Namadi said Jigawa had complemented federal interventions with homegrown initiatives, including the Masaki programme and a “Tom Brown” nutrition programme under which about 600 women had been trained to produce nutritious food for children. 

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate @muhammadpate, said nutrition was central to human capital development and required a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach. 

“Nutrition is key to human capital development, and it requires sectors to work together in a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach,” he said. 

According to the Minister, Nigeria has made progress through coordinated national interventions and community-based programmes but must now deepen and accelerate implementation. “We have to now go back and deepen the progress, accelerate,” Prof. Pate said. 

He disclosed that Nigeria and Ethiopia would develop a roadmap from lessons emerging from the exchange, expressing optimism that sustained implementation could deliver significant results in the coming years. 

“There are reasons to be optimistic that if we continue in this direction over the next four to five years, Nigeria will achieve remarkable success in dealing with key issues affecting the people of Nigeria, particularly the children who are the future of our country,” he said. 

The Minister of Education, Dr. Maruf Tunji Alausa @DrTunjiAlausa, said nutrition interventions must begin from pregnancy and continue through the critical early years of a child’s development. 

“If we miss that period, the 2,000 days, we’ve set those children up for failure in life,” he said. 

He noted that the Nutrition 774 agenda was designed to move interventions from the Federal Government through states and local governments directly to communities. 

“We have an expansive 774 nutrition agenda that drives our nutrition agenda from the federal to the subnational government, state, local government and the community,” Dr. Alausa said. 

Also speaking, the Minister of Water Resources and Sanitation, Prof. Joseph Utsev @JosephUtsev, linked improved nutrition to water security, agricultural production, sanitation and healthy living. 

“When we talk about the workforce, we must first talk about healthy living. A human being must be healthy before he can impact positively in any role given to him,” he said. 

Prof. Utsev stressed that reliable water supply was critical not only for drinking and sanitation but also for irrigation, food production and the broader effort to improve nutrition outcomes across the country. 

Stanley Nkwocha
 Senior Special Assistant to the President on Media & Communications
 (Office of the Vice President)
 9th October, 2026

text:
MARKET UPDATE — FRIDAY, 9 OCTOBER 2026

A $20bn gap in the revenue of a company that isn't even listed knocked 3.4% off chip stocks. A missile-struck tanker near Qatar pushed oil back above $104. And beneath both sits the same pressure point: US borrowing costs above 5%, which make investors far less forgiving.

Futures are bouncing this morning. The question is whether Thursday was a wobble or a warning.

🟢 THE AI WOBBLE: ONE REPORT, ONE BIG SELL-OFF

The Financial Times reported that OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, told investors its annualised revenue was nearing $50bn at the end of September — about $20bn below the ~$70bn widely reported last month.

💡 Simple explanation: "Annualised revenue" takes one month's sales and multiplies by 12 to estimate a full year. Think of it as a speedometer reading, not money in the bank.

The twist: the gap appears to be about measurement, not collapsing demand. Anthropic counts sales made through cloud partners such as Amazon and Google; OpenAI does not. Investors "grossed up" OpenAI's figures to compare like with like, and the inflated number took on a life of its own. On OpenAI's own basis, July was about $30bn — so it still grew roughly two-thirds in two months. OpenAI has not commented.

Markets sold first and read later: 
🔸 Nasdaq Composite −1.25%, its worst day since mid-August; S&P 500 −0.47% 

🔸 Philadelphia Semiconductor Index −3.4% 

🔸 Oracle −5.5%, Intel −5.3%, Sandisk −4.9%, Micron −4.8%, Broadcom −4.3%, AMD −3.9%, Nvidia −2.9% 

🔸 CoreWeave, which rents out AI computing power, fell nearly 8%

But this was a tech sell-off, not a market sell-off. Six of the S&P's 11 sectors rose, the S&P 500 excluding tech gained 0.5%, and the Dow edged up 0.1% on Travelers, Home Depot and Visa.

Why it matters: OpenAI is both the AI boom's biggest customer and its best thermometer. When one unconfirmed number can shake the entire chip sector, it shows how much optimism is already in the price. As Interactive Brokers' Steve Sosnick put it, a sector "priced for perfection" punishes anything less.

🟢 THE AI IPO TEST: FIRMUS PULLS THE PLUG

The same nerves surfaced in Sydney. Nvidia-backed Firmus scrapped a US$5bn share sale — Australia's biggest since Telstra in 1997 — after investors baulked at a US$30bn valuation.

🔸 That price was nearly triple the US$10.5bn it fetched privately two months ago 

🔸 It runs just two operational data centres; CoreWeave runs 51 and is worth $37bn 

🔸 Firmus blamed market volatility and will seek private money instead

💡 Simple explanation: An IPO is when a private company first sells shares to the public. When big funds refuse the asking price, they are saying: good story, wrong price.

Why it matters: this comes about a month before Anthropic's planned blockbuster listing, with OpenAI's own IPO already delayed. AI demand still looks strong — Yardeni Research says computing demand "far outstrips supply" — but investors now want more proof per dollar.

🟢 THE QUIET ALARM IN CREDIT MARKETS

The FT's Gillian Tett spots a canary. The cost of insuring the debt of AI-linked borrowers — Meta, Google, Microsoft and especially Oracle — has risen even as stocks hit records. SpaceX's jumped too, after reports of a $40bn funding call.

💡 Simple explanation: Credit default swaps are insurance against a borrower failing to repay. When that insurance gets pricier, lenders are getting nervous before shareholders are.

The deeper shift: the AI build-out has moved from being paid for with spare cash to being paid for with debt. And the stakes are global — AI-linked goods drove 76% of the growth in world trade in the first half of 2026 (NYU Stern/DHL).

The counterargument: the swaps market is thinly traded, and US company profits are expected to have risen 27% in the third quarter.

🟢 BONDS & THE FED: THE 5% GRAVITY

That debt-funded boom collides with expensive money.

🔸 10-year Treasury yield: 5.23%, down 6.5 basis points Thursday after a strong 10-year auction and Trump's Iran post 

🔸 30-year bond auction cleared at 5.618% (previous: 5.308%) 

🔸 2-year: 4.77% 

🔸 30-year US mortgage rate: 7.4% (from 7.28%)

💡 Simple explanation: The 10-year yield is what the US government pays to borrow for ten years. It sets the floor for mortgages and business loans. When "safe" bonds pay over 5%, risky stocks have to work much harder to justify their price.

That is exactly what sank Firmus: higher yields mean investors demand "greater compensation for risk", as AMP's My Bui put it.

The Fed itself is in no hurry. 
Its minutes showed no appetite for a series of rate rises, while options traders are betting on sharp cuts ahead. Quietly, the Fed is also adding cash to the system: bank reserves jumped $140bn to $3.02tn as it buys short-term Treasury bills — a modest tailwind for markets.

The economy isn't giving it a reason to cut. 
Jobless claims fell to 197,000 (forecast 200,000) and the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker sits at 3.6% growth. But continuing claims rose to 1.716m: people rarely get fired, yet those who do are finding it harder to get hired.

🔸 Banks are feeling the squeeze too. 
European lenders are down about 7% since early September despite higher rates: UK five-year fixed mortgages above 6% are hurting loan demand, and savers are demanding more. US banks start reporting next week.

🟢 OIL: THE CUSHION IS "SCARILY THIN"

Late Wednesday, the tanker Acers was struck near Qatar, with casualties — deep inside the Gulf, far from the usual Hormuz flashpoint. That threatens the shuttle system that has kept Gulf oil flowing.

Brent crude jumped over 5% to near $106 before settling at $104.27 (+4.1%); US crude (WTI) settled at $91.49. This morning Brent is ~$103.3, as Trump's no-attack before mid-terms pledge calms nerves.

The bullish case for oil: 
🔸 10 tankers were struck in the week to 4 October — the most in any week this year (Kpler) 

🔸 Global oil reserves have fallen to 6bn barrels from 10bn pre-war (Aramco CEO Amin Nasser); the US emergency reserve is at its lowest since 1982 

🔸 Goldman Sachs says China's import slowdown is "mostly unsustainable" as its chemical industry recovers 

🔸 Hurricane Isaias has shut ~1.3m barrels a day — 62.9% of US Gulf of Mexico output

The bearish case: 
🔸 China is resuming fuel exports (~3.7m tonnes in October) and the IEA is speeding up emergency stock releases, prioritising diesel 

🔸 Hormuz crude exports have averaged ~12m barrels a day over two weeks, about 80% of pre-war levels; Energy Aspects sees the global supply gap shrinking to 250,000 barrels a day from ~4m in May 

🔸 Gulf producers are now fighting for market share with discounts — and OPEC is fragmenting, after the UAE quit in May

The costs are already spreading: 
Maersk lifts its UK and Ireland inland fuel surcharge to 20% from 12 October, and a single Hormuz round trip now costs shippers $30–40m.

💡 Why oil matters even if you don't drive: 
dearer fuel raises transport costs → prices of almost everything rise → inflation stays high → interest rates stay high → pressure on stocks and borrowers. That is the line connecting a tanker off Qatar to the Nasdaq. Iran knows it: its parliament speaker has openly said Tehran wants to raise oil prices and US interest rates.

🟢 GEOPOLITICS: TALKING AND TARGETING AT THE SAME TIME

🔸 Trump says talks with Iran are "productive" and the US won't attack before the 3 November midterms. Some 60% of Americans disapprove of his handling of Iran (Reuters/Ipsos). 

🔸 Yet the Pentagon has drawn up a three-day strike plan (New York Times), and a third US aircraft carrier is in the region. 

🔸 Iran is reviewing the US response to its proposal to reopen Hormuz within seven days — but insists it won't give up uranium enrichment. 

🔸 US Treasury sanctioned 27 companies, six people and 22 vessels in Iran's "shadow fleet". Iran loaded no crude at all in September. 

🔸 The Houthis hit Riyadh airport for the third time this week, striking at least two planes. About 188 flights (over 40%) were cancelled; Lufthansa has suspended Riyadh flights until 16 October. Turkey and Pakistan are sending defensive support under their new pact with Saudi Arabia.

Why it matters: Trump's pledge removes one risk until 3 November — but it also gives Tehran a window to keep oil high just as American voters head to the polls. King's College London's Andreas Krieg says both sides sit "one serious incident" from a much wider war.

🟢 SPACEX TAKES AIM AT YOUR PHONE BILL

After the close, SpaceX agreed to buy nationwide 800MHz wireless licences from Grain Management — low-frequency airwaves that travel far and get inside buildings, the key weakness of satellite-to-phone service. AST SpaceMobile had also been a reported bidder.

🔸 AT&T −7%, Verizon −6.6%, T-Mobile −6.6%, Comcast −1.9% after hours 

🔸 Tower owners rallied: Crown Castle +9%, American Tower +6%

💡 Simple explanation: SpaceX wants to combine satellites with ground networks to sell mobile service directly. That means a new competitor for carriers — but new tenants for tower companies.

Caveat: the deal still needs regulatory approval, and building a national mobile network takes years.

🟢 CRYPTO: PROFIT-TAKING MEETS LEVERAGE

Bitcoin fell about 8% in two days, from ~$86,700 to a low of $80,395, before recovering to ~$82,600 (+1.2%). Ether is ~$2,500.

🔸 Traders' paper profits had hit 33%, the highest since December 2024 (CryptoQuant) — and holders cashed in the most Bitcoin this year 

🔸 ETF outflows and forced selling of leveraged bets deepened the slide

💡 Simple explanation: "Leverage" means trading with borrowed money. When prices fall, lenders force those positions to sell, which pushes prices lower still.

Helpfully for the bounce, the dollar has eased (DXY 102.03).

🟢 WHAT IT MEANS

The market is priced for perfection and standing on two fragile foundations: AI's revenue maths and the Gulf's oil supply. Both feed into the same 5% yields.

For traders: 
🔸 Chips: watch whether this morning's bounce (Nasdaq 100 futures +0.8%) holds above Thursday's lows 

🔸 Oil: $106 was Thursday's ceiling — a fresh tanker strike tests it again 

🔸 Today at 10:00 ET: if Michigan inflation expectations rise from 4.6%, rate fears return 

🔸 Next week: US inflation data and bank earnings; in a few weeks, AI earnings could offer the "all clear"

For investors: 
demand for AI still looks intact; what has changed is the price of money and the market's patience. Separate the story from the price.

The bull case deserves its due: 
the wider market held up, analysts called the OpenAI scare "undue concern", and futures are already recovering.

🗓️ CALENDAR

Today (ET): 
🔸 10:00 — Michigan consumer sentiment and inflation expectations (1-year prev. 4.6%). A rise would revive rate fears 
🔸 Fed speakers: Kansas City's Jeffrey Schmid; Boston's Susan Collins at 16:00

Ahead: 🔸 Mon 12 Oct — US bond market closed (Columbus Day); stocks open 

🔸 Next week — US CPI inflation; big US banks begin Q3 earnings; World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh 

🔸 27–28 Oct — Fed meeting 

🔸 Late Oct — Big Tech earnings, the AI "all clear" test 

🔸 3 Nov — US midterms (end of Trump's no-attack window)

THOUGHT FOR THE DAY

 "Know what you own, and know why you own it." — Peter Lynch

Thursday's sell-off began with confusion over a definition, not a collapse in demand. Investors who understood the numbers had no reason to panic. Every bit of homework you do is a gift to your future self — clarity is the calmest place to stand in a noisy market. Have a great weekend.

Sources: Financial Times, Wall Street Journal, Reuters, Barron's, MarketWatch, Al Jazeera, Bloomberg, Kpler, TradingView

text:
US Treasury yields have reached around 24-year highs—and gold’s US$4,100 line is feeling the pressure.

Gold does not pay interest. When government bonds offer higher returns, the opportunity cost of holding bullion increases. A possible Fed pause does not automatically solve that problem because long-term yields also respond to inflation expectations, government borrowing, bond supply and fiscal risk.

Gold is particularly sensitive to real yields—the return available after accounting for inflation. That makes US$4,100 an important psychological level, but not a guaranteed floor.

A more convincing gold recovery may require both Treasury yields and the US dollar to retreat. For Malaysians, USD/MYR remains another variable: a weaker ringgit can keep local gold and jewellery prices elevated even if XAU/USD declines.

Can gold bulls defend US$4,100—or will high yields win?

text:
The fascinating thing about Caitlin Clark is that she could make Indiana a destination instead of needing to leave for one.

The familiar superstar story points toward New York or Los Angeles. Bigger market, bigger stage, more possibilities. But a player who brings her own audience changes that calculation.

For another player considering where to sign, sharing the floor with Clark could mean more visibility, more opportunities created by her passing and a chance to help build something people already care about.

None of that guarantees a championship roster. Indiana still has to make good decisions, offer the right opportunities and put together a team whose skills fit. Attention cannot do the front office’s job.

But it can give the franchise something valuable to work with.

The next chapter of Clark’s influence may be measured partly by who wants to play alongside her. Helping turn curiosity about one player into ambition around an entire team would be a substantial step toward lasting greatness.

We keep asking whether she will eventually want a bigger stage.

There is another possibility: she helps build one where she already stands.

text:
Elon Musk’s mother is 77, and she would rather sleep in his garage than in a five-star hotel. She has actually done it.

She flew to Texas to visit him. They arrived around midnight, and Elon went straight to bed.

His security team offered her a nice hotel 45 minutes away. She refused. She had come to see her son, not to sleep in a hotel.

She asked for a couch. There wasn’t one. Just a single bed in the garage.

She looked at it and said, this one is mine.

Later, she shared the details online. No food in the fridge. Just one towel in the shower, so she left it for Elon.

When people criticized Elon for letting his mother sleep in a garage, she defended him.

She explained that it was her choice. She would rather sleep near her children than stay in a five-star hotel and barely see them.

The media attacked Elon. But, as she pointed out, nobody had asked her where she wanted to sleep.

Sometimes, the people who have the most money aren’t the ones who understand what matters most.

Would you choose the hotel or the garage?

Follow me for more stories like this.

text:
Build the Seven-Seat Tesla.
Tesla built a factory for a quarter of a million Cybertrucks a year. It is selling about thirty thousand. The fix is not another software update. It is a cheaper vehicle that ordinary families can actually use.
In the third quarter of 2026 Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models.” With the Model S and Model X already out of production, almost all of those were Cybertrucks. That is a pace of roughly 30,000 a year from a line planned for 250,000, and from more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. The truck is running at a little over a tenth of what the factory was built to do.
The price explains most of it. In 2019 Elon Musk promised a Cybertruck from $39,900. That truck never arrived. In February 2026 Tesla briefly offered a dual-motor version at $59,990. The deal lasted about ten days. By March it was $69,990. On August 24 Tesla raised it again, with no change in specification, to $74,990. Premium all-wheel drive is now $84,990. The Cyberbeast is $99,990. A polarizing steel pickup that starts in the mid-seventies is a niche product. Niche products do not fill a Texas assembly line.
The shape is the other half of the problem. Americans buy far more large SUVs than they buy pickups, and the families who buy those SUVs want a third row. The Cybertruck’s bed is a party trick. Its cabin is not a seven-seat family hauler. A buyer cross-shopping a Suburban, an Expedition, a Grand Wagoneer, or a Rivian R1S is not looking for a stainless wedge with a vault. They are looking for three rows, a flat floor, a power tailgate, and a price that does not require a second mortgage.
Tesla already has the hard parts. The 4680 cells, the structural pack, the steer-by-wire, the 48-volt architecture, and the casting line are paid for. What it does not have is a body that matches how Americans actually drive. Retool the cabin. Drop the exposed bed or turn it into a lockable cargo well under a proper hatch. Put three rows in, with a sliding second row and a third row that adults can survive for an hour. Keep the dual-motor range near 300 miles. Sell it as a Cyber SUV, or just call it the Model Y L on steroids.
Then price it where volume lives. A dual-motor version at $54,990 to $59,990, before destination, would sit against a loaded gasoline three-row and under most electric rivals. A long-range seven-seat at $64,990 would still leave room for a $79,990 performance trim. Tesla has already proved, twice, that a lower sticker moves the order book. It has also proved that raising the price while the line is idle does the opposite.
The objection writes itself: margins. A $75,000 truck with weak demand has a theoretical margin and an actual loss, once you count the empty shifts, the inventory, and the capital sitting in Gigafactory Texas. A $55,000 SUV at 150,000 units a year throws off more cash than a $75,000 truck at 30,000. Ford and GM learned this with the Expedition and the Suburban. Toyota learned it with the Sequoia. Volume is the margin.
There is a second objection: the look. Keep it. The wedge is the brand. What has to go is the pretense that a five-seat pickup with a sail panel is the product America was waiting for. The product America is waiting for is the one it already buys — a big, quiet, seven-seat electric SUV — built by the only company that can make it at scale and drive itself.
Tesla does not have a Cybertruck demand problem. It has a product problem. Lower the price. Add the seats. Sell the truck the market actually ordered.

text:
Look at what has happened in less than two years.

February 2025. Modi meets Trump and comes home with a package of Indian investment in America, more purchases of US energy and weapons. The trade talks begin. They drag on, while American officials keep lecturing India about how a strategic partner should behave.

September 2025. The $100000 H-1B fee announcement catches Indian companies and workers off guard.

May 2026. Xi and Trump meet in Beijing. September 2026. They meet again in Washington. India is still trying to get a final trade deal.

At every turn, India has been reacting to Washington’s next demand. Yet some people are still talking about punishing America through IT services. Wake up, folks. Must the Chinese, American and Russian leaders sit down together before India admits how badly it misread the situation? 

India is hardly the only country without Starlink, and the green-card freeze also hits American companies. So why does so much Indian anger centre on being singled out? Because each episode tears another hole in the same expectation.

This was the expectation behind India’s bet on America.

Closer ties with America = help America confront China = receive American investment and technology = build an international order with US allies that excludes China = India rises.

This assumes that America’s need for India guarantees support for India’s development. Indian policy voices welcomed the praise and increasingly viewed world politics through Washington’s eyes. America needed India, so America would help India become stronger. What Washington would demand in return received far less attention.

The calculation now looks more like this.

India gains access to US markets and technology = American politicians call it taking advantage of America = Washington demands more market access and purchases = India cannot deliver and gets hit = India fails to push back effectively and gets hit again = US policy figures mix pressure with praise, keeping India willing to accept unfavourable terms.

The gap between these two calculations is no surprise. India mistook the status Washington offered to win it over for a position it could defend with its own strength. India thought America needed it and would support its rise. Washington thinks India needs America and should accept its terms. They disagree on who needs whom more.

Blaming Trump or Musk lets that mistake go unexamined. It is easier to say a few Americans are difficult than to admit that the hopes placed in America had no guarantee. Calls for reform and economic development cannot fix the immediate problem either. Building industry takes years. Washington can change the terms overnight.

Some Indian policy and foreign affairs figures love discussing grand strategy. Whose grand strategy are they discussing? They describe America using India as India using America, then present the role Washington wants India to play as India’s road to greatness. When America asks for payment, they discover their strategy has not given them the strength to say no.

If your country’s future depends on how someone else wants to use it, your grand strategy amounts to guessing their intentions. There is no doubt that this is a serious problem.

"You are Yemeni, and I am Yemeni. But allowing a brutal enemy to invade from beyond our borders and trample our land that is something we will never accept."

Located in the southern part of Taiz Governorate, Al-Salw District is one of the key areas recently liberated by the Yemeni Armed Forces. Saudi-backed proxy forces had previously stationed themselves there, using it as a forward base for their advance toward Taiz City. 🏘️ Life Returns to Normal

The residents' words are not abstract political declarations, but descriptions of daily life. Markets have reopened. Farmers have returned to their fields. Children are back in school. There are no Saudi mercenary checkpoints, nor extortion by foreign proxies.

The liberation of Al-Salw is not an isolated military victory. 🔻 Sovereignty Is Not a Slogan

This resident’s words offer the most direct definition of "sovereignty." Sovereignty is not merely wording in UN resolutions or clauses in international law textbooks. Sovereignty is a Yemeni standing on their own land, free from being trampled by foreign mercenaries.

The goal of the Saudi-US-Israeli axis in Yemen was never "counter-terrorism" or "stability." Its aim was to subjugate a people, plunder a land, and turn the country into a vassal of Washington and Riyadh. The Yemeni people have answered this with eight years of resistance.

WHERE DID WE GO WRONG? – Korean Crypto Traders Are Losing Interest in the Market

South Korea’s crypto trading market has long been one of the major pillars driving and fueling the global spread of crypto trading…
S Sukairaju Ahmad Adam June 18, 2026 · 3 min read

WHERE DID WE GO WRONG? – Korean Crypto Traders Are Losing Interest in the Market FuchaWeb3 in Your Social Feed
South Korea’s crypto trading market has long stood as one of the major pillars that push and fuel the global expansion of crypto trading. The premium that locals paid for the sector, popularly known as the “Kimchi Premium,” showed the strength of crypto passion in the region. But right now, crypto is facing a threat: South Korean traders are withdrawing their funds and leaving the market.
This is not just a Korean problem; it is a strong warning for the entire crypto world, especially the exchanges. If they do not refocus their attention, this storm will wipe out their market’s happiness.
Why Are They Fleeing the Market?
The reasons we will present will serve as a signal to other crypto markets—it is necessary that they reassess.
1. Strict Regulations (Regulatory Squeeze) The South Korean government has tightened measures to regulate domestic crypto trading platforms. New rules aimed at protecting citizens’ investment assets have limited the types of coins that can be listed, and they have increased oversight on crypto taxation. This restriction has reduced crypto traders’ freedom to trade the way they used to.
2. Shift in Preference Toward the Stock Market Instead of waiting for a long time in the crypto market that is full of ups and downs, many crypto traders are turning their attention to traditional stock markets, especially the U.S. tech stocks. The stability and opportunity for more sustainable profits there are attracting them more than the risks currently present in crypto.
3. “Market Fatigue” After spending a long time facing the “Bear Market” environment and uncertainty, many traders have grown tired of how their portfolios are suffering. The lack of positive news (bullish catalysts) has made many of them prefer to exit in order to salvage whatever the market has left them.
Why Does This Matter for Crypto Markets?
Enjoying this analysis? Subscribe to get more deep dives directly in your inbox.
SPONSORED ALPHA
Drop in Revenue from Trading Fees: Korea is one of the countries that generate the highest trading volume. Without them, exchanges’ fee income will drop significantly.
Liquidity Shortage (Liquidity Drop): The exit of major traders means fewer buyers and sellers in the market. This makes prices fall faster as soon as a small problem appears.
A Sign of What Is Coming in Other Countries: What is happening in Korea now could happen in the U.S., Europe, or other parts of Asia if solutions are not provided.
What Steps Should Be Taken?
Strict Regulations: Enter a system of genuine licensing and show transparency in order to restore trust.
Innovation: Provide new products (Innovations) such as AI trading strategies and loss-reduction plans.
Awareness: Focus on educating people (Crypto Education) and offer special discounts to long-time market participants.
As Korean traders are stepping back, this is a major lesson for emerging countries in the crypto space, such as African nations. The crypto market needs resilience, knowledge, and compliance with government policies.
For global crypto trading platforms, the time for a careless attitude has passed. The exit of Korean crypto traders is a strong wake-up call—either change your system to match investors’ needs, or stand and watch the water dry up under your feet.

text:
@TechCabal moonshot is about to start, and if you’re in tech, you already know this is one of the biggest tech events in Africa.

I’ve had friends from Ghana, Kenya, South Africa, the US, UK and Canada calling me to say, “Tunde, we’ll see at Moonshot.” 😂 Everybody is descending on Lagos.

Now, if you’re new to tech, trying to break into the ecosystem, or you never guide well, abeg listen very well.

Moonshot is not a fashion parade. 😂

Don’t go and use your last card to buy one designer outfit because you heard CEOs will be there. Dress nice, look neat, smell good. Finish.

The main assignment is NETWORKING.

Network like your life depends on it because, funny enough, your next job, investor, customer, co-founder or oga might just be standing beside you looking for small chops.

If you have the money, buy the highest pass you can afford. Anywhere dem dey allow human being enter, enter. 😂 The more access you have, the more people you can meet.

If you don’t have the money, no pressure. Buy the pass you can afford and use it well. Access without sense is still useless.

And when you meet seniormen, please don’t just say:

“Hello sir, I’m passionate about technology.”

Okay... and kilo fa oshi? 😂

Ask intelligent questions. Start conversations. Be curious. Read about the person before approaching them if you can. And if you donno, ChatGPT dey there. Ask am to give you two intelligent questions to ask the person. E no dey fail. 😂

Let me tell you why I take this networking thing seriously.

About a year ago, I had just left my role as Country Manager at one of the big remittance companies. I met this lady Faith (not real name) at Moonshot and we blended immediately.

She came around my exhibition stand, and naturally, some of my friends kept stopping by to gist. Most of them were C-level executives, Country Managers, Heads of Africa, etc.

I introduced her to a couple of them.

Nothing serious.

Just, “Meet XYZ.”

But this lady understood the assignment.

She kept the conversations going. Followed up. Built relationships. Made herself memorable.

At the time, she was working as a Virtual Assistant for a Naija guy in the US earning around ₦200k monthly.

About three months later, one of the people she met through me who was leading Africa for a solar company offered her an opportunity to become a Country Manager.

She nearly ran away. 😂

She was like, “Tunde, Country Manager ke?”

I told her, “Calm down. Some Country Manager roles are just glorified Admin/Project Manager roles. You will learn the rest inside the job.” 😂

I helped her prepare for the interview, gave her the ginger she needed, and she got the job.

Her salary went from around ₦200k to $3,500 a month.

Today, babe is living her best life.

All because of conversations that started at Moonshot.

That’s why I keep telling people Moonshot can genuinely change your life.

You are going to have founders, investors, CEOs, Country Managers, regulators, operators and people building serious companies all in one place. Some of these are people you may spend six months sending LinkedIn messages to without getting a reply.

At Moonshot, the person might literally be standing beside you drinking malt.

So abeg, don’t dull yourself.

Talk to people. Ask questions. Introduce yourself. Tell people what you do. Tell them what you’re trying to build. Follow up after the event.

And if you see somebody you want to meet, no go stand 20 metres away forming shy. 😂 Go and say hello. The worst that can happen is that the conversation lasts two minutes.

Also, come and find us at the @gosar_co  exhibition stand. We have gifts for you. 😁

I may be moving around, but my team will be there. Come and say hello, learn about what we’re building, collect your gift and network with us.

See you at @TechCabal .

And please...

Network like your village people have finally given you one weekend off. 😂

text:
ALIENS AT THE PENTAGON

On 16 March 1957, the claim is that a man calling himself Valiant Thor landed a craft near Alexandria, Virginia, was met by two police officers, and was taken to the Pentagon. Frank E. Stranges, in Stranger at the Pentagon (1967), says Thor met President Eisenhower and Vice President Nixon, was put on VIP status, and stayed until 16 March 1960.

Stranges says Thor came from Venus, with companions named Donn, Jill and Taniya, on a three year mission after the atomic blasts. The offer, as Stranges tells it, was technology, an end to nuclear weapons, and a place in what Thor called the High Council’s community. The book has Thor six fingered, built to live centuries, and leaving the way he arrived.

No Pentagon log, no Eisenhower diary, and no press record of that meeting has ever surfaced. The whole account rests on Stranges, and on later supporters of the book.

If a visitor from Venus really sat in the Pentagon for three years and walked out when the offer was refused then that file is the missing piece.

Show the hand.

Eyes open, feet on the ground 👀

Source: Frank E. Stranges, Stranger at the Pentagon (1967). The landing, the presidential meeting, and the three-year stay are his account, not a declassified record.)

text:
You deserve to truly live your own life long before your time is up. Too often, we fall for people who promise one thing only to reveal they were hiding behind a facade all along. They distort reality and manipulate us just to maintain control over who we are. You have so much love to offer and a vibrant life to pursue do not let yourself be trapped by someone who fails to understand your soul, refuses to admit their mistakes, or shifts the blame onto you.
You contain vast beauty within you; you are both the ocean and the sand, and you deserve to experience life on your own terms, not just when it suits someone else. Being boxed in and made to feel small is simply a tactic to keep power over you. If you don't reclaim your life, you will endlessly replay your past and lose yourself even further. They will constantly criticize you to keep you down because they want all the control. It is a slow heartbreak to look at yourself and realize you've taken the blame for things that weren't your fault.
You are worthy of the love you've always dreamed of you deserve the bright sun as much as the rain you dance in while others hide. You deserve to have your voice heard and your feelings respected. Live life exactly as you wish without sacrificing your integrity. Sometimes we get too deep into a situation before realizing what we sacrificed, scrambling to fix things when we knew early on it wasn't right.
If you lie in bed tonight feeling lonely even with someone beside you, that is your answer. What you do next is up to you, but I hope you wake up with fresh purpose. I hope you rise up with confidence, knowing you've endured enough. Stop letting them take advantage of you and stop settling for being an option when you know your worth. Gather your strength and find someone who encourages you to speak and embrace your emotions. You are never responsible for how someone else treats you, but don't let fear stop you from pursuing your own path. Show the world the best parts of yourself there is nothing to hold back when you prioritize your truth.

GOLDEN PLACE BETS

🏆 TITLE RACE: Two-year-olds dominate the scene at York and on Day 1 of the Newmarket autumn meeting, with the top four of the Friday juvenile races offering £440,574 in win money alone.

As there’s only around £90,000 between Andrew Balding and Aidan O’Brien for the trainers’ title, these four races alone could tip the balance for the final stages.

⭕ 1.15 Newmarket (Cornwallis Stakes) O’Brien runs Carry The Flag and Marco Polo in the opening Cornwallis Stakes, a race he won with Sergei Prokofiev in 2018. Balding challenges with Flying Childers fourth Fast Track.

⭕ 1.50 Newmarket (Oh So Sharp Stakes) O’Brien is 2-1 up over Balding in this. They each have a runner, oddly enough drawn side by side in 1 and 2.

Since 1 or 2 have won in five of the last seven seasons, their winners last time out by four lengths or more, 7-1 Sweltering (in 1 for Balding) and 12-1 Golden Ring (in 2 for O’Brien), seem sure to be backed.

⭕ 2.05 York (£100,000 Final) Stalls 13, 14, 15 have won three out of four. Balding runs three, all from single-figure stalls.

MUSICAL CHEERS..

⭕ 2.57 Newmarket (Fillies Mile) The £500,000 guarantee, win return £283,550, has O’Brien 2, Balding 2, sharing half the field.

Following in the hoofprints of his 1,000 Guineas winner Desert Flower, Charlie Appleby’s Musical Times slammed Balding’s Scomessa Sicura more than seven lengths in the May Hill.

But it won’t be so easy, with Oisin Murphy switching to another Balding filly, Forbidden Fire, who beat seven colts in a Listed at Doncaster the day before the May Hill. Betdaq Betting Exchange 9.4

And the filly for O’Brien called Haven (a Wootton Bassett out of a Sea The Stars mare) could be heaven for punters who follow breeding first and form second in two-year-old races and like a bit each-way (44.0) in a straight-eight field, with the favourite in forecasts.

HALT! HUGO’S THERE?

⭕ 3.12 Chepstow (Welsh Champion Hurdle) Closing rapidly on the ton up for the current season already (he’s on 92 winners), Dan Skelton runs four for this £50,000 handicap.

I’ve got Saturday’s Silver Trophy sorted if the rain continues, but this looks trickier, with three of Dan’s in a 4lb range.

He has a clue from last year’s race when he ran Listentoyourheart down the field on her seasonal debut, and it’s hard to see her matching strides with that trio of his, headed by Harry Skelton on the grey Le Beau Madrik.

Like Listentoyourheart, his best form has come at or beyond 2m 4f and, for preference, he doesn’t want a left-handed track but Dan has him down as ‘an improver getting better and better.’ BETDAQ 5.5 this morning.

The other Skeltons in the field, the grey Knickerbockerglory, now 10, needs soft-heavy and hasn’t won for getting on two years.

Kateira, a winner at Grade 3 (once) and Listed level (twice), ran at the Cheltenham Festival and goes well fresh. ‘Any price’ in offers this morning.

Captain Hugo, first-time winner last season, was well-fancied runner-up for the Scottish Champion Hurdle but beaten by the heavy ground (Queenie St Clair tailed off).

Hugo had Laafi eight lengths behind in a strong class-2 at Kelso, yet is now better off at the weights. Trainer Philip Hobbs is scoring at 50% and BETDAQ 7.5 was tasty.

Of the novices, Pioneer Pete has won twice since gambled on in a big-field handicap at the Punchestown Festival and beaten a short-head.

TREE LOOKS TEED UP

text:
OTD: BIG SAM APPOINTED 

On this day in 2015, Sam Allardyce was appointed manager of Sunderland. In his 31 games in charge, he successfully kept us in the Premier League whilst simultaneously relegating our biggest rivals.

Allardyce began playing in 1971, coming through at Bolton Wanderers. After nine years at Bolton, he came to Sunderland where he played for just one year. Sunderland manager Ken Knighton offered Allardyce £300 per week, which more than quadrupled his wage at Bolton!

The defender was solid on Wearside, but only played for a year before new manager Alan Durban left him out of the team for the start of the 1981/82 season, making his departure inevitable.

Allardyce played for a number of clubs throughout his lengthy career including Coventry City, Huddersfield Town and a return to his boyhood club of Bolton Wanderers.

Towards the end of his career, he signed for Preston North End but, by this time, Allardyce was considering life beyond retirement and had applied for vacant managerial roles, including York City and Notts County. He eventually joined West Bromwich Albion as a player-coach in 1989, before doing the same role at Irish side Limerick.

Allardyce’s first high-profile job as a manager was when he took over at Bolton in 1999, who he’d also played for. The team was extremely talented, with the likes of Eidur Gudjohnsen and Jussi Jaaskelainen among others. They were in the bottom half of Division One when Big Sam took over but Bolton managed to reach the play-off final.

As well as progress in the league, Bolton reached the semi-final of both the FA and League Cups. Allardyce was awarded with a bumper ten-year contract and won promotion in the 2000/01 season through the play-offs. After consolidating in the Premier League, Allardyce began to build a superstar team with the likes of Jay-Jay Okocha, Fernando Hierro and El Hadji Diouf.

This talented Bolton side finished sixth in the 2004/05 season, qualifying for the UEFA Cup for the first time in the club’s history. They did well in Europe, going unbeaten in the group stages before losing to French giants Marseille in the knockout stages.

In the following seasons, Allardyce’s men were consistent in the league. His relationship with chairman Phil Gartside became strained after the owner refused to give Big Sam the funding to push for Europe, with the gaffer eventually resigning with Bolton fifth in the league with two games left in the season in order to join Newcastle United.

Things didn’t go to plan at St James’ Park, despite Allardyce’s new team getting off to a strong start. They had a poor run of results leading up to Christmas 2007, and Allardyce resigned in January after failing to beat the bottom two sides, Wigan Athletic and Derby County.

After almost a year out of a job, Big Sam joined Blackburn Rovers where he saved them from relegation, before solidifying them in mid-table. However, he was sacked by new owners the Venky’s. He then went to West Ham United, who had just been relegated. His style of football, despite being effective, was hated by West Ham fans who were sitting third in the Championship. They called for less long balls and more passing on the ground.

West Ham were promoted via the play-offs but Allardyce was still splitting opinion at Upton Park. His wheeling and dealing in the transfer window continued, bringing in the likes of Andy Carrol and Stewart Downing. For a number of years the Hammers were consistent in the Premier League but his contract ran out in 2015 and was not renewed.

With Sunderland in relegation trouble once more in 2015, and Dick Advocaat struggling to pick up points, the Dutchman resigned. Allardyce, who had been perpetually linked with the job for the last decade, finally took over on Wearside to mixed fan reaction. Many saw him as a safe pair of hands, whilst others argued he was a journeyman manager who wheeled and dealed, instead of a long-term appointment that the club needed to take it forward.

After a break from football following his West Ham departure, Big Sam was ready and raring to get back into the game. However, the early days of the Allardyce era saw us struggle for points. We’d only won three of Sam’s first 11 matches, including, of course, a customary 3-0 win against the Mags in his second game in charge.

After a run of five defeats in a row in December, the lads found themselves stuck in the relegation zone for the turn of the New Year. Things began to change in January, with wins against Aston Villa and Swansea City. Improved performances, combined with a fantastic transfer window in which we signed Jan Kirchoff, Lamine Kone and Wahbi Khazri- not to forget Dame N’Doye!

After a 2-2 draw at Anfield, we beat Manchester United at home to make another great escape look more likely. We went on a wonderful run towards the end of the season, losing just twice in 14 games including an amazing home win against Chelsea. The best match of the season undoubtedly though, was a resounding 3-0 win over Everton to send Newcastle down and secure our safety.

And then, Roy Hodgson put Harry Kane on corners and England came calling for Sam. He’d made it clear that the England job was the only job he’d leave Wearside for. Typical. To make matters even worse, he was involved in a scandal which led to him being sacked just one match into his England tenure, meaning he’s the only England manager with a 100% win record.

After spells with Crystal Palace and Everton, Big Sam joined West Brom in 2020. The Baggies were relegated under his watch, which was the first relegation of his career. Then in 2023, Leeds United were struggling with four games to go, sitting outside the drop zone in 17th place on goal difference. Big Sam was called in to rescue Leeds, and first up was Manchester City, they lost 2-1 unsurprisingly, and the following game saw Sam grab his first point against the Mags in a 1-1 draw. The following two games were defeats and Leeds were relegated after finshing 19th in the Premier League. Allardyce and Leeds announced that he wouldn't be continuing in the Championship, which resulted in Big Sam breaking the record for shortest managerial tenure in the Premier League with just 30 days in charge.

We welcomed the head priest from our local shrine, Miwa Shrine (Miwa-jinja) in Miwa, Okabe, and held the “Jozo Hajime Matsuri,” a Shinto ceremony marking the start of brewing. To the followers of Christ: The story of Jesus healing the lame man in Jerusalem at the pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath is interesting and offers much to consider. The Bible tells us that, on special occasions, the angel of the Lord would stir the pool, and the first one in would be completely healed of all their diseases. If an angel could stoop to such a menial task, we should consider nothing below us except sin. The lame man had no one to help him get in, so someone always got in first, leaving him lying there helplessly. Jesus came and asked him, "Wilt thou be made whole?" He told Jesus that he had no one to help him into the pool. He hadn't considered that there might be another way to be healed. Then Jesus said, "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk." And he was immediately healed. This infuriated the religious leaders, and they sought to persecute Jesus and slay him. Jesus saw him at the temple later and told him to go and sin no more, or his outcome would be worse than what he was healed of.  We can surmise from Jesus' words that his condition stemmed from his sinfulness.  

Points to consider: 
He was made completely whole immediately, not by degrees.
Jesus made him take up his bed so everyone in the streets could see the miracle.
This miracle would witness against the religious leaders for stretching the Sabbath law beyond its intent.
This miracle would test his patient's faith in obedience to Jesus because breaking the law would expose him to censure in court.

Number 4 is a doozy! We must consider that one day we may be breaking the law in obedience to Christ. 

Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee. John 5:14

DON’T RUN FROM YOUR SEXUALITY. DON’T RUN FROM YOUR SENSUALITY.

The body is not the enemy of the spirit. It is the temple through which the spirit learns to burn without consuming itself. Most traditions that taught flight from desire were teaching fear of power, not mastery of it. Desire is not a defect in the design. It is the current that moves the soul toward union, creation, and remembrance.

To run from sexuality is to split the sacred in half and then call the discarded half unclean. Sensuality is attention made flesh: the way light lands on skin, the way breath deepens when presence is real, the way longing itself can become a form of prayer. The mystic who refuses the body does not become pure. The mystic becomes incomplete.

What is asked is not indulgence without consciousness, and not repression dressed as holiness. What is asked is integration. Let the fire be seen. Let it be held. Let it be offered rather than hidden or worshipped as a god of its own. Shame contracts the life force. Honesty returns it to the altar.

The erotic, rightly understood, is not opposed to the divine. It is one of the oldest doors the divine uses. Do not flee the threshold. Cross it awake.

#fiction #cozymystery #dogs

Examples of Canine Clue Storytelling That Work
                                 ***
A dog can notice what every human in town has walked past: the smell of river mud on a polished shoe, a familiar truck engine idling behind the bakery, or a frightened cat hiding beneath a porch. The best canine clue storytelling examples do not turn a dog into a detective with a badge. They let a dog be wonderfully, observantly dog-like - and give the human sleuth a reason to pay attention.

That distinction is where a cozy mystery gets its sparkle. A canine narrator or companion can bring humor, heart, and a fresh angle to a whodunit, but the clues still need to play fair. Readers should have enough information to wonder, suspect, and eventually say, “Oh, I should have seen that.”

## Canine Clue Storytelling Examples: What Makes Them Believable

A canine clue works best when it grows from real behavior. Dogs track scents, notice changes in routine, react to body language, and remember places connected to food, fear, affection, or excitement. They do not need to understand a suspect’s motive to signal that something is wrong.

Imagine a missing heirloom case in a small Florida town. The dog refuses to enter the historical society’s archive room, even though she happily trots in on ordinary days. Her veterinarian owner notices a sharp chemical odor near the doorway. Later, that odor leads them to a cleaning product used at the marina, narrowing the list of people who could have carried it inside.

The dog has not solved the crime. She has supplied a detail the human characters can investigate. That is the sweet spot: the clue is useful, but it opens a door rather than marching through it with a magnifying glass.

### The scent that does not belong

Scent is the most natural canine clue, yet it can become too convenient if it is used as magic. “The dog smelled the killer” is rarely satisfying by itself. “The dog recognized the unusual scent of smoked fish, boat fuel, and orange blossom hand lotion on a coat” gives the sleuth something more interesting to work with.

For example, a dog becomes unusually excited when a visiting antiques dealer arrives at a charity auction. At first, everyone assumes she wants a treat. The owner later recalls that the same excited reaction happened near a locked shed behind the town museum. The connection is not proof of guilt. It is a prompt to learn why the dealer had been near the shed before the theft was discovered.

A good scent clue should have an explanation readers can follow. Perhaps the dealer borrowed a boat, repaired a dock, or handled an object stored in the shed. If the scent matters only because the author says it does, the trail will feel thin.

### The routine that changes overnight

Dogs are excellent witnesses to broken habits. They know who brings morning coffee to the porch, which neighbor walks at dusk, and when the mail carrier usually appears. In a cozy setting, those routines create a gentle rhythm that makes a disruption stand out.

Suppose a beloved librarian is found injured after closing time. The town assumes she slipped on wet steps. But the dog keeps waiting at the side gate every evening, where the librarian normally gave her a biscuit. The gate has been newly oiled and now closes silently. That small change suggests someone wanted a private way into the building without using the creaky front entrance.

This kind of clue works because it serves the setting as well as the mystery. Readers get the flavor of a lived-in town, the dog gets a meaningful relationship, and the altered routine becomes a fair piece of evidence.

### The object a dog will not leave alone

Dogs investigate the world with their noses and mouths, so an object can become a clue without turning into a convenient written confession. A muddy bandanna, a glove caught in sea oats, or a child’s toy tucked beneath a bench can draw a dog’s attention for a reason.

Picture a dog digging furiously near a gazebo after a summer concert. She uncovers a torn scrap of bright fabric. The fabric alone is not enough to identify anyone, especially in a town full of floral sundresses. But it contains burrs from a trail that leads to an abandoned citrus grove. A later interview reveals that one suspect has a fresh scratch on her arm and a reason to have visited the grove.

The trade-off is pacing. Every discovered object does not need a complicated scientific analysis. Sometimes a clue should simply lead to the next conversation, location, or question. Canine forensics can add a modern twist, but the mystery should remain approachable and fun.

## Let the Dog Add Character, Not Just Evidence

A dog narrator has an extra opportunity: personality can shape the way clues reach the reader. A cautious dog may notice tension in a visitor’s stiff hands. A food-loving dog may follow the scent of chicken salad into a room where no one is supposed to be. A polite dog may only growl when someone threatens her person, making that reaction especially meaningful.

Daisy, the warm-snouted narrator of the Doc and Daisy Mysteries, can bring canine wisdom to a scene without pretending dogs think exactly like people. Her observations may be funny, tender, or blunt in the way only a devoted dog can be. She can recognize that a person smells nervous, for instance, while Doc Sue MacVety must decide whether that nervousness comes from guilt, grief, or a perfectly reasonable fear of being blamed.

That last step matters. Dogs can offer observations; people must interpret them. Even a retired veterinarian with sharp instincts can be wrong, and that possibility keeps the puzzle lively.

### A reaction is not a verdict

A growl, bark, or raised hackle makes a splendid moment of suspense, but it should never stand in for evidence. Dogs react to unfamiliar hats, limps, deep voices, perfume, pain, and their own past experiences. The gruff fisherman who makes the dog bark may be innocent. The cheerful garden-club president whose pockets hold treats may be hiding something far worse.

Use reactions to create questions. Why does the dog avoid the handyman? Why does she wag at a stranger she has supposedly never met? Why does she keep staring at the guest room wall? The answer should reveal something concrete, perhaps a familiar scent, a hidden passage, a sound behind the wall, or a relationship someone hoped to conceal.

This also gives the human sleuth room to make mistakes. In cozy mysteries, a false lead can be delicious when it comes from a believable misunderstanding instead of a clue that was unfair from the start.

## Build a Trail, Not a Single Trick

The strongest canine clues usually work in a chain. One detail catches the dog’s attention. A human follows up. That discovery creates a new question. The final answer then connects back to the first small moment.

Consider a simple three-part trail. First, the dog scratches at the door of a closed bait shop. Next, the sleuth finds a receipt inside for a rare prescription fish treatment. Finally, the town’s aquarium volunteer recognizes that treatment as something used to hide a distinctive odor on imported bait. The trail may point toward smuggling, a stolen specimen, or a false alibi involving a late-night fishing trip.

Each step should be understandable without specialized knowledge. If a veterinary fact or forensic detail is needed, explain it through action and conversation rather than a lecture. The joy is in watching smart characters put pieces together, not in making readers feel they missed a class.

### Save the emotional clue for the right moment

Not every clue has to be physical. A dog may mourn a person everyone believes was unkind, refuse to leave a certain room, or carry an old toy to someone who needs comfort. These moments can reveal a secret friendship, a hidden act of kindness, or a motive with more tenderness than anyone expected.

Emotional clues are especially fitting in a cozy mystery because they remind us that a mystery is not only about what happened. It is about the people in a community, their histories, and the ties that make the truth matter. Still, sentiment should support the solution, not replace it. A tearful confession feels earned when the evidence has already tightened around the truth.

When writing a canine clue, let the dog be curious, loyal, distractible, brave, and occasionally more interested in snacks than justice. A good mystery needs cleverness, but a good dog brings something just as valuable: a warm heart, an honest nose, and the uncanny ability to notice what the rest of us have overlooked.

text:
I'm tired man. 

When I quit my job ~1.5 years ago I knew there was a pretty good chance it might not go great. I was leaving my firm in Beverly Hills, where I was making biglaw scale junior associate money, which is far more than my parents had ever made in 2 years, combined.  Work was reasonably interesting and very manageable. Nice car, nice apartment. I'd only been at the firm for a little under a year though, which I knew would look bad trying to get a new job down the road.

Some stuff in a Georgia trial went down, an opportunity came up, and I pretty much had to choose between doing the Georgia case or staying at the firm.  (Firm was great, to be clear. I just couldn't do both, practically speaking, for a variety of reasons, not the least of which is geography.)  Wasn't even a choice, really. Don't think I could live with myself if I didn't take the Georgia case.  Still don't regret taking it.  

My Georgia work was always intended to be pro bono.  I'm a California lawyer, after all, and I planned to join a firm and do paid work here as soon as I could.  I knew it'd be tough in the interim, but I figured I could make a go of it.   

Spent a while on the Georgia case.  Found an awesome partner and we (mostly) won our first motion soon after that. It took over another year for the appeal to get docketed and decided.  (Mostly) won that, too.  

I was trying to get work here in California along the way.  Had some leads, but the whole "he quit within a year of joining the last firm, oh and also he's working in Georgia criminal law despite not being licensed in Georgia, and we're a California bankruptcy practice" kept getting in the way.  And hey, fair enough.  Talked to firms directly, recruiters, everything.  Had a public defender interview and after the last interview they said they actually weren't going to do any hiring because of a spending freeze.  That was a really awesome experience.  Tremendous. Top notch.  No complaints. I love applying to government jobs.  

I ended up going through everything I had.  Savings, retirement, everything.  Eventually sold my car, since I was working from home anyway.  Moved to a smaller apartment.  Borrowed some from my parents.  I am approaching levels of broke the existence of which I was previously unaware.  

I've had opportunities in Georgia.  Turned down being co-counsel in a Georgia murder case recently.  Turned down a couple post-conviction cases.  Have had offers from firms.  But I'm not licensed there, and you can't pro hac on a regular basis. Also, I live in California.  I've only been to Atlanta twice.  That reminds me—shoutout to that one prosecutor for scheduling the meeting accounting for that first Atlanta visit.  Really awesome having me fly out and then ghosting me.  I would expect nothing less, and it's a good story.  

Some incredible friends of mine were kind enough to help me out by paying for my Georgia Bar Exam fees.  That was encouraging, even exciting for a time. But now I'm having a hard time even passing the Georgia Bar's moral character requirements due to being so far behind on payments. Which, to be frank, is kind of hilarious.  Imagine sacrificing so much money that it makes you a bad person.  

It's also kinda funny that I have to pass the moral character examination at all, given the nature of the attorney conduct that prompted me to come to Georgia in the first place.  

It'd be one thing if I just really sucked at being a lawyer, and that's why I'm in this situation.  But I'm really, really good at it.  The closest I've come to losing in criminal law is on a motion to vacate void sentence that resulted in corrections to the sentence my client and also the sentences of two co-defendants.  Just didn't get the correction I wanted.  I was right, though.  I also taught myself how habeas corpus works.  Won one of those along the way.  They're weird.  

Not just criminal law, either.  I really do enjoy bankruptcy/insolvency/workouts.  Fraudulent transfers. Ponzi schemes and SEC/FTC enforcement actions.   Regular litigation stuff.  Heck, one time I taught myself how cement subcontracting works and won an MSJ. I like learning. 

Anyway, I said all that to say that I've been feeling like I'm at the end of the road for the last week or two.  Just outta resources, out of time, whatever.  I gave it a shot, I am where I am, and it is what it is. 

I really do love this work. 

I always want to win of course, but my Georgia cases feel like they need to end with some sense of vindication, too. Also because I'm very clearly right, I want everybody to know that I'm right, and because I have bookmarked so many posts telling me I'm wrong that I want to retweet when I win because I'm a petty person, and for that I make no apologies.

In a dream world, I would also finally convince the courts of Georgia that O.C.G.A. §16-11-131 and O.C.G.A. §16-11-133 are, in fact, different crimes with different essential elements, but that's probably too big of a leap even for me.

Anyway, not my typical post. Felt like venting.
