text:
No One Was Paying Attention to Gina Hinojosa a Month Ago. Now Republicans Are Worried.

NYT Gift Article link
Listen · 18:54 min
09OCT2026
By Michelle Goldberg
https://t.co/8PQWFKHojZ
Opinion Columnist, reporting from East Texas.

Lynn Davenport, a lifelong conservative, met Donald Trump backstage at a Texas rally in 2016. On Jan. 6, 2021, she was at his Stop the Steal rally in Washington, though she left before the Capitol was sacked. In 2024, she was a delegate to Texas’ Republican convention and a Republican precinct chair.

And in May, she filmed an ad for Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running a surprisingly competitive race to become governor of Texas.

The two women have been friends for years, since Hinojosa, a state representative from Austin, helped lead opposition to a crusade by the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, to privatize Texas’ public school system. Abbott’s agenda was bitterly opposed by some conservative Texans, particularly rural ones in places where public schools are the center of the community. (Think “Friday Night Lights.”) Davenport was impressed by Hinojosa’s willingness to listen to her, and by her mastery of education policy. Still, as a committed Republican, she didn’t think she’d ever vote for her.

But Davenport has grown increasingly disgusted with Abbott, over both schools and the data centers he invited into Texas. The governor, she said, is a “globalist. Which to me is scarier than a communist, a socialist or a Marxist, because what Abbott is imposing is technocracy. He’s giving the tech giants carte blanche in Texas.” So she decided not just to support Hinojosa’s bid for governor, but to do it publicly. “Gina is someone that I can work with, whereas Abbott doesn’t care what I think,” she told me.

The premise of Hinojosa’s surprisingly competitive campaign is that there’s a critical mass of voters like Davenport in Texas. The opportunity for Democrats, Hinojosa believes, lies not with moderate, affluent Republicans put off by Trump’s norm-smashing vulgarity, but with disappointed MAGA populists. “The conventional political wisdom is that it is those country club Republicans who will swing over,” she told me before I traveled to Texas. “I think it’s always been MAGA.”

I was skeptical of this analysis then, and after seeing her campaign last week, I’m still not wholly convinced. Trump’s appeal has never been only or even primarily economic; he taps into fear and rage about a country growing less white, less Christian and less deferential to male authority. And Hinojosa seems, at least on paper, ill suited to appeal to Trump’s base. A Latina and a former labor lawyer, she comes from the heart of Texas’ Democratic establishment: Her father led the state Democratic Party from 2012 until 2025. Though she now calls herself a “populist” rather than a “progressive,” she’s one of the more liberal members of the Texas House.

Still, Hinojosa has a group of supporters like Davenport, people furious at Abbott over school privatization and data centers. Mary Lowe, an education activist and a self-described “fundamental Christian,” told me that Abbott is “a globalist. He’s a tyrant. He’s a great deceiver.” And though she’s voted Republican in almost every primary and every general election since 1979, she’s voting for Hinojosa in November. “She’s a good human,” said Lowe. “She’s one of us.”

Several polls still show Hinojosa trailing by a couple of points, but three recent ones, including a New York Times/Siena poll released on Saturday, have her ahead. The polling aggregator Real Clear Politics now rates the race as a tossup, and last week Cook Political Report moved it from “likely” to “lean” Republican. Over the past week, national Democrats have started investing more heavily in the race: Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois and the Democratic Governors Association each gave Hinojosa $1 million.

“She certainly has a much better chance than I did in ’22,” said Beto O’Rourke, who challenged Abbott four years ago and lost by more than 10 points.

Part of that chance derives from Trump’s unpopularity and the country’s economic misery, which is particularly stark in Texas. Campaigning, Hinojosa talks about how the state has more people without health insurance than any other, and some of the nation’s highest rates of small-business bankruptcies. She describes blood plasma centers popping up in middle-class areas — she visited one next to a Sephora — as more people seek to sell their plasma to make ends meet. Hinojosa told me about meeting a lobbyist for the plasma center industry who was excited about all the opportunity in the state. “That’s, I think, a shocking example of where we are in Texas in 2026,” she said.

But her surge can’t be attributed entirely to the economic environment: Hinojosa seems to be hitting her stride as a politician. She’s long had a talent for making people feel heard, but O’Rourke said she’s become dramatically better on the stump. “I campaigned with her in El Paso a few weeks ago, and I’ve never seen her speak so well,” he said.

Her message is simple: Life has gotten too hard for hard-working people in Texas. Schools are underfunded — hundreds have gone to four days a week — and new artificial intelligence initiatives are no substitute for a good teacher in the classroom. Data centers are both a blight and a symbol of Abbott’s misplaced priorities. “It’s impacting people’s homes and lives, and it is a demonstration of the governor doing the bidding of moneyed interests and leaving the people to fend for themselves,” Hinojosa told me. Taking a page from Trump, she’s promising $1,500 checks for every Texan from the state’s plush rainy-day fund — she calls it the “Greg Abbott Corruption Tax Refund” — and to “DOGE” the Department of Education’s dodgy vendor contracts.

It’s a platform, she insists, that can break through with those who in the past have felt alienated from the Democratic Party. “When I sit down with people who voted for Trump, with people who voted for Abbott, and hear them, and they hear me, there’s an opportunity for connection and alliance,” she said. Democrats have a chance, she insists, to move past the cultural battles that have kept them perennially on the defensive. “If we try to be post-culture wars, we can be post-culture wars,” she said. “I’ve experienced it. I’ve seen it.”

Of course, deep rifts over religion, race and gender can’t simply be wished away. But if Hinojosa can find a way to make them less salient, it could portend not just seismic change in Texas, but the beginning of a political realignment. If some fraction of socially conservative voters conclude that rapacious billionaires threaten them more than supercilious liberals, it would remake America’s political map. For decades now, we’ve lived in an era dominated by what scholars call post-material politics, in which values, identity and self-expression have often taken precedence over economic concerns. What if that era is coming to an end? What opportunities would that open up, and what ideological sacrifices would it require?

In May, speaking to my colleague Lulu Garcia-Navarro, Tucker Carlson said that culture war issues — the issues on which he’d built much of his demagogic career — were becoming less important than matters of concentrated wealth and financial precarity. “Most of the debates about race, ethnicity, religion, to some extent immigration, are less resonant long-term than debates about economics,” he said. Hinojosa’s campaign is a bet that he was right.

She is, of course, far from the only Democrat running as a populist and seeking to persuade disaffected Trump supporters. Zohran Mamdani started his mayoral campaign by interviewing working-class Trump voters in Queens and the Bronx, and he won over a small but meaningful chunk of them. A New York Times/Siena poll showed the populist Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan — whom Carlson has all but endorsed — winning 8 percent of people who voted for Trump in 2024.

But it’s one thing to run as an economic progressive in places that regularly elect Democrats. It’s quite another to do it in Texas, in many ways the spiritual home of the modern right. Sure, Texas looks more promising for Democrats this year than it has in decades, with the party’s Senate candidate, James Talarico, maintaining a consistent lead over the Republican Ken Paxton. But Paxton is singularly sleazy and widely despised. As astonishing as a Talarico victory would be, Republicans could explain it away as the fault of a particularly bad candidate.

They won’t be able to do that if Hinojosa wins. Abbott has been elected governor of Texas three times by double-digit margins. If Hinojosa even comes close to beating him, it will be because the Republican coalition that Trump assembled is collapsing, and a new Democratic one is perhaps starting to take shape. “There are people who are responding to our message the same way they were responding to Trump’s message,” she said. “They want power. They want to feel like they’re in control of their lives again, and I think that they want to return to a time that feels like it makes sense again, where hard work pays off.”

A big part of the reason Hinojosa is pulling ahead is that Latinos, who swung toward Republicans in 2024, have soured on the party due in large part to Trump’s brutal mass deportation campaign. At a Spanish-language town hall last week, Hinojosa, whose mother is a Mexican immigrant, mentioned ICE’s fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who’d been in the country for 35 years. “They thought he was someone else, they killed him, and then they realized that he was only going to work,” she said. “When that’s happening, none of us are safe.”

But Hinojosa is also trying to chip away at Abbott’s — and Trump’s — white, rural base. No one thinks she’s going to win these voters outright; the goal is to lose them by less. “There’s definitely a backlash against Abbott over vouchers and over data centers in rural Texas,” said Suzanne Bellsnyder, who writes a newsletter called Texas Rural Reporter. “The question is, does that anger against Abbott translate into a vote for Gina?”

Bellsnyder is trying to make sure it does. A former field director for Abbott, she’s now working for Hinojosa’s campaign. “If I didn’t think she had a chance, I promise you, I wouldn’t be putting my entire Republican credentials on the line,” she told me.

Like Davenport, Bellsnyder got to know Hinojosa during the fight against Abbott’s education agenda. The centerpiece of this battle was Abbott’s voucher bill, which gives most qualifying private school parents about $10,000, reducing funding that otherwise would have gone to public schools. When Abbott tried to pass the law in 2023, he was foiled by 21 Republican holdouts. Abbott then supported primary challenges, partly funded by the Pennsylvania billionaire Jeff Yass, against 15 of the Republicans who thwarted him. Most of them lost, and the law passed in 2025. The wounds among anti-voucher conservatives are still raw.

At an Hinojosa rally in Longview, a city in East Texas, last week, I met Steve Clugston, a 58-year-old school superintendent. Clugston told me he last voted for a Democrat back in the 1990s, when conservative local officials in his part of the state still belonged to the party. “They’re now probably Republicans,” he said.

Clugston voted for Donald Trump in 2024, believing he did a “pretty good job” in his first term. He is, he said, an “old school conservative,” which is reflected in his approach to education. “I still swing the paddle,” he said. (Texas is among a minority of states that allow corporal punishment in schools.) “I believe in kids acting right and learning how to work hard and how to show up and be dependable.”

But he was livid about Abbott’s relentless push for vouchers. “Our governor took billionaire money and then used it to beat Republicans that us Republicans elected,” he said. As he soured on Abbott, he’d also grown disillusioned with Trump and his flagrant, gluttonous corruption. “When you’ve lied to me enough,” said Clugston, “and sold us out for billionaires, I get to the point I’m done.”

Hinojosa’s inroads with the populist right might have been limited to those most committed to public schools, were it not for Abbott’s enthusiasm for data centers. The governor has aggressively sought tech investment in Texas; he’s offered billions in tax incentives to attract data centers and last year boasted that the state was “the epicenter of A.I. development.” Texas now has more in operation than any other state.

Many rural Texans who either live near these behemoths, or fear they will soon, detest them. Anger is so intense that Sid Miller, the state’s outgoing agriculture commissioner — he lost his primary after a series of scandals — told Rolling Stone that it could cost Abbott the election.

In June, Cheryl Shadden, who lives across from a sprawling bitcoin mine in Hood County, showed up at an Hinojosa event in Glen Rose, Texas, wearing a homemade T-shirt that said “Break Rank.” She meant break ranks with the Republican Party, which has failed to protect her from the ugly, noisy facility that she said has upended her life.

“My community is blasted with horrific noise 24/7,” Shadden told me. “I mean, inside of our homes, outside of our homes. We’ve got health problems associated with it.” She says the value of her property — 10 acres and a barn — has plummeted. And the Republicans she’s reached out to for help have ignored her. “I hit everybody and their mother, and crickets, and then Gina Hinojosa’s staff is like, ‘Gina would like to speak to you.’”

Abbott has realized that fury over data centers is a political threat, and he recently issued a moratorium on new development, pending an audit of their energy and water usage. But the pause has loopholes, and the audit, conveniently, is due to be finished right after the election, which means he can restart his data center push once the political danger is gone. “It just stinks. It’s just not right,” said Michael Ellis, a 70-year-old Republican battling plans for a new data center in Texas’ Navarro County.

I met Ellis and his wife, Jennifer, in the town of Corsicana, about an hour southeast of Dallas, where Hinojosa stopped to meet with a small group of anti-data-center organizers. Ellis had come with a binder; he had blueprints of a proposed 80-acre facility slated to go up a mile from his home. He was worried about noise caused by generators, water usage and the danger of an industrial disaster in an area with only a volunteer fire department. He blamed Abbott for welcoming such projects in with virtually no oversight.

Michael was still undecided about who he was voting for, but Jennifer was leaning toward Hinojosa. “Just to walk in and sit down with us and meet with us, to me, that goes a long way,” she said. “That’s massively impressive.”

Then I asked her about the Senate race. She said she’d probably vote for Paxton, despite his many scandals, because of trans issues. “I don’t do all the gender thing,” she said.

It was a reminder of the culture wars’ endurance. Hinojosa still isn’t terribly well known in Texas; in September, she told me that some 20 percent of the electorate wasn’t familiar with her. I wondered what voters like Ellis would think of her after Abbott, who is outspending Hinojosa around 6 to 1, blankets Texas with attack ads. One recent spot tried to brand her as “gender bender Gina,” a radical out to “trans your kids.”
Hinojosa has tried to pre-empt this caricature in her own advertising, seeking to distance herself from social liberalism without recanting her previous positions. In one ad, she declared, “My pronouns are ‘mom,’ ‘Texan’ and soon to be ‘governor.’” In another, she described deciding, 23 years ago, to carry a pregnancy to term even though her baby had no chance of survival. “I chose her,” she said. The spot doesn’t mention the law that now denies Texas women the choice that she had. If I saw it without knowing who Hinojosa was, I might have thought she was anti-abortion.

She’s not, but on the campaign trail, she doesn’t talk about abortion unless she’s asked. Even then, she says her priority in office will be fixing the law that prevents doctors from treating some women with doomed pregnancies until they’re near death. “Reproductive choice is just one of those issues that divide us,” she told me. “I’m running to be governor to work on an agenda that the vast majority of us agree on.”

I could probably write a whole column picking apart this strategy. Reproductive rights are popular, even in red states. It would be disastrous for Democrats to decide, at this moment of intense social backsliding, that women’s health and freedom should be subject to compromise. And abortion rights can’t really be separated from economics — being forced to carry an unwanted pregnancy is financially calamitous.

But I have to be honest: When I try to flesh out this critique, my heart isn’t in it. In 2014, Wendy Davis ran a boldly pro-choice campaign for governor and lost by more than 20 points. In 2022, some predicted that the end of Roe v. Wade could endanger Abbott; it didn’t. It’s hard to blame Hinojosa for trying something new.

Besides, as she often says, even if she wins, she will almost certainly have a Republican legislature. The best that can be hoped for, probably, is legislation to make Texas’ abortion ban less deadly. If Hinojosa wants to escape the culture wars in Texas, maybe it makes sense to admit defeat, at least temporarily. “While we’ve been fighting those fights, we’ve lost economic power in this state and in this country, and we’re hurting,” she said. “We need to come together to take back that power.”

Whether Texans are ready to do that is anyone’s guess. Jim Henson, the director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, still thinks Abbott is favored. He points out that in the polls, Democratic voters are significantly more committed to voting for Hinojosa than Republicans are to voting for Abbott. On the surface, that looks like good news for her, but it means that Abbott has more room to improve his standing with his base. “Abbott still has time to consolidate some of the Republicans that are not yet committed,” said Henson.

Still, he said, something is changing in Texas. A few weeks ago, Henson thought an Hinojosa victory was nearly impossible. Now he just thinks it’s unlikely. If only Talarico were to win, as he’s increasingly favored to do, “it’s going to be an earthquake,” said Henson. If Talarico and Hinojosa win, it will be a whole other order of magnitude. “People are feeling the ground shaking,” he said. “It’s just a matter of how big it is going to be.”

If it’s big enough, we’ll feel the reverberations from coast to coast. Conservatives triumphed when they were able to brand the Democratic Party as the stronghold of elites. Hinojosa thinks she can turn that association around, showing voters that Republicans represent heedless, exploitative oligarchs. “It’s 99 percent of us against like 15 billionaire dudes and the weak leadership that allows them to get away with whatever they want,” she said. If that argument can prevail in Texas, it can probably prevail most anywhere.

text:
$SBUX $CMG merger offers the wrong kind of synergy.  The overlap between the two brands is unlikely to be enough to justify a takeover premium.

The Financial Times
October 9, 2026

Putting the band back together is surely a great feeling, but a dubious corporate strategy. Starbucks chief Brian Niccol has considered a merger with Chipotle, his $41bn rival — and former employer — the FT reported on Thursday. However neat the match might seem from Starbucks’ corner office, it makes little sense for shareholders.

Niccol knows Chipotle very well indeed. He ran the Mexican-themed restaurant chain for six years before decamping in 2024 to the world’s biggest coffee chain, which was then in a state of considerable disarray. Seen from afar, the two do faintly similar things, serving comestibles to customers who are in a hurry. Both have large, sometimes restive workforces.
Moreover, the ways in which they differ might seem from a distance like opportunities. Chipotle’s balance sheet is free of debt; gearing it up a little could provide low-hanging fruit. And while Starbucks has a sprawling global network, Chipotle has yet to venture outside the US, apart from a smattering of international stores. 

But do these companies really belong together? Not really. For one, the overlap is unlikely to be enough to justify a takeover premium. Imagine Niccol could shave 10 per cent off Chipotle’s food, drink and packaging costs and halve its general overheads. That would save $770mn a year, Lex reckons using Royal Bank of Canada forecasts, giving an after-tax return on investment of just 6 per cent. Anything below 10 per cent should make investors nervous.

More importantly, Niccol hasn’t finished fixing up his present employer, making this a poor time to take on his old one. Starbucks shares have gone sideways since the day his appointment was announced. Profitability isn’t yet where it used to be. Same-store sales growth of 8 per cent in the latest quarter suggests the company has turned a corner, but recent numbers are still flattered by the previous year’s decline.

Chipotle has fared much worse, as has most of the US restaurant sector. But for Niccol to argue he can do a better job than its current leadership might be somewhat problematic, since Chipotle chief Scott Boatwright was his direct report for six years. Conversely, keeping the brand separate and its leaders in place — the Starbucks boss spent more than a decade at multi-brand restaurant group Yum Brands — would further trim the potential cost savings.

Perhaps it’s just that Niccol could use some more motivation. After all, the generous $100mn-plus package he received in 2024, linked to the company’s share price, has mostly failed to pay out. Worse, having started his role in sunny California, he now spends significant time in rainy Seattle. Starbucks should want to keep Niccol engaged, but buying Chipotle is too high a price.
john.foley@ft.com

text:
How come a Dutchman became King of England?

William of Orange became King of England because English elites invited him to overthrow James II in 1688, and Parliament then offered the crown jointly to him and his wife Mary.

James II had become king in 1685. He was openly Catholic, appointed Catholics to military and civil posts, and was seen as trying to restore Catholic power and rule without Parliament.

 His second wife, Mary of Modena, gave birth to a son in June 1688 (James Francis Edward Stuart). That son would have taken precedence over James’s Protestant daughters and raised the prospect of a lasting Catholic dynasty
.
 A group of leading English politicians—the “Immortal Seven”—then wrote to William, stadtholder of the Dutch Republic and husband of James’s elder daughter Mary, inviting him to intervene.

William already had strong reasons to act. He was the leading Protestant prince in Europe, locked in rivalry with Louis XIV of France, and feared that a Catholic, pro-French England would isolate the Dutch.

 In November 1688 he landed at Torbay with a Dutch army and English and Scottish supporters. James’s support collapsed;
 he fled to France in December. The episode is known as the Glorious Revolution because it involved relatively little fighting in England.

In early 1689 a Convention Parliament declared that James had abdicated by fleeing and offered the throne to William and Mary together. Mary was the legitimate Protestant heir in the line of succession; William insisted on being king in his own right, not merely consort, and was accepted as such.

 They reigned jointly until Mary’s death in 1694; William then ruled alone until 1702. 
The settlement was confirmed by the Bill of Rights (1689), which limited royal power and barred Catholics from the throne.

So the “Dutchman” was not a foreign conqueror in the ordinary sense. He was the Protestant nephew and son-in-law of the deposed king, brought in by English invitation to secure a Protestant succession and a constitutional monarchy aligned against France.

So how many Dutch soldiers did he have compared to James?

Thought for 1s

I’ll check the contemporary estimates for William’s landing force and James II’s army in 1688.William landed with fewer soldiers than James could field, but they were better troops, and James’s army fell apart before a real battle.

William’s invasion force in November 1688 was mostly Dutch regulars from the States Army. The usual figures are about 15,000 Dutch soldiers—one detailed count is 15,269—plus roughly 1,000 to 5,000 volunteers, mainly English and Scottish exiles and French Huguenots.

 Overall estimates for the army he brought ashore run from about 14,000–16,000 to around 21,000. They came in a fleet of roughly 400–500 ships.
 To cover the Dutch border against France, the Republic hired German and other troops to replace the units sent to England.

James II had expanded the English army after the Monmouth rebellion. On paper it was around 30,000 men, sometimes given as high as the mid-30,000s, with Scottish and Irish contingents in England pushing the theoretical total nearer 40,000. 

Trained, available troops were closer to 25,000–30,000; many were new recruits, and others were tied down in garrisons. 

At Salisbury Plain his concentrated force is said to have outnumbered William’s by about two to one—on the order of 24,000–30,000 ordered to assemble there.

The numbers never decided the campaign. James’s officers, including John Churchill (later Duke of Marlborough), defected;
 large parts of the army melted away; and James lost confidence and withdrew toward London, then fled to France. By early December only a few thousand of the Salisbury force remained. William’s Dutch Guards later took over the palace at Whitehall. So James started with the larger army; William had the more reliable one, and political collapse did the rest.

How many soldiers did James have at Salisbury Plain

Why did James's army melt away?

What was the difference in quality between the armies?

So how did he have so many men to start with, why did they all quit?

James had a large army because he had deliberately expanded it after 1685, and it fell apart because key officers had already decided not to fight for him and his own confidence collapsed.

After the Duke of Monmouth’s rebellion in 1685, James used the scare to turn a modest peacetime force into a standing army of roughly 30,000 men in England, sometimes listed on paper in the low-to-mid 30,000s.

 Before that the English establishment was nearer 9,000–16,000. He kept many of the new regiments, paid them from revenue that did not need fresh parliamentary grants, reviewed them on Hounslow Heath, and put Catholics into commands.

 Scottish and Irish units brought into England pushed the theoretical total higher still. A lot of the extra men were recent recruits, not long-service professionals.

They did not all quit at once, and the rank and file were less disloyal than the officers. What happened at Salisbury in late November 1688 was a chain of defections at the top.

 Several senior officers, including John Churchill, later Duke of Marlborough, had already been in touch with William. On the night of 23–24 November Churchill went over; other officers followed. James, already ill with heavy nosebleeds and convinced he could not trust the army, ordered a retreat toward London even though his men on the plain outnumbered William’s by about two to one.

 Once the retreat started, units dispersed. By 10 December only about 4,000 of the roughly 30,000 ordered to concentrate were still with the colors, and James fled to France.

The motives were mostly political and professional, not pay.
 Protestant officers disliked James’s Catholic appointments, his use of the dispensing power, and the risk of a Catholic dynasty after the birth of his son in June 1688.

 Many also saw William, husband of the Protestant heir Mary, as the safer side once the invasion was ashore.
 Irish Catholic troops in the army were widely distrusted by English soldiers, which made cohesion worse. 
Commissions were property; officers who feared a purge or a lost cause had a strong incentive to switch early. The Dutch professionals opposite them stayed intact, so the larger English army never fought a pitched battle.

So how many of his men would have been Protestant? How many catholic? how many Irish?

Thought for 3s

I’ll look up the religious and national makeup of James II’s army in 1688.
Most of the army James had in England in 1688 was still Protestant and English.

 Catholics and Irishmen were a minority, but a very visible one.
On the English establishment, John Childs’s figures—the standard ones—put Catholic officers at about 11 percent, a little over 200 men. 

That share was higher at the top: about 27 percent of field officers, and a disproportionate number of regimental commanders.
 Among the rank and file, Catholics were roughly 15 percent. James himself thought there were no more than about 1,000 Catholic soldiers; later counts suggest more than that, largely because of the Irish units he had shipped over.

 A recent survey of commissions finds under 10 percent of English officers were Catholic. So of an English army of around 30,000, something like 25,000 or more were Protestant.

The Irish contingent in England was small but politically explosive. 
James ordered about 2,500–2,800 men over from the Irish army in late 1688—battalions of the Foot Guards, Granard’s, Hamilton’s, and related units. 

They were not exclusively Catholic or exclusively Irish: when they were later counted, those regiments still contained 200 or more Protestants.

 Propaganda treated them as a Catholic Irish occupation force anyway.
 The separate Irish army at home was much more Catholic. By 1686, of about 7,500 men, roughly two-thirds of the rank and file and 40 percent of the officers were Catholic, and Tyrconnell’s purge continued after that. 

Those troops mostly stayed in Ireland; only the detachments above reached England. A Scottish contingent of nearly 3,000 was also brought south.
That mix helps explain the collapse.

 The bulk of the English regiments were Protestant, and their officers had little reason to fight a Protestant heir’s husband once senior men such as Churchill changed sides. 

The Irish Catholic companies were the part of the army the English public and many English soldiers already distrusted, so they sharpened the panic without being numerous enough to hold the force together.

So basically his soldiers were Protestants and they would not fight for a Catholic King

Mostly Protestant, yes. A simple refusal to fight for a Catholic king, no.

The English army in 1688 was overwhelmingly Protestant—about 85 percent of the rank and file, and close to 90 percent of the officers.
 Those men had already fought for James against the Protestant rebel Monmouth in 1685.

 Religion alone did not make them unwilling to serve him.
What broke the army was narrower. 

Senior Protestant officers, Churchill chief among them, had decided James’s Catholic policies and the birth of a Catholic heir made his regime a bad risk, and some were already in touch with William.
 
When those officers defected at Salisbury, James lost his nerve and ordered a retreat even though he still outnumbered William.
 Units then dispersed. Ordinary soldiers followed their officers or went home once the army started to fall apart; they did not stage a mass mutiny on confessional grounds.

The Irish Catholic detachments, only about 2,500–2,800 men, made the politics worse without being large enough to hold the force together.

 So the army was Protestant, and that mattered, but it quit because its leaders changed sides and the king stopped trusting it, not because Protestant soldiers as a body would not fight for a Catholic monarch.

What happens when survivors seek justice, but gaps in coordination, limited support and unclear institutional mandates stand in the way?

From overlapping institutional mandates and inadequate funding to provide basic necessities for survivors and perpetrators, to the lack of appropriate custody facilities for children in conflict with the law; participants confronted realities demanding urgent attention. 

Yet, the SGBV Information Hub offers hope for stronger collaboration, coordinated advocacy and improved responses.

The question is no longer just what the law says, but how effectively it protects people.

Let’s collaborate, coordinate and strengthen accountability for a safer Cross River.

•  9:5, the so-called sword verse: when the sacred months end, “kill the polytheists wherever you find them and capture them and besiege them and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they should repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, let them go on their way.” The exit offered is conversion and Islamic practice, not a permanent peace with unbelief. Ibn Kathir records the view that this verse abrogated earlier peace agreements; al-Hasan al-Basri is quoted as calling it valid until the Day of Judgment. Other classical exegetes, including al-Tabari, limited it to treaty-breaking Arab polytheists of that campaign. Both readings exist; the expansive one is not a modern invention.
•  9:29: “Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day… from those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled.” Ibn Kathir treats this as the order, after the pagans were subdued, to fight Jews and Christians until they accept Islam or pay the poll tax in a state of submission. The stated ground is their refusal of Islamic belief and law, not only a specific attack.
•  8:12, tied to Badr: God tells the angels he will “cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike them upon the necks and strike from them every fingertip.” 8:60 tells believers to prepare force “to terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy.” 3:151 repeats the casting of terror into unbelievers’ hearts. “Terror” here is a Quranic term for the psychological effect of military violence, not a later slogan.
•  47:4: “When you meet those who disbelieve, strike their necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, then secure their bonds,” after which ransom or release is allowed. 8:39 and 2:193 say fight until fitnah ends and “religion is for Allah.” 9:111 frames killing and being killed in God’s cause as a purchased bargain with paradise.

•  “I have been ordered to fight the people until they testify that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish prayer, and pay zakah.” (Sahih al-Bukhari 25; also Muslim.) The condition for stopping the fight is Islamic confession and practice.
•  “I have been made victorious through terror (cast into the hearts of the enemy).” (Sahih al-Bukhari 2977.)
•  “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.” (Sahih al-Bukhari 6922; also in other collections.) Classical jurists of the four Sunni schools treated unrepentant apostasy as a capital offense. The Quran itself threatens apostates with hell (3:86–91, 4:89) but does not spell out an earthly death penalty; the death penalty comes from hadith and fiqh. Some modern writers limit the hadith to treason in wartime. That is a narrowing, not what the standard legal manuals say.

text:
Pentagon confirms Fort Hood shooter’s firing squad execution will be livestreamed

The Pentagon has said the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, a revelation about plans for the first military execution in more than 65 years.

The Army announced this week that the execution would take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in the 2009 shooting at the base.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had earlier told Real America’s Voice, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” Pentagon officials clarified on Thursday that it would be livestreamed, with more details to follow, The Associated Press reports.

Experts offered mixed reactions. Fordham law professor Deborah Denno said it could make the process “much more transparent.” UC Berkeley’s Elisabeth Semel, however, questioned the government’s motivation, saying, “This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver.”

Hasan could file a habeas petition in civilian court, which experts say could significantly delay the execution.

🇮🇳⚓ INS Mangrol to Join Indian Navy on 12 October | Indigenous Anti-Submarine Warfare Ship Ready for Commissioning...
The Indian Navy is set to commission INS Mangrol, its third Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft (ASW-SWC), at the Naval Dockyard in Mumbai on 12 October 2026. Built by Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL), Kochi, the ceremony will be presided over by Vice Admiral Sanjay Vatsayan, Flag Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Western Naval Command.
⚓ Built with over 80% indigenous content, INS Mangrol is designed to detect and counter underwater threats in coastal and shallow waters. Its equipment includes the Abhay hull-mounted sonar, lightweight torpedoes, an indigenous anti-submarine rocket launcher and the Mareech Advanced Torpedo Decoy System.
Powered by three diesel engines with waterjet propulsion, the vessel offers high manoeuvrability in shallow waters. It can also undertake underwater surveillance, low-intensity maritime operations and mine warfare-related tasks.
🇮🇳 Named after the coastal town of Mangrol in Gujarat, the warship reflects India's growing indigenous capabilities in naval shipbuilding and anti-submarine warfare. Its induction will strengthen the Indian Navy's ability to protect ports, harbours and coastal approaches against underwater threats.

Analysis and Answer by Grok on Starlink in Bharat!.
@AshwiniVaishnaw
@narendramodi
@NitinNabin, @sambitswaraj
@ncbn, @PawanKalyan
@gauravbhatia,
Starlink is not yet commercially available in India (as of October 2026). It holds a GMPCS licence and IN-SPACe authorisation, but security assessment, FDI approval, and spectrum assignment are still pending for Starlink and the other licensed satcom operators. Expected drawbacks, based on global experience and Indian conditions, are as follows.

Cost and affordability
Hardware (dish + router) is widely estimated at roughly ₹20,000–35,000 (some reports cite around ₹33,000). Monthly plans are expected in the ₹3,000–7,000 range, with some estimates near ₹3,000–4,200.
That is several times the price of fibre or fixed wireless from Jio, Airtel, or BSNL (often ₹900–1,600 for hundreds of Mbps). India Today and survey coverage note the service could take a large share of average household income and that most users want prices closer to existing broadband.
Without subsidies, it is poorly suited to mass rural or low-income use.
Capacity and performance limits
Officials have said Starlink-type capacity in India may support only about 2 million connections in total, on the order of 40,000–50,000 per district, with speeds typically capped around 200 Mbps.
It cannot replace fibre or 5G fixed wireless at scale in cities. Real-world speeds vary with congestion, and heavy use (4K streaming, large downloads, gaming) can face throttling after priority data is used.
Latency is usually better than older geostationary satellite links but still higher and less consistent than fibre, which matters for competitive gaming and some real-time applications.
Weather, heat, and power
Heavy rain, dense cloud, and fog can temporarily slow or interrupt the link (rain fade).
User terminals have been reported to throttle or shut down in extreme heat; Indian summers are a practical risk.
The dish needs continuous power. Areas with load-shedding or unstable voltage lose service unless the user adds solar or UPS backup, raising the real cost.
Installation and coverage constraints
A clear view of the sky is required. Buildings, trees, and dense urban clutter block the signal, so it is weaker as a city broadband substitute.
Setup is more involved than plugging in a fibre ONT or mobile hotspot.
Security, control, and sovereignty issues
Indian rules require traffic through local gateways, lawful interception, no routing that bypasses Indian gateways via inter-satellite links, border monitoring zones, and the ability to deny service in specified areas. Analysts (including Takshashila) note these are hard to verify independently in orbit and depend heavily on the operator.
Precedents (Ukraine/Crimea coverage decisions, unlicensed use reported in places such as Iran) have fuelled concern that a foreign operator could keep service on, or turn it off, in ways that diverge from Indian government priorities during a crisis.
Border and coastal spillover is a related issue: beams do not stop at the frontier, and service authorised in neighbouring countries can complicate control.
Data-handling and AI-training clauses in Starlink’s privacy terms have also been flagged in Indian commentary.
Market fit
In cities and many towns, fibre and 5G already offer cheaper, often faster, lower-latency service. Starlink is mainly relevant for remote, hilly, island, maritime, disaster, or enterprise sites where terrestrial networks are absent or unreliable.
Competition from OneWeb (Bharti-backed) and Jio’s satellite plans, plus ongoing security reviews, adds regulatory and commercial uncertainty.
In short, the main disadvantages for India are high upfront and recurring cost, limited capacity, weather and power sensitivity, and unresolved questions of governmental control over a foreign-operated constellation. It is best viewed as a niche complement to terrestrial networks, not a mass-market replacement, once it is actually cleared to launch.

You are not contradicting my point, but rather confirming it:

1. Tribute ≠ dependence. Medri Bahri paid tribute (like livestock) purely to maintain autonomy or secure protection, stopped paying entirely during other eras, and at one point paid dual tribute to both Ethiopia and the Ottomans simultaneously just to safeguard its independence.

2. Wasn’t I referring to short-lived presences? Rulers of the Eritrean highlands held sea access since the medieval era, which is why Ethiopia sought a connection by granting the autonomous territory kingdom status as Medri Bahri. This gave Ethiopia coastal access only from 1448 until the 1557 Ottoman invasion, followed by nothing until 1955—meaning just 100 out of the last 1,300 years. 
3. Ethiopia simply wanting sea access is not the point. Their goal is establishing a military naval presence while requesting Eritrean sovereignty. Commercial sea access has already been offered and welcomed by Eritrea, as it benefits both nations economically.

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. text:
No One Was Paying Attention to Gina Hinojosa a Month Ago. Now Republicans Are Worried.

NYT Gift Article link
Listen · 18:54 min
09OCT2026
By Michelle Goldberg
https://t.co/8PQWFKHojZ
Opinion Columnist, reporting from East Texas.

Lynn Davenport, a lifelong conservative, met Donald Trump backstage at a Texas rally in 2016. On Jan. 6, 2021, she was at his Stop the Steal rally in Washington, though she left before the Capitol was sacked. In 2024, she was a delegate to Texas’ Republican convention and a Republican precinct chair.

And in May, she filmed an ad for Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running a surprisingly competitive race to become governor of Texas.

The two women have been friends for years, since Hinojosa, a state representative from Austin, helped lead opposition to a crusade by the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, to privatize Texas’ public school system. Abbott’s agenda was bitterly opposed by some conservative Texans, particularly rural ones in places where public schools are the center of the community. (Think “Friday Night Lights.”) Davenport was impressed by Hinojosa’s willingness to listen to her, and by her mastery of education policy. Still, as a committed Republican, she didn’t think she’d ever vote for her.

But Davenport has grown increasingly disgusted with Abbott, over both schools and the data centers he invited into Texas. The governor, she said, is a “globalist. Which to me is scarier than a communist, a socialist or a Marxist, because what Abbott is imposing is technocracy. He’s giving the tech giants carte blanche in Texas.” So she decided not just to support Hinojosa’s bid for governor, but to do it publicly. “Gina is someone that I can work with, whereas Abbott doesn’t care what I think,” she told me.

The premise of Hinojosa’s surprisingly competitive campaign is that there’s a critical mass of voters like Davenport in Texas. The opportunity for Democrats, Hinojosa believes, lies not with moderate, affluent Republicans put off by Trump’s norm-smashing vulgarity, but with disappointed MAGA populists. “The conventional political wisdom is that it is those country club Republicans who will swing over,” she told me before I traveled to Texas. “I think it’s always been MAGA.”

I was skeptical of this analysis then, and after seeing her campaign last week, I’m still not wholly convinced. Trump’s appeal has never been only or even primarily economic; he taps into fear and rage about a country growing less white, less Christian and less deferential to male authority. And Hinojosa seems, at least on paper, ill suited to appeal to Trump’s base. A Latina and a former labor lawyer, she comes from the heart of Texas’ Democratic establishment: Her father led the state Democratic Party from 2012 until 2025. Though she now calls herself a “populist” rather than a “progressive,” she’s one of the more liberal members of the Texas House.

Still, Hinojosa has a group of supporters like Davenport, people furious at Abbott over school privatization and data centers. Mary Lowe, an education activist and a self-described “fundamental Christian,” told me that Abbott is “a globalist. He’s a tyrant. He’s a great deceiver.” And though she’s voted Republican in almost every primary and every general election since 1979, she’s voting for Hinojosa in November. “She’s a good human,” said Lowe. “She’s one of us.”

Several polls still show Hinojosa trailing by a couple of points, but three recent ones, including a New York Times/Siena poll released on Saturday, have her ahead. The polling aggregator Real Clear Politics now rates the race as a tossup, and last week Cook Political Report moved it from “likely” to “lean” Republican. Over the past week, national Democrats have started investing more heavily in the race: Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois and the Democratic Governors Association each gave Hinojosa $1 million.

“She certainly has a much better chance than I did in ’22,” said Beto O’Rourke, who challenged Abbott four years ago and lost by more than 10 points.

Part of that chance derives from Trump’s unpopularity and the country’s economic misery, which is particularly stark in Texas. Campaigning, Hinojosa talks about how the state has more people without health insurance than any other, and some of the nation’s highest rates of small-business bankruptcies. She describes blood plasma centers popping up in middle-class areas — she visited one next to a Sephora — as more people seek to sell their plasma to make ends meet. Hinojosa told me about meeting a lobbyist for the plasma center industry who was excited about all the opportunity in the state. “That’s, I think, a shocking example of where we are in Texas in 2026,” she said.

But her surge can’t be attributed entirely to the economic environment: Hinojosa seems to be hitting her stride as a politician. She’s long had a talent for making people feel heard, but O’Rourke said she’s become dramatically better on the stump. “I campaigned with her in El Paso a few weeks ago, and I’ve never seen her speak so well,” he said.

Her message is simple: Life has gotten too hard for hard-working people in Texas. Schools are underfunded — hundreds have gone to four days a week — and new artificial intelligence initiatives are no substitute for a good teacher in the classroom. Data centers are both a blight and a symbol of Abbott’s misplaced priorities. “It’s impacting people’s homes and lives, and it is a demonstration of the governor doing the bidding of moneyed interests and leaving the people to fend for themselves,” Hinojosa told me. Taking a page from Trump, she’s promising $1,500 checks for every Texan from the state’s plush rainy-day fund — she calls it the “Greg Abbott Corruption Tax Refund” — and to “DOGE” the Department of Education’s dodgy vendor contracts.

It’s a platform, she insists, that can break through with those who in the past have felt alienated from the Democratic Party. “When I sit down with people who voted for Trump, with people who voted for Abbott, and hear them, and they hear me, there’s an opportunity for connection and alliance,” she said. Democrats have a chance, she insists, to move past the cultural battles that have kept them perennially on the defensive. “If we try to be post-culture wars, we can be post-culture wars,” she said. “I’ve experienced it. I’ve seen it.”

Of course, deep rifts over religion, race and gender can’t simply be wished away. But if Hinojosa can find a way to make them less salient, it could portend not just seismic change in Texas, but the beginning of a political realignment. If some fraction of socially conservative voters conclude that rapacious billionaires threaten them more than supercilious liberals, it would remake America’s political map. For decades now, we’ve lived in an era dominated by what scholars call post-material politics, in which values, identity and self-expression have often taken precedence over economic concerns. What if that era is coming to an end? What opportunities would that open up, and what ideological sacrifices would it require?

In May, speaking to my colleague Lulu Garcia-Navarro, Tucker Carlson said that culture war issues — the issues on which he’d built much of his demagogic career — were becoming less important than matters of concentrated wealth and financial precarity. “Most of the debates about race, ethnicity, religion, to some extent immigration, are less resonant long-term than debates about economics,” he said. Hinojosa’s campaign is a bet that he was right.

She is, of course, far from the only Democrat running as a populist and seeking to persuade disaffected Trump supporters. Zohran Mamdani started his mayoral campaign by interviewing working-class Trump voters in Queens and the Bronx, and he won over a small but meaningful chunk of them. A New York Times/Siena poll showed the populist Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan — whom Carlson has all but endorsed — winning 8 percent of people who voted for Trump in 2024.

But it’s one thing to run as an economic progressive in places that regularly elect Democrats. It’s quite another to do it in Texas, in many ways the spiritual home of the modern right. Sure, Texas looks more promising for Democrats this year than it has in decades, with the party’s Senate candidate, James Talarico, maintaining a consistent lead over the Republican Ken Paxton. But Paxton is singularly sleazy and widely despised. As astonishing as a Talarico victory would be, Republicans could explain it away as the fault of a particularly bad candidate.

They won’t be able to do that if Hinojosa wins. Abbott has been elected governor of Texas three times by double-digit margins. If Hinojosa even comes close to beating him, it will be because the Republican coalition that Trump assembled is collapsing, and a new Democratic one is perhaps starting to take shape. “There are people who are responding to our message the same way they were responding to Trump’s message,” she said. “They want power. They want to feel like they’re in control of their lives again, and I think that they want to return to a time that feels like it makes sense again, where hard work pays off.”

A big part of the reason Hinojosa is pulling ahead is that Latinos, who swung toward Republicans in 2024, have soured on the party due in large part to Trump’s brutal mass deportation campaign. At a Spanish-language town hall last week, Hinojosa, whose mother is a Mexican immigrant, mentioned ICE’s fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who’d been in the country for 35 years. “They thought he was someone else, they killed him, and then they realized that he was only going to work,” she said. “When that’s happening, none of us are safe.”

But Hinojosa is also trying to chip away at Abbott’s — and Trump’s — white, rural base. No one thinks she’s going to win these voters outright; the goal is to lose them by less. “There’s definitely a backlash against Abbott over vouchers and over data centers in rural Texas,” said Suzanne Bellsnyder, who writes a newsletter called Texas Rural Reporter. “The question is, does that anger against Abbott translate into a vote for Gina?”

Bellsnyder is trying to make sure it does. A former field director for Abbott, she’s now working for Hinojosa’s campaign. “If I didn’t think she had a chance, I promise you, I wouldn’t be putting my entire Republican credentials on the line,” she told me.

Like Davenport, Bellsnyder got to know Hinojosa during the fight against Abbott’s education agenda. The centerpiece of this battle was Abbott’s voucher bill, which gives most qualifying private school parents about $10,000, reducing funding that otherwise would have gone to public schools. When Abbott tried to pass the law in 2023, he was foiled by 21 Republican holdouts. Abbott then supported primary challenges, partly funded by the Pennsylvania billionaire Jeff Yass, against 15 of the Republicans who thwarted him. Most of them lost, and the law passed in 2025. The wounds among anti-voucher conservatives are still raw.

At an Hinojosa rally in Longview, a city in East Texas, last week, I met Steve Clugston, a 58-year-old school superintendent. Clugston told me he last voted for a Democrat back in the 1990s, when conservative local officials in his part of the state still belonged to the party. “They’re now probably Republicans,” he said.

Clugston voted for Donald Trump in 2024, believing he did a “pretty good job” in his first term. He is, he said, an “old school conservative,” which is reflected in his approach to education. “I still swing the paddle,” he said. (Texas is among a minority of states that allow corporal punishment in schools.) “I believe in kids acting right and learning how to work hard and how to show up and be dependable.”

But he was livid about Abbott’s relentless push for vouchers. “Our governor took billionaire money and then used it to beat Republicans that us Republicans elected,” he said. As he soured on Abbott, he’d also grown disillusioned with Trump and his flagrant, gluttonous corruption. “When you’ve lied to me enough,” said Clugston, “and sold us out for billionaires, I get to the point I’m done.”

Hinojosa’s inroads with the populist right might have been limited to those most committed to public schools, were it not for Abbott’s enthusiasm for data centers. The governor has aggressively sought tech investment in Texas; he’s offered billions in tax incentives to attract data centers and last year boasted that the state was “the epicenter of A.I. development.” Texas now has more in operation than any other state.

Many rural Texans who either live near these behemoths, or fear they will soon, detest them. Anger is so intense that Sid Miller, the state’s outgoing agriculture commissioner — he lost his primary after a series of scandals — told Rolling Stone that it could cost Abbott the election.

In June, Cheryl Shadden, who lives across from a sprawling bitcoin mine in Hood County, showed up at an Hinojosa event in Glen Rose, Texas, wearing a homemade T-shirt that said “Break Rank.” She meant break ranks with the Republican Party, which has failed to protect her from the ugly, noisy facility that she said has upended her life.

“My community is blasted with horrific noise 24/7,” Shadden told me. “I mean, inside of our homes, outside of our homes. We’ve got health problems associated with it.” She says the value of her property — 10 acres and a barn — has plummeted. And the Republicans she’s reached out to for help have ignored her. “I hit everybody and their mother, and crickets, and then Gina Hinojosa’s staff is like, ‘Gina would like to speak to you.’”

Abbott has realized that fury over data centers is a political threat, and he recently issued a moratorium on new development, pending an audit of their energy and water usage. But the pause has loopholes, and the audit, conveniently, is due to be finished right after the election, which means he can restart his data center push once the political danger is gone. “It just stinks. It’s just not right,” said Michael Ellis, a 70-year-old Republican battling plans for a new data center in Texas’ Navarro County.

I met Ellis and his wife, Jennifer, in the town of Corsicana, about an hour southeast of Dallas, where Hinojosa stopped to meet with a small group of anti-data-center organizers. Ellis had come with a binder; he had blueprints of a proposed 80-acre facility slated to go up a mile from his home. He was worried about noise caused by generators, water usage and the danger of an industrial disaster in an area with only a volunteer fire department. He blamed Abbott for welcoming such projects in with virtually no oversight.

Michael was still undecided about who he was voting for, but Jennifer was leaning toward Hinojosa. “Just to walk in and sit down with us and meet with us, to me, that goes a long way,” she said. “That’s massively impressive.”

Then I asked her about the Senate race. She said she’d probably vote for Paxton, despite his many scandals, because of trans issues. “I don’t do all the gender thing,” she said.

It was a reminder of the culture wars’ endurance. Hinojosa still isn’t terribly well known in Texas; in September, she told me that some 20 percent of the electorate wasn’t familiar with her. I wondered what voters like Ellis would think of her after Abbott, who is outspending Hinojosa around 6 to 1, blankets Texas with attack ads. One recent spot tried to brand her as “gender bender Gina,” a radical out to “trans your kids.”
Hinojosa has tried to pre-empt this caricature in her own advertising, seeking to distance herself from social liberalism without recanting her previous positions. In one ad, she declared, “My pronouns are ‘mom,’ ‘Texan’ and soon to be ‘governor.’” In another, she described deciding, 23 years ago, to carry a pregnancy to term even though her baby had no chance of survival. “I chose her,” she said. The spot doesn’t mention the law that now denies Texas women the choice that she had. If I saw it without knowing who Hinojosa was, I might have thought she was anti-abortion.

She’s not, but on the campaign trail, she doesn’t talk about abortion unless she’s asked. Even then, she says her priority in office will be fixing the law that prevents doctors from treating some women with doomed pregnancies until they’re near death. “Reproductive choice is just one of those issues that divide us,” she told me. “I’m running to be governor to work on an agenda that the vast majority of us agree on.”

I could probably write a whole column picking apart this strategy. Reproductive rights are popular, even in red states. It would be disastrous for Democrats to decide, at this moment of intense social backsliding, that women’s health and freedom should be subject to compromise. And abortion rights can’t really be separated from economics — being forced to carry an unwanted pregnancy is financially calamitous.

But I have to be honest: When I try to flesh out this critique, my heart isn’t in it. In 2014, Wendy Davis ran a boldly pro-choice campaign for governor and lost by more than 20 points. In 2022, some predicted that the end of Roe v. Wade could endanger Abbott; it didn’t. It’s hard to blame Hinojosa for trying something new.

Besides, as she often says, even if she wins, she will almost certainly have a Republican legislature. The best that can be hoped for, probably, is legislation to make Texas’ abortion ban less deadly. If Hinojosa wants to escape the culture wars in Texas, maybe it makes sense to admit defeat, at least temporarily. “While we’ve been fighting those fights, we’ve lost economic power in this state and in this country, and we’re hurting,” she said. “We need to come together to take back that power.”

Whether Texans are ready to do that is anyone’s guess. Jim Henson, the director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, still thinks Abbott is favored. He points out that in the polls, Democratic voters are significantly more committed to voting for Hinojosa than Republicans are to voting for Abbott. On the surface, that looks like good news for her, but it means that Abbott has more room to improve his standing with his base. “Abbott still has time to consolidate some of the Republicans that are not yet committed,” said Henson.

Still, he said, something is changing in Texas. A few weeks ago, Henson thought an Hinojosa victory was nearly impossible. Now he just thinks it’s unlikely. If only Talarico were to win, as he’s increasingly favored to do, “it’s going to be an earthquake,” said Henson. If Talarico and Hinojosa win, it will be a whole other order of magnitude. “People are feeling the ground shaking,” he said. “It’s just a matter of how big it is going to be.”

If it’s big enough, we’ll feel the reverberations from coast to coast. Conservatives triumphed when they were able to brand the Democratic Party as the stronghold of elites. Hinojosa thinks she can turn that association around, showing voters that Republicans represent heedless, exploitative oligarchs. “It’s 99 percent of us against like 15 billionaire dudes and the weak leadership that allows them to get away with whatever they want,” she said. If that argument can prevail in Texas, it can probably prevail most anywhere.

This clown has a late night advertisement claiming, "Trump is the biggest fraud".  The irony.   Ellison caught on audio with a questionable relationship with the Somali fraudsters.   

From Grok
The audio is a roughly 55-minute secret recording of a December 11, 2021 meeting between Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and people later tied to the Feeding Our Future fraud case.

It was made without Ellison’s knowledge, apparently by Ikram Mohamed, who was later charged and pleaded guilty in the scheme. The file sat on the evidence list in Aimee Bock’s federal trial and was first published in April 2025 by the Center of the American Experiment. It resurfaced again in late 2025 and 2026 as more defendants pleaded guilty and as Republicans questioned Ellison in Congress.

Feeding Our Future was the nonprofit at the center of what prosecutors called the largest pandemic fraud case in the U.S.: about $250 million in federal child-nutrition money claimed for meals that were largely never served. FBI raids came in January 2022, about a month after this meeting.

What is on the tape, according to reporting from CBS Minnesota, Fox News, American Experiment, and others:

- Attendees, including later defendants such as Salim Said (convicted) and Ikram Mohamed, presented themselves as the “Minnesota Minority Business Association.” They said state agencies were cutting off reimbursements because of racism, xenophobia, and Islamophobia, and they asked Ellison to intervene.
- Ellison is heard treating the complaints as legitimate. Reported lines include “Of course, I’m here to help,” “Let’s go fight these people” (referring to the state agencies checking the claims), “I’m telling you, sue, sue, sue,” and that he already had his team looking into it and would call education officials for explanations. He also said this had not come to his attention until then, and that Governor Tim Walz agreed agencies were unfairly driving small East African businesses out.
- The group talked about votes and campaign money as the way to protect their interests. Ellison is reported to have replied “That’s right” to a comment about putting dollars behind candidates who would protect them. His office says he rejected an implicit offer of campaign support.

Nine days later, on December 20, 2021, Ellison’s campaign accepted four $2,500 contributions ($10,000 total). One donor was Gandi Mohamed, Ikram’s brother and a later defendant. Critics say that undercuts Ellison’s claim that he took nothing from people connected to the meeting. His campaign says the donations were returned once the fraud links were known; reporting indicates some returns came only in 2025, after the tape became public. A separate later donation from defendant Liban Alishire was returned in 2022.

Ellison’s position is that he met constituents in good faith, did not know they were involved in fraud, did nothing they asked, and later helped federal prosecutors. In an April Star Tribune op-ed he wrote that he “took a meeting in good faith with people I didn’t know and some turned out to have done bad things. I did nothing for them and took nothing from them.” His office has also said his September 2022 claim of being “deeply involved for two years” in holding Feeding Our Future accountable referred to the office’s legal work, not personal knowledge of this meeting.

Critics, including House Majority Whip Tom Emmer and Sen. Josh Hawley, argue the tape shows him offering to use the AG’s office against the agencies investigating the group, then accepting related donations, and that this clashes with later statements that he knew little and took no money. No criminal charge has been filed against Ellison over the meeting.

text:
Can someone explain to me exactly how Rob Pelinka supposedly lowballed Marcus Smart? Because the numbers tell a rather interesting story. 🤔

The Lakers reportedly offered approximately $9 MILLION for one season.

Houston signed him for $12.43 MILLION over TWO seasons, approximately $6.06 million in the first year and $6.37 million in the second, with a player option.

So Smart reportedly turned down roughly $9 million for one season to accept about $6 million in his first season with Houston.

And somehow we’re supposed to believe Pelinka insulted him financially? 😂

Now, let’s be fair. Smart apparently wanted more long-term security, and that’s perfectly understandable. But wanting a longer contract and being lowballed are two different things.

He averaged 9.3 points per game during the regular season. Yes, he played good defense and had a strong playoff run. Nobody is denying his contribution.

But he’s also 32 years old, with an injury history. Was Pelinka supposed to ignore all that and hand him a lucrative multiyear contract simply because Smart believed he deserved one?

What exactly did Smart expect? $15 million annually? $20 million? Three or four guaranteed years?

If Houston offered him the situation he preferred, including a reunion with Ime Udoka and being closer to family, good for him. That’s his decision.

But don’t confuse a disagreement over contract length and guarantees with being financially disrespected.

And since the exact Lakers offer hasn’t been fully disclosed, perhaps Smart should explain the complete terms before repeatedly accusing the organization of lowballing him.

Because from what has been reported, Pelinka offered him more money for the coming season, Smart chose Houston for less, and now Pelinka is somehow the villain.

Sorry, but something isn’t adding up. 💜💛

ES Morning Market Report | October 9, 2026

As discussed in yesterday’s end of day report, the Globex session was going to be critical in determining which side could capitalize on yesterday’s volatility. With an overnight high of 7853.50, buyers have pushed ES back into a neutral to bullish position and, more importantly, reclaimed 7830.

Yesterday sellers had everything they needed. They broke 7800, printed an RTH low of 7783, and had an opportunity to establish value inside the lower distribution. They failed. Buyers reclaimed 7815.75 into the close, and overnight they have now carried that momentum through 7830. That sequence represents important market generated information.

Over the last two weeks, ES has methodically worked through 7757, 7763, 7780, 7800, 7815.75, 7830 and 7848, eventually reaching 7897.50, just short of the 7905.50 ATH. Despite multiple attempts to auction lower, buyers continue to defend the structure and rebuild value at higher prices.

The key this morning is 7830. As long as buyers continue developing time and volume above this level, the auction remains constructive. The weekly high and 7905.50 ATH become the natural magnets above. Buyers do not need to sprint higher. Holding 7830 and allowing value to migrate higher would arguably be the healthier development.

Buyer Scenario

Buyers have already completed the first objective by reclaiming 7830. The next test is whether they can hold it during RTH. Acceptance above 7830 keeps 7848 and the 7853.50 Globex high immediately in play. Above there, attention shifts back toward 7897.50 and the 7905.50 ATH.

The strongest bullish setup would be a controlled test of 7830 that attracts responsive buyers, followed by value developing higher. That would reinforce the argument that yesterday’s break below 7800 was a failed auction and potentially provide the foundation for another ATH attempt.

Seller Scenario

Sellers are now back in a difficult position, but they are not eliminated.

Their first opportunity is rejection of the 7848, 7853.50 area followed by a move back below 7830. Losing 7830 would return 7815.75 to the board.

Below there, 7800 remains the structural line in the sand.

We have now seen repeated penetrations of 7800 without sustained acceptance. If sellers want to materially change this auction, they need more than another sweep. They need time and volume below 7800. Accomplish that and 7780, 7763 and 7757 reopen. Fail again and another population of shorts risks becoming fuel for buyers.

The two week structure is telling us something important. Sellers have repeatedly generated downside movement, but they have struggled to convert that movement into lower value. Buyers, meanwhile, continue reclaiming lost territory.

That keeps the advantage with buyers as long as 7830 holds.

text:
@Soteriology101 @Whosoeverwills @DPGBehler 
A working sketch of Bobby Grow’s @cum_granosalis books on Evangelical Calvinism vis-à-vis Christ’s vicarious humanity: two volumes co-edited with Myk Habets: 
•Evangelical Calvinism: Essays Resourcing the Continuing Reformation of the Church 
•Evangelical Calvinism, Volume 2: Dogmatics and Devotion 
→ 
The second volume is organized around the vicarious ministry of Christ. The same program is developed at length on his blog and in the fifteen theses that introduce the project.

The first move is methodological. Grow argues that many modern debates about salvation—classical Calvinism versus Arminianism, sovereignty versus free will, limited versus general atonement—begin in the wrong place. They start from soteriology, usually inside what he calls a Latin or Augustinian frame, and then try to fit Christ into that frame. He wants the order reversed. Thinking should begin with Christology, specifically with the hypostatic union: the place where Almighty God and humanity “kiss.” 

Jesus is not an instrument executing a prior decree. He is the electing God and the elected human in one person. Election, atonement, faith, and human agency are then read from that center rather than from an abstract mass of humanity standing before an abstract will of God.

That center is the vicarious humanity of Christ. 

The Son assumes real human nature, not a generic or partial humanity, and in that nature lives the whole human response to the Father: faith, repentance, obedience, worship, and intercession. The point is not only that Christ dies instead of us, but that Christ is human for us. Our humanity has its true ground in his recreated, resurrected humanity. Grow often puts this in Athanasian rather than Augustinian terms: salvation is ontological and participatory before it is merely juridical. God does not first set up a contract and then apply its benefits to selected individuals. God gives himself. Grace is “all the way down.” There is no independent natural platform from which a fallen person first decides to join God.

From this follow two claims that must be held together.

First, Christ’s work is for all humanity. Thesis 11 states that Christ lived, died, and rose again for all, so Evangelical Calvinism affirms universal atonement. Grow follows Torrance here: this is a finished work, not a mere possibility. By the incarnation there is a “carnal” or objective union of the Son with humanity as such. 

Election is christologically conditioned: humanity is elect in the Son’s assumption of human nature, not by an absolute decree that first splits the human race into two classes. The gospel can therefore be preached as already true of the hearer: Christ has bound himself to you before and apart from your believing.

Second, this is not universalism. Thesis 12 is explicit. Universal redemption does not entail that all will finally be saved. Grow distinguishes the objective inclusion of humanity in Christ from the subjective, Spirit-given realization of that inclusion. “Spiritual union” is a sharing in the one union already wrought in Jesus. Faith is not an independent human contribution that completes an incomplete work. It is the Spirit enabling a person to echo Christ’s own Yes to the Father—often with appeal to *pistis *Christou as the faith of Christ. Baptism and conversion, on this telling, are a living into a reality that is already true, not the first creation of that reality.

Rejection remains real. Grow can say that some “opt out,” refuse the grace given in Christ, and so condemn themselves. He cites Torrance to the effect that Christ has already made the person his own, and that even if someone refuses him and damns himself, that love does not cease. The refusal does not undo the incarnation or turn Christ’s Yes into a No. It is a contradiction of what God has done, and that contradiction becomes its own judgment.

What this is not, on Grow’s own terms, is a symmetric libertarian choice to “stay or leave,” as if the human will stood outside the work of Christ and then selected one of two equal options. He affirms something like total inability: fallen humanity is *incurvatus *in *se and cannot move toward God from an abstract free will. The initiative is Christ’s. Our Yes is participation in his Yes. Our No is possible, tragic, and self-condemning, but it is not the same kind of act as a first decision to join God. 

Grow thinks the usual dilemma—either God irresistibly saves the elect, or the human will is the decisive co-cause—still belongs to the older causal and contractual grammar. He wants agency relocated inside the vicarious humanity of the Son and the ministry of the Spirit, rather than treated as a rival sovereignty.
The resulting picture can be summarized without slogans:

•God has already said Yes to humanity in the incarnate Son.
•All humanity is objectively included in that Yes; redemption is not a limited offer waiting to be activated by the right kind of decision.
•No one is saved apart from personal faith, but that faith is a sharing in Christ’s own response, not a climb from outside into God’s favor.
•Final exclusion is possible as refusal of a gift already given, not as proof that Christ never represented that person.
•The “limit” of the atonement is not a restricted list of individuals chosen in a decree. It is the vicarious humanity of Jesus himself: the One for the many.

That is the framework Grow is gesturing toward when he tells interlocutors that starting from soteriology keeps Calvinists and non-Calvinists at loggerheads, and that the place to begin is the hypostatic union. As a description of what he is saying, this seems to be the shape.
