Walter Bezanson on the "Melville conspiracy" at Yale:

>> I am still grateful for the privilege offered to Yale graduate students of American literature in 1937. It was a turning point in the re-discovery of Melville and his works. Merton Sealts, Harry Hayford, and I, after sharing a seminar, became co-conspirators to rescue Herman for posterity. Then Stanley Williams, our mentor, called me into his study one day and said, “Walter, I have a great topic for your dissertation. How would you like to work on— Cooper’s Sea Tales? There’s room for a good book there.” I thanked him, but clung to the Melville conspiracy. As for Cooper? “I’d prefer not to,” I told him. 

For I had already discovered that Melville in his late years was reported to have written the longest poem in American literature, and that it was still unavailable to an audience, unread, and declared un-readable. Melville, an unreadable poet? What a challenge! In all innocence, I bet a Ph.D. that I could read, and perhaps rescue, Clarel, a Poem and Pilgrimage in the Holy Land; 2 vols. 1876—if I could find a copy." <<

text:
The Marshmallow Test – Why Civilizations Live and Die on Patience

At Stanford, around 1970, a psychologist put a marshmallow in front of a four-year-old and offered a deal: eat it now, or wait fifteen minutes and get two. Then he left the room. Years later, the children who waited did better at school, at work, and in life. Everyone took the lesson to be about children. The real lesson is about civilizations.

1. The test. Watch the videos and you will laugh. Children cover their eyes, sing to themselves, kick the table, and lick the marshmallow without biting it. Some eat it before the door closes. You know these people – some of them are your colleagues, and one of them is you at 11 pm in front of the fridge.

2. The twist. In 2012, researchers ran the test again with one change. First, an adult promised the children better crayons and came back with nothing. Then came the marshmallow, and those children barely waited. Children whose promise had been kept waited four times longer. Patience is not only character. It is trust: you wait only if you believe the second marshmallow will really come.

3. Economists call this time preference: how much you value now over later. The interest rate is simply the price of waiting. Every civilization is a marshmallow test at scale. You plant a tree whose shade you will never sit in, you build a cathedral over three generations, you save for children you have not yet had.

4. The broken promise. Communism was the crayon experiment run on a whole nation. In Poland, money lost its value, savings vanished, and the state could take what you built. So people learned to eat now. If something appeared in the shop, you bought it, whether you needed it or not. It wasn’t because Poles were impatient. It was because they had learned the adult never comes back.

5. The four-year child. A politician has four years, and the bill arrives after he leaves. Public debt is a simple trick: we eat the marshmallow, and our children pay for both.

6. Money that rots. Inflation tells you that waiting is for fools. A decade of near-zero interest rates told every saver in Europe that the second marshmallow had been cancelled. So we got "buy now, pay later", credit for holidays, and an economy built around eating it now. Then the phone finishes the job: one-click buying, endless scrolling, a new reward every few seconds. It’s a machine designed to make sure you never have to wait for anything again.

7. The lesson. Civilization is not having more marshmallows. It is the ability to wait for them, and that ability rests on trust: stable money, safe property, promises kept. Destroy that trust and you get a nation of four-year-olds eating sweets, which is exactly what you then complain about.

The West blames its people for living for today. But it was never the children who failed the test. It was the adults who broke the promise – and then sold them more marshmallows on credit.

text:
"Socialism heroically fights problems unknown in any other system."

Yes – this guy was one of our most brilliant intellectuals. Meaning a guy producing real understanding – not vapid commentary dressed up as depth. One sentence of his explains more than a shelf of political science.

1. The law. First the system creates the problem. Then it creates an office to fight the problem. Then it blames the people for the problem. Then it asks for more power to fight harder. Every step looks like a solution, and the whole thing is a trap.

2. The proof. In Poland we lived under these absurdities for 45 years. The state fixed the price of meat, so meat disappeared. Then came ration cards for meat. Then people sold meat privately at its real price, so the state made that a crime called "speculation" and set up special bodies to hunt the speculators. It was a problem unknown in any other system, and the state fought it heroically.

3. The queue. We got to know the machine deeply, from the inside, standing in line. You queued first and asked what was being sold later. People walked home wearing toilet paper rolls on a string around their necks, like trophies. And we learned to laugh about it. A man walks into a shop: "No meat?" "No, sir, here we have no fish. No meat is across the street."

4. The merriest barrack. We were called the merriest barrack in the communist camp. Other barracks were grimmer. We laughed at the queues, at the Party, and at ourselves, with jokes whispered at work and told loudly at weddings. The system had the army, the police and the press. We had the punchline.

5. The joke as knowledge. The laughter was not an escape. It was understanding. A good joke is a model of the system that fits into ten seconds. "They pretend to pay us, and we pretend to work" is a whole economics textbook in one line. The communists could censor newspapers, but they could never censor the joke.

6. The man. Stefan Kisielewski, known as Kisiel – the name of a sweet fruit jelly. He was a composer and a columnist, and readers opened the Catholic weekly from the last page, where his column was. He was the only public figure in communist Poland to openly praise capitalism from the parliament rostrum. In 1968 he called the regime a dictatorship of dimwits. Days later, "unknown attackers" beat him in the street. The tongue out was his method: a regime that demands to be taken seriously fears nothing more than a man who laughs at it – and is right.

7. The West today. Germany shut down its nuclear plants, then fought an energy crisis. Berlin capped rents, then fought a shortage of flats. Brussels writes rules that strangle industry, then launches plans to save European competitiveness. Each time, the problem is new to them. It was not new to us.

We laughed because we knew. The West does not laugh yet, because it still believes. The jokes come later – right after the queues.

text:
Parkinson’s Law – Why the State Bureaucracy Grows When the Work Shrinks

In 1955, a British naval historian wrote a joke for The Economist. Seventy years later, it remains one of the most accurate descriptions of the modern state ever written. Everyone knows the slogan: work expands to fill the time available. Almost no one knows the mechanism underneath it. That mechanism explains Europe.

1. The evidence. Between 1914 and 1928, the Royal Navy lost two thirds of its largest warships. Over the same years the Admiralty – the office that ran the ships – grew by three quarters. There were fewer ships and more men behind desks. Then there was the Colonial Office, which kept growing while the colonies left one by one. It was hiring while the empire was shrinking.

2. The first mechanism. An official who feels overworked has three choices. He can resign, he can share the work with a colleague, or he can ask for two subordinates. He never chooses the colleague, because a colleague is a rival. Two subordinates are a rank. So one tired man becomes three. Then each of the two subordinates feels tired.

3. The second mechanism. Seven people now do what one did, and they keep each other busy with drafts, approvals, and comments on the approvals. Everyone works hard, and nothing is produced. You have been in this meeting. You have been copied on this email. You have watched three people sign the form that one person filled in.

4. The law of triviality. Parkinson noticed that a committee will approve a nuclear reactor in minutes, because nobody understands it. The same committee will debate the bicycle shed for an hour, because everybody does. Bureaucracy does not avoid the important question by accident. It avoids it by design – the small question carries no risk, and on the big one, someone’s name goes on the decision.

5. The ratchet. A business that fails closes. A department that fails gets a bigger budget, because the problem is now bigger. Failure is the bureaucracy’s best argument for itself. This is why the state never shrinks on its own: every problem it does not solve becomes a new office for solving it.

6. The civilizational lesson. Burnham described the managers taking over. Parkinson showed how they breed. Put the two together and you get Brussels. You get France, where the state spends more than half of everything the country produces and still cannot fix a hospital. This is not because the people inside are wicked. It is because the machine works exactly as Parkinson said it would.

7. The vindication. Parkinson was dismissed as a humorist. Then Milei cut Argentina’s ministries in half – and the country did not collapse. It barely noticed, except on the bill. The lesson is simple: you cannot reform a bureaucracy by asking it what to cut. It will always propose to cut the ships – and hire someone to manage the cut.

text:
I'll say what a lot of people in finance won't say out loud.

Plenty of jobs out there still pay $16 to $22 an hour. Full-time, that's roughly $2,770 to $3,810 a month before taxes.

Now go find rent under $1,600. Add a car payment, insurance, gas, groceries, utilities, your phone bill.

That's before health insurance comes out of your check. Before student loans. Before a kid gets sick and you're out $300 at urgent care. Before your car needs new brakes you didn't budget for.

I've worked in personal finance for over a decade, so believe me, I'm not anti-budget. Budgets matter.

But there's a point where telling someone making $19 an hour to "cut back more" stops being useful advice.

You cannot budget your way out of $3,600 in unavoidable monthly costs on a $2,900 paycheck. The math isn't a discipline problem.

Sometimes the spreadsheet isn't broken. The income is just too low to cover what it costs to be alive right now.

🎬 Monasteries, Visas, and Drones: How the Head of Rybar Was Preparing an Operation Against Montenegro Under the Cover of a “Documentary” ‼️‼️

New details surrounding the high-profile detention of Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the pro-Kremlin Rybar network, in the Montenegrin town of Risan confirm that Russian operatives came to the Balkans as more than just bloggers. Their objective was to produce a large-scale propaganda film aimed at undermining Montenegro’s European integration.

When Montenegrin police and the National Security Agency (ANB) detained Zvinchuk, his wife Valeria, and three associates, professional drones and electronic equipment were seized from the group.

Now, new information has emerged about what exactly this group was attempting to film — a network whose members are the subject of a US reward offer of up to $10 million for information.

Rybar’s Official Version: “We Were Just Filming a Monastery”

Following the detention, Rybar’s official channels immediately released a statement insisting that the group was in Montenegro entirely legally.

Their official cover story appeared as “innocent” as possible: they claimed to have arrived to film the Cetinje Monastery, the principal religious site of the Metropolitanate of Montenegro and the Littoral, and even claimed to have obtained official permission from the clergy.

The use of religious themes is a classic hallmark of Russian intelligence services seeking to legitimise their presence in the Balkans, where religious issues are particularly sensitive.

The Real Objective: Targeting Tourism and European Integration

However, sources within Montenegro’s defence sector speaking to the newspaper Vijesti revealed plans that were far less “spiritual”.

Montenegrin intelligence services had reportedly been monitoring the Russians from the moment they entered the country.

According to these reports, the real purpose of Zvinchuk’s “documentary” was to produce manipulative content surrounding Montenegro’s alignment of its visa policy with European Union standards.

What was the alleged information operation designed to achieve?

• Discrediting the EU: Russian propagandists allegedly intended to convince Montenegrins that complying with Brussels’ requirements to tighten visa regulations would supposedly “kill” the country’s economy.

• Targeting tourism: The film was allegedly intended to generate panic over Montenegro losing tourists — and, consequently, tourism revenue.

• Promoting the “Serbian World”: The central narrative of the film allegedly portrayed the European path as destructive, while presenting a return to a pro-Russian alliance with Belgrade as Podgorica’s only salvation.

Government Response: Defending Montenegro’s European Future

Montenegro’s Prime Minister, Milojko Spajić, quickly commented on the detention of Zvinchuk, whom some analysts identify as a colonel in Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.

He emphasised that state institutions had acted decisively and pre-emptively:

“The message following today’s successful operation, in which the head of the Rybar information network was detained, is clear: Montenegro is defending its interests, and no one will jeopardise our European future.”

This incident is further evidence of how Russia treats filmmaking, media, and religion as weapons.

The detention of Zvinchuk’s group in Risan is not simply the arrest of bloggers. It represents the disruption of an alleged large-scale Kremlin hybrid operation being prepared directly in NATO’s backyard.

📌 Sources: Vijesti, RTCG, Meduza, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, UK Government.

🎥 #America_suffered_a_strategic_defeat_against_Iran: #Robert_Pape and #Netanyahu set victory at a #mobilization_of_900000_to_1_5_million ground troops and an #invasion_of_Iran, a country of #93_million and #80_percent_mountain. The Iran war exacts a storm penalty at the midterms👇👇

👈 Malcolm Nance @MalcolmNance, former U.S. military-intelligence analyst and author, speaking with Anna Smith on The Trump Report:

✅ 1 – Claims
🔺1.1 No American president has ever joked about nuclear weapons, or about another country using them against the United States. Trump’s remark on Los Angeles and San Diego is of that kind, and the joke cannot be separated from the intent.
🔺1.2 The United States has suffered a strategic defeat in the Iran war: momentum, initiative, and escalation dominance are gone. Robert Pape’s condition for victory is mobilization; Benjamin Netanyahu put the figure at 900,000 to 1.5 million ground troops and an invasion of Iran, a country of 93 million and 80 percent mountain. The blockade neither zeroes out oil nor secures passage.
🔺1.3 The price of gasoline and diesel, not deportation and ICE, is the storm penalty of this war at the midterms. Taking Congress does not, by itself, stop the war.

✅ 2 – Arguments
🔺2.1 The claim that the nuclear remark is unprecedented is historical, not an intelligence reading. If no president has ever, even in jest, spoken of an enemy’s nuclear strike on the United States, the case is unique, whether or not the adversary takes it seriously.
🔺2.2 Joke and intent must be distinguished, and on this reading they cannot be. He offers the remark as entertainment, yet the psychological analysis treats it as joking and not joking. The sole power to unleash atomic war, without anyone else’s consent, turns the same sentence from a quip into a danger.
🔺2.3 Pathological lying is why intent cannot be read. If the documented count stopped at 33,000 in the first term and the estimate is now 83,000, the listener has no separate standard for believing this sentence. Age about 80, bodily infirmity, and clear signs of rising dementia increase that ambiguity.
🔺2.4 The target is not the opposing city. San Diego is relatively liberal, yet it is the West Coast bastion of the U.S. military, and on this estimate about 60 percent Republican. California is the world’s fourth-largest economy. Hatred of whatever is not Trump himself has taken the place of conservatism.
🔺2.5 The intelligence reading follows the citizen’s. The adversary hears domestic rhetoric meant to excite a base of hate, not an operational threat. If Trump is serious only when the matter touches his family and his wallet, then from the Soviet contact of 1987 through Putin, Kim, and Xi he is unserious and easily manipulated.
🔺2.6 Justification of the war is not the enemy’s capability. Iran has no intercontinental ballistic missile; “let them take out Los Angeles” justifies a war he started. North Korea has such missiles, an unstable ruler, and tested, viable atomic weapons, and Trump says nothing to Kim. One side wishes death on domestic enemies at the hands of foreign enemies; the other gives a pass to those who could actually hurt the United States.
🔺2.7 Strategic defeat is not one battle. If the momentum and initiative of the first weeks are gone, the United States is dancing to Iran’s tune. Air power and blockade do not replace ground force. Pape’s only way to win is mobilization; Netanyahu stated the 900,000 to 1.5 million. That is a condition, not a plan now under way.
🔺2.8 Mountains and population make the condition heavier. If Iran’s mountains make Afghanistan look like a flat beach, and if Iranians know America better than Americans know Iran, an insurgency would make the first ten years in Iraq look like child’s play. The figure is a condition of winning, not a guarantee.
🔺2.9 Cover is not escort. A plotted point, helicopters, and aircraft cover the ship; daily anti-ship missiles and drones do not. Safe passage is therefore a claim. The quieter reporting of strikes comes from the end of ship-for-ship retaliation, not from safer water.
🔺2.10 Zero exports are not zero oil. Oil remains in the ground and in tanks, and neighbors still trade. An economic-outcast plan, if no one accepts it, does not complete a blockade. With no regional port open, and steaming times of days to weeks, the blockade cannot be sustained.
🔺2.11 The midterm penalty is separate from tolerance of authoritarianism. The base accepted mass deportation, children in court, and ICE; it cannot tolerate expensive gasoline, long assumed cheap and plentiful. Diesel moves food and goods, and every extra dollar is passed to the public.
🔺2.12 What Congress can do and what will happen are different. Purse strings from January are possible, but if the White House treats Congress as a Duma and refuses to seat the winners, the result is not an end to the war. A near-civil-war scenario is possible, not established.

✅ 3 – Evidence and indications
🔺3.1 At a Nebraska rally, on energy costs and the Iran war, Trump called the war a small price and said let them take out Los Angeles and San Diego. Staff tried to clean it up; he doubled down. As he spoke, USS Abraham Lincoln was returning after a year underway, with Pete Hegseth aboard.
🔺3.2 The lie count stopped at 33,000 in the first term; the estimate now is 83,000. The speaker was conservative most of his life, “up there with Co and Pal,” and now, on the chart, lower-left.
🔺3.3 San Diego centers the West Coast military. The estimate offered is about 60 percent Republican. California is the world’s fourth-largest economy.
🔺3.4 First contact was the Soviet Union in 1987. Putin is cast as a mentor, Kim Jong Un as a dictator who summarily executes, Xi Jinping as taking the lead in global production.
🔺3.5 Iran has no ICBM capability. North Korea has ICBMs, an unstable ruler, and tested, viable atomic weapons.
🔺3.6 The only way to win, as Professor Robert Pape is cited, is mobilization and invasion. The figure of 900,000 to 1.5 million ground troops is attributed to Benjamin Netanyahu. Iran has 93 million people and is 80 percent mountainous. The speaker has been to Afghanistan and says Iran’s mountains make it look like a flat beach. Children would throw rocks, women Molotov cocktails.
🔺3.7 Oil pushed past $100 a barrel. Iran–Oman transit talks did not lower the risk. The Navy is not escorting; it holds the eastern side of the Strait of Hormuz, perhaps putting service personnel or merchant captains aboard. Ships black out, run at night, and hug the coast.
🔺3.8 UKMTO, not Lloyd’s, documented 13 successful ship attacks in seven days. They are heard less because Trump stopped ship-for-ship retaliation.
🔺3.9 The speaker lived in the UAE for ten years and went to Fujairah regularly; about 200 ships are always in the harbor. Outflow figures count oil piped from Habshan to Fujairah and loaded there. A ship was hit in Fujairah the day of the interview.
🔺3.10 Day 223 of the regular war, day 85 of the second phase. That phase began after small drones broke two tankers’ windows, then weeks of coastal bombardment and a blockade. Neighbors still trading: Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Russia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Turkey, and Iraq. Six Pakistani crossings. Diesel in Iran is about 10 cents a gallon. About 20 oil carriers southwest of India are running down.
🔺3.11 Scott Bessent was put in charge of Operation Economic Outcast, called an Israeli-inspired blockade of sea and neighbors; no one complied. No regional port is open, not even Oman. At the last Oman servicing call, drones hit the hotel, and Iranian television phoned live to ask if there was a fire. Bahrain and Kuwait are called destroyed. The UAE does not want warships in Fujairah. Nearest ports: Seychelles, Diego Garcia, Singapore — two weeks, ten days, and three days’ steaming. The other route is the Red Sea, the Houthis, and Israel.
🔺3.12 A car-transporter move was $600 to $700 before the war and is $3,000 to $4,000 now, prepaid, because road diesel is more than triple. A FedEx letter demands several hundred dollars in tariff on a shipment from Britain. The Supreme Court held the tariffs illegal; FedEx still bills the customer. The minimum wage is given as £525. A billion dollars is cited for a ballroom, and a cemetery plot for a memorial arch.
🔺3.13 The midterms are less than four weeks away. The claim is that 85 percent of independents have flipped and almost all Latino support is gone, after a 2024 win among Latino men. Deportation of 20 million is cited, including cleaners at Mar-a-Lago, and 5,000 children under 10 in court alone, with cartoons. John Fetterman is named as the Pennsylvania Democrat said to be talking of flipping. A reported plan would place 10,000 personnel of a Spanish security firm, named Surigore, at post offices, and ICE, the FBI, and the military around polls. The speaker is 65; his family served from 1864 to last year, almost 162 years.

✅ 4 – Conclusions
🔺4.1 The city remark is both unprecedented and domestic rhetoric. The world reads it as excitement of the base, not as Iranian capability. The capability that exists is North Korea’s, and Trump says nothing to Kim.
🔺4.2 There is no coming back on present means. Pape’s only way is mobilization and invasion; Netanyahu’s figure is 900,000 to 1.5 million, against 93 million people and 80 percent mountain, at the price of an insurgency worse than Iraq’s first decade. The blockade can drive exports toward zero; it does not zero the oil, and the United States lacks the will, the economic capacity, and the ports to sustain it.
🔺4.3 Cover does not make passage safe. Thirteen hits in seven days, and Fujairah oil counted as safe outflow, show that a barrel figure is not an escort.
🔺4.4 The midterm penalty is gasoline and diesel, not ICE. If Democrats take the House, and perhaps the Senate, control of the purse from January is not the same as being seated. Refusal to seat them is a dangerous scenario, not a fact. This is the worst the speaker has felt in his life.

text:
🎥#آمریکا_در_جنگ_از_ایران_شکست_استراتژیک_خورد: #رابرت_پِیپ و #نتانیاهو خواهان #بسیج_۹۰۰_هزار_تا_یک_و_نیم_میلیون نیروی زمینی برای #حمله_به_ایران_۹۳_میلیونی_و_۸۰_درصد_کوهستانی اند. مجازات طوفانی جنگ ایران در میان‌دوره‌ای‌ها👇👇

👈 مالکوم ننس @MalcolmNance، تحلیلگر پیشین اطلاعات نظامی آمریکا و نویسنده، در گفت‌وگو با آنا اسمیت در برنامهٔ ترامپ ریپورت:

✅ ۱ – ادعاها
🔺۱.۱ هیچ رئیس‌جمهور آمریکا دربارهٔ خوردن شهر خودی با سلاح هسته‌ای دشمن شوخی نکرده است. حرف ترامپ دربارهٔ لس‌آنجلس و سن‌دیگو از این جنس است و شوخی از قصد جدا نمی‌شود.
🔺۱.۲ آمریکا در جنگ ایران شکست استراتژیک خورده است: شتاب، ابتکار و برتری تشدید رفته. رابرت پِیپ و بنیامین نتانیاهو راه پیروزی را بسیج ۹۰۰ هزار تا یک‌ونیم میلیون نیروی زمینی و حمله به ایرانِ ۹۳ میلیونی و ۸۰ درصد کوهستانی می‌دانند. محاصره نه صادرات را صفر می‌کند و نه عبور امن می‌سازد.
🔺۱.۳ هزینهٔ بنزین و گازوئیل مجازات طوفانی همین جنگ در میان‌دوره‌ای‌هاست، نه اخراج و پلیس مهاجرت. گرفتن مجلس هم به‌خودی‌خود جنگ را متوقف نمی‌کند.

✅ ۲ – استدلال‌ها
🔺۲.۱ بی‌سابقگی حرف هسته‌ای ادعای تاریخی است، نه خوانش اطلاعاتی. اگر هیچ رئیس‌جمهوری حتی به‌شوخی نابودی شهر خودی را به دشمن نسپرده باشد، این مورد یکتا است، مستقل از آنکه دشمن آن را جدی بگیرد یا نه.
🔺۲.۲ تفکیک شوخی و قصد لازم است و، به این خوانش، شدنی نیست. حرف سرگرمی است، اما تحلیل روان‌شناختی آن را نا‌شوخی می‌کند. قدرت یک‌نفرهٔ گشودن جنگ اتمی همان جمله را از لطیفه به خطر تبدیل می‌کند.
🔺۲.۳ دروغ بیمارگونه مقدمهٔ نخواندن قصد است. اگر شمار دروغ از دورهٔ اول گذشته و هنوز بالا برود، شنونده معیار جدا برای باور این جمله ندارد. سن حدود ۸۰، ناتوانی بدن و نشانهٔ زوال عقل این ابهام را بیشتر می‌کند، نه کمتر.
🔺۲.۴ هدف حرف شهر مخالف نیست. سن‌دیگو لیبرال نسبی است، اما پایگاه نظامی غرب آمریکا و، به این برآورد، اکثریت جمهوری‌خواه. کالیفرنیا موتور چهارمین اقتصاد بزرگ جهان است. پس نفرت از هرچه خود ترامپ نباشد جای محافظه‌کاری را گرفته است.
🔺۲.۵ خوانش اطلاعاتی بعد از خوانش شهروندی می‌آید. دشمن حرف را تبلیغات داخلی برای پایگاه نفرت می‌فهمد، نه تهدید عملیاتی. اگر جدیت ترامپ فقط کیف پول و خانواده باشد، از تماس شوروی در ۱۹۸۷ تا پوتین، کیم و شی او را نا‌جدی و دست‌کاری‌پذیر می‌بینند.
🔺۲.۶ توجیه جنگ و قابلیت دشمن یکی نیست. ایران موشک قاره‌پیما ندارد؛ جملهٔ «بگذارید لس‌آنجلس را بزنند» توجیه جنگی است که خود شروع کرده. کرهٔ شمالی قاره‌پیما، حاکم ناپایدار و سلاح آزمایش‌شده دارد و ترامپ به کیم چیزی نمی‌گوید. یک سو مرگ برای دشمن داخلی است، سوی دیگر گذر برای دشمنی که می‌تواند بزند.
🔺۲.۷ شکست استراتژیک از یک نبرد نیست. اگر شتاب و ابتکار هفته‌های اول رفته باشد، ادامه با آهنگ ایران است. هوا و محاصره جای نیروی زمینی را نمی‌گیرد. به همین دلیل رابرت پِیپ و نتانیاهو شرط پیروزی را همان بسیج ۹۰۰ هزار تا یک‌ونیم میلیون می‌گذارند، نه طرحی که اکنون در جریان است.
🔺۲.۸ کوه و جمعیت همان شرط را سنگین‌تر می‌کند. اگر کوه ایران افغانستان را هموار نشان دهد و جمعیت ایران آشناتر به آمریکا باشد تا آمریکا به ایران، شورش دههٔ اول عراق بازی کودک است. پس رقم نیرو شرط بردن است، نه تضمین بردن.
🔺۲.۹ پوشش غیر از اسکورت است. نقطه، بالگرد و هواپیما کشتی را می‌پوشاند؛ موشک ضدکشتی و پهپاد روزانه را نمی‌پوشاند. پس تضمین عبور امن ادعا است. کم‌شنیده‌شدن ضربه‌ها هم از توقف مقابلهٔ کشتی‌به‌کشتی است، نه از امن شدن آب.
🔺۲.۱۰ صفر شدن صادرات غیر از صفر شدن نفت است. نفت در زمین و مخزن می‌ماند و مسیر همسایه باز است. طرح اخراج اقتصادی، اگر پذیرفته نشود، محاصرهٔ دریایی را کامل نمی‌کند. بدون بندر منطقه‌ای و با چند روز تا چند هفته بخار، محاصره پایدار نیست.
🔺۲.۱۱ مجازات میان‌دوره‌ای از تحمل استبداد جدا است. پایگاه با اخراج، کودک دادگاهی و پلیس مهاجرت مسئله نداشت؛ با بنزین گران مسئله دارد، چون بنزین در آمریکا ارزان فرض شده. گازوئیل غذا و کالا را جابه‌جا می‌کند و هر دلار به مصرف‌کننده می‌رسد.
🔺۲.۱۲ توان قانونی مجلس غیر از توان واقعی است. کنترل خزانه از ژانویه ممکن است، اما اگر دولت کنگره را مهر لاستیکی ببیند و نشستن را نپذیرد، نتیجه توقف جنگ نیست. سناریوی جنگ داخلی نزدیک ممکن است، نه ثابت.

✅ ۳ – شواهد و قرائن
🔺۳.۱ زمینه: ترامپ در تجمع نبراسکا جنگ ایران را بهای کم خواند و گفت بگذارید لس‌آنجلس و سن‌دیگو را بزنند. کارکنان کاخ سفید خواستند جمعش کنند؛ او روی حرف ماند. همزمان ناو هواپیمابر آبراهام لینکلن پس از یک سال دریا به بندر برمی‌گشت و پیت هگست، وزیر دفاع، روی کشتی بود.
🔺۳.۲ شمار دروغ تا ۳۳ هزار در دورهٔ اول، و برآورد کنونی ۸۳ هزار. گوینده خود را بیشتر عمر محافظه‌کار خواند، هم‌تراز کو و پال، و امروز در نمودار سیاسی پایین چپ.
🔺۳.۳ سن‌دیگو مقر ناوگان غرب است. برآورد مصاحبه حدود ۶۰ درصد جمهوری‌خواه. کالیفرنیا چهارمین اقتصاد بزرگ جهان.
🔺۳.۴ تماس شوروی با ترامپ ۱۹۸۷. پوتین رئیس‌جمهور روسیه و در این خوانش مرشد؛ کیم جونگ اون رهبر کرهٔ شمالی و اعدام‌کنندهٔ خلاصه؛ شی جین‌پینگ رهبر چین و در حال گرفتن صدر تولید جهانی.
🔺۳.۵ ایران فاقد موشک قاره‌پیما. کرهٔ شمالی دارای قاره‌پیما و سلاح اتمی آزمایش‌شده.
🔺۳.۶ رقم نیرو از رابرت پِیپ، استاد دانشگاه، و از بنیامین نتانیاهو، نخست‌وزیر اسرائیل، است: ۹۰۰ هزار تا ۱.۵ میلیون نیروی زمینی برای حمله به ایران. جمعیت ۹۳ میلیون و سرزمین ۸۰ درصد کوهستانی. گوینده خود به افغانستان رفته و کوه ایران را در برابر آن ساحل هموار خواند.
🔺۳.۷ نفت از ۱۰۰ دلار بشکه گذشت. گفت‌وگوی عبور ایران و عمان ریسک را پایین نیاورد. ناو شرق تنگهٔ هرمز را نگه داشته، شاید کاپیتان تجاری سوار کند. عبور شب، چراغ‌خاموش، چسبیده به ساحل، به امید به‌گل ننستن.
🔺۳.۸ یوکی‌ام‌تی‌او، مرکز تجارت دریایی بریتانیا، نه لویدز، ۱۳ حملهٔ موفق را در ۷ روز ثبت کرد. دلیل کم‌شنیده‌شدن توقف سیاست ضربه در برابر ضربه است.
🔺۳.۹ گوینده ده سال در امارات بوده و فجیره را مرتب دیده؛ همیشه حدود ۲۰۰ کشتی در بندر. رقم خروج هرمز نفت خط لولهٔ حبشان به فجیره را هم می‌شمارد. امروز یک کشتی در فجیره خورده است.
🔺۳.۱۰ روز ۲۲۳ از شروع جنگ منظم و روز ۸۵ از فاز دوم. فاز دوم پس از شکستن پنجرهٔ دو نفتکش با پهپاد کوچک، سپس بمباران ساحل. همسایه‌های هنوز در تجارت: پاکستان، افغانستان، ترکمنستان، روسیه، ارمنستان، آذربایجان، ترکیه، عراق. شش گذرگاه پاکستان. گازوئیل داخل ایران حدود ۱۰ سنت گالن. ناوگان حدود ۲۰ کشتی جنوب‌غرب هند ته کشیده است.
🔺۳.۱۱ اسکات بسنت، وزیر خزانه‌داری، مسئول طرح «اخراج اقتصادی» شد؛ مصاحبه آن را الهام‌گرفته از اسرائیل خواند و گفت هیچ همسایه‌ای نپذیرفت. بندر باز منطقه‌ای هیچ. آخرین پهلوگیری در عمان با پهپاد به هتل نیرو همراه شد و تلویزیون ایران زنده زنگ زد. بحرین و کویت نابودشده. امارات ناو در فجیره نمی‌خواهد. نزدیک‌ترین بندر سیشل، دیه‌گو گارسیا و سنگاپور است: دو هفته، ده روز، سه روز بخار. راه دیگر دریای سرخ، حوثی، اسرائیل.
🔺۳.۱۲ جابه‌جایی خودرو با تریلی پیش از جنگ ۶۰۰ تا ۷۰۰ دلار بود و اکنون ۳ تا ۴ هزار، پیش‌پرداخت. گازوئیل سر راه بیش از سه‌برابر. نامهٔ فدکس تعرفهٔ چندصددلاری از بریتانیا می‌خواهد، هرچند دیوان عالی تعرفه را غیرقانونی خواند. حداقل دستمزد ماهانه معادل ۵۲۵ پوند.
🔺۳.۱۳ میان‌دوره‌ای کمتر از چهار هفته. ۸۵ درصد مستقل‌ها برگشته و حمایت لاتین‌تبار تقریباً رفته. اخراج تا ۲۰ میلیون، از جمله نظافتچی مارالاگو، و ۵ هزار کودک زیر ده سال تنها در دادگاه با کارتون توضیح. جان فترمن، سناتور دموکرات پنسیلوانیا، در حرف چرخش به جمهوری‌خواهان. طرح ۱۰ هزار نیروی شرکت امنیتی اسپانیایی سوریگور در پست، و استقرار آیس، اف‌بی‌آی و ارتش دور صندوق. خانوادهٔ گوینده از ۱۸۶۴ تا پارسال در ارتش، حدود ۱۶۲ سال. سن او ۶۵.

✅ ۴ – نتایج
🔺۴.۱ حرف شهرهای آمریکا هم بی‌سابقه است و هم تبلیغات داخلی. جهان آن را هیجان پایگاه می‌خواند، نه قابلیت ایران. قابلیت واقعی به کرهٔ شمالی داده می‌شود و ترامپ آنجا ساکت است.
🔺۴.۲ جنگ ایران شکست استراتژیک خورده است. رابرت پِیپ و نتانیاهو شرط پیروزی را بسیج ۹۰۰ هزار تا یک‌ونیم میلیون و حمله به ایرانِ ۹۳ میلیونی و ۸۰ درصد کوهستانی می‌گذارند، و همان هم بردنی نیست مگر به قیمت شورشی بدتر از عراق. محاصره صادرات را کم می‌کند، نفت را صفر نمی‌کند، و بندر پایدار برای خودش ندارد.
🔺۴.۳ پوشش دریایی عبور امن نمی‌سازد. ۱۳ ضربه در ۷ روز و شمارش نفت فجیره نشان می‌دهد رقم خروج غیر از اسکورت است.
🔺۴.۴ مجازات طوفانی میان‌دوره‌ای هزینهٔ بنزین و گازوئیل است، نه اخراج و آیس. اگر دموکرات‌ها مجلس را بگیرند، کنترل خزانه غیر از نشستن نماینده است. امتناع از نشستن سناریوی خطرناک است، نه امر واقع. این بدترین احساس تمام عمر گوینده است.

✅اول، ریک، خیلی ممنون که دعوتم کردید.
🔺و به‌عنوان یک پدر، می‌دانم پر کردن باک چقدر خرج دارد. ۸۰ دلار برای یک باک بنزین. دیوانگی است.
🔺و بله، از توقف مالیات فدرال بنزین حمایت می‌کنم.
🔺اما یک چیز است که واقعاً این وضع را ساخته: جنگ در ایران. جنگی که رقیبم از همان اول برایش هورا کشیده و آن را برد، برد، برد خوانده.
🔺وقتی سر باک می‌روم، حس نمی‌کنم کشورمان در حال بردن باشد.
🔺هفت ماه گذشته، هشت ماه گذشته؛ این تا کی ادامه دارد؟
🔺می‌توانیم خیلی بهتر از این عمل کنیم. اما اگر این جنگ را متوقف نکنیم، اگر همین حالا متوقفش نکنیم، باز هم تماشا می‌کنیم که رژیم ایران تنگهٔ هرمز را در چنگ دارد، قیمت انرژی بالاتر می‌رود، و شما هم سر باک هزینه می‌دهید و هم در خواربارفروشی.

Washington is handing Greece $4B for defense. If it is Foreign Military Financing, almost all of it must be spent on American equipment.

That is how FMF works. The cash lands in Athens on paper and returns to US primes through FMS cases. The joint statement offers Greek industry one verb on cooperation. Explore.

Greece hosts the US Navy at Souda Bay and the port at Alexandroupolis moves US supplies toward Eastern Europe. Read that way, the package is payment for access, filed as interoperability. It suits Washington. For Athens it feeds a fleet of F-16s, Rafales and F-35s on 3 support chains, with the largest funding stream pulling toward one of them.

Alliance-wide interoperability is a standardization job the alliance works through its own bodies. A bilateral package tunes Greece to US forces first.

Watch whether the first FMS cases under the plan name Greek workshare.

text:
An older Black woman climbed down into a hole in a Houston street and lay flat on her back in the dirt, because it was the only way left to stop the digging. Her name is Dorris Ellis Robinson, and the gap she was lying in was exactly forty-five bricks wide, which happens to be the size of a grave. Those bricks were paid for and laid by hand by freed families after the city told them no for seven straight years.

The hole in the road was forty-five bricks wide.

That is not a figure of speech. A crew had lifted exactly forty-five of them out of Andrews Street in Houston's Fourth Ward, and the gap they left behind was roughly the length and width of a grave.

An older woman stood at the edge of it and looked down. Her name is Dorris Ellis Robinson, and she had spent years by then trying to keep machines off that particular stretch of pavement.

She had gotten a restraining order once. She had sat in meetings and written letters and stood in front of the city council, and none of it had worked, because the digging had started again that morning and it was still going.

She asked them to stop and they kept going, so she asked again.

"They didn't stop digging," she said later. "I mean, they were adamant."

Then she got down on her hands and knees at the edge of the hole, and lowered herself into it, and lay flat on her back in the dirt where the bricks used to be.

Forty-five bricks was just enough room for a woman's body.

That photograph now hangs at the entrance of an exhibit at the African American Library at the Gregory School, so it is the first thing a visitor sees walking in. A Black woman lying full length in a Houston street, staring up at the sky, surrounded by pavement that people keep trying to take.

"So I did whatever it took to save them," is how she put it. To understand why a woman would lie down in a road, you have to know what those forty-five bricks cost the first time.

Emancipation reached Texas on June 19, 1865, and within months the walking started. Freed families came up out of the Brazos River plantations along San Felipe Road, which ran straight into Houston from the southwest, and about a thousand of them stopped on the swampy south bank of Buffalo Bayou just west of downtown.

One formerly enslaved man remembered his owner, Charles Longcope, gathering everyone in June 1865 and reading them the proclamation from the doorway of his mansion. Then Longcope offered each of them a building lot out in the Fourth Ward, which tells you precisely what he thought that land was worth.

It flooded.

That was the whole reason it was available to Black people at all.

They took it and built on it anyway, and they named it Freedmen's Town. Within fifteen years it held the overwhelming majority of Black Houston, and by the 1930s it had produced more than four hundred Black-owned businesses.

People there still call it the Mother Ward, because Third Ward and Fifth Ward were poured out of it. One of the men who came was a Virginia-born preacher named Jack Yates, who had been enslaved and who reached Houston after the war.

In 1869 he bought a lot on Andrews Street, and in 1870 he built his house on it. Hold onto Andrews Street, because every single thing in this story happens on Andrews Street.

Three years after he laid his foundation, Yates did something they should teach in every school in Texas. On July 10, 1872, he and Richard Allen and Richard Brock and the Reverend Elias Dibble, all four of them formerly enslaved, closed on ten acres of land in Third Ward, bought from the Wellborn heirs for eight hundred dollars scraped together out of two congregations.

They bought it so Black Houston would have one piece of ground to hold Juneteenth on that nobody could put them off of.

They named it Emancipation Park, and it is still there.

Seven years out of bondage, and they were buying real estate for a holiday.

Now understand what those same families were living with underfoot. There was no pavement on their streets and there never had been, because the city of Houston did not pave Black neighborhoods.

When it rained, and in that part of Houston it rains, the road turned to standing mud. Catherine Roberts of the Rutherford B. H. Yates Museum has described the ordinary daily consequence of that, and it is the detail that stays with me.

Women in long skirts and petticoats had to step down off the walk and into the mud to reach the trolley.

Picture that on a Sunday morning.

Your good clothes, the ones you paid for and pressed, and you are ankle-deep in filthy water before you have gone twenty feet from your own door. In a neighborhood that flooded, that was a health problem before it was ever an indignity.

So they asked the city to pave the street. They asked in 1907.

They asked again in 1908, and in 1909, and in 1910, and the answer came back the same way every time.

No.

Six or seven years of petitions, from a community that by then had thirteen blacksmiths and thirty-four brick makers and installers living inside its own boundaries. These were not people who lacked the skill.

They lacked the permission. The city finally relented around 1914, and it attached a condition.

The work had to be given to a white contractor. Then the white contractor read the address and refused the job.

His reasoning is the part that should be printed on a wall somewhere. There were still unpaved streets in white Houston neighborhoods, and he was not going to be the man who handed Black residents something white residents did not have yet.

So the permit went out with a white-owned firm's name on it, Eureka Paving. And Eureka turned around and hired the brick men who already lived in Freedmen's Town, the same men whose neighbors had been petitioning for seven years, and charged the community a steep price for the work.

Sit with that arrangement, because it is the whole American arithmetic in one sentence.

They were not allowed to pave their own street until a white company was paid to hire them to pave their own street.

Some of the brick came out of a works owned by the Reverend Ned Pullum, a Fourth Ward minister who built a fortune on Pullum Standard Brick. A Black-owned brickyard, supplying a Black neighborhood, for a road the city refused to build.

They paid for it out of their own pockets. Then they went out after their own workdays and laid it themselves, by hand, one brick at a time.

Because they were the ones installing it, they got to decide how it went down. The families have always said the pattern set into that pavement came from home, carried across the water and pressed into a Texas road by people whose parents had been somebody's property.

Here the record deserves honesty instead of drama, because the sources disagree about which tradition it was. Roberts has described it as Yoruba, while others have pointed toward BaKongo cross designs out of West Central Africa.

The archaeologist Carol McDavid, who has worked in Freedmen's Town for years, has taken the position that the question deserves serious study before anybody tears the street up rather than after. Which is a careful scholar's way of saying the question is real and nobody has bothered to answer it.

What nobody disputes is whose hands were in the dirt.

For a stretch of decades that street was the center of everything Black Houston had. Then the twentieth century came for it, and it came in pieces, and every single piece was a decision made by somebody sitting in an office.

In the 1930s, land was cleared for the City Hall complex and Black residents were moved off it. In 1944 the housing authority opened San Felipe Courts, a thousand units of public housing for white families only, built on top of blocks of the oldest part of Freedmen's Town.

They sited it next to the city incinerator. It did not admit a single Black family until 1968.

In the 1950s the freeway came through and cut what was left of the ward in half. Then the arithmetic did the rest, and none of the arithmetic is disputed.

The Fourth Ward held nearly seventeen thousand people in 1910. By 1980 the remaining residential strip was down to fewer than 4,400.

Almost half of them were living below the poverty line. Only five percent owned the roof over their heads.

That is the neighborhood a young photographer walked into in 1970 with a camera he had bought himself.

Earlie Hudnall Jr. was born in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, in 1946. His father took pictures of the family, but it was his grandmother Bonnie Jean who made him what he became.

She sat out on the porch in the summer with a can of Garrett snuff and told stories out of the family album. That book was not just birthdays.

She kept obituaries in it. She kept newspaper clippings in it, and two of those clippings never left him.

One was about a Navy flyer shot down in Korea, which was Jesse L. Brown, out of Hattiesburg. The other was about a man taken out of a jail in Poplarville, Mississippi, by a mob in 1959.

He was ten years old when his parents sat him down and told him what had happened to Emmett Till.

Those clippings and his father's pictures, he has said, taught him young that somebody had to write down what happened to their own people. Then he added four words about it.

"That was the start."

He carried a small camera into Vietnam as a Marine. When his tour ended he wanted to reenlist and his mother refused to hear it, so he applied to the art program at Texas Southern University instead, hopped the Greyhound, and rode across the South to Houston at twenty-two.

At TSU he found the muralist John Biggers, who became his mentor and gave him a three-word instruction he has been repeating for fifty years. Art is life, Biggers told him, so draw on your own family and your own community and what we are all about.

Then a dean named Thomas Freeman came looking for a photographer. Freeman was running the local end of the Model Cities Program, part of the War on Poverty, and he needed somebody to go out on Tuesday and Thursday evenings and photograph how people in Houston actually lived.

Hudnall took the job for the money and stayed sixty years. It put him on foot in the Third Ward and the Fourth Ward and the Fifth Ward, in Sunnyside and South Park, at the exact moment every planning document in the city was writing those neighborhoods off.

He did not see a problem to be solved.

He saw Hattiesburg.

"It was a kindred kind of connection," is how he described walking into the Fourth Ward the first time. He talks about the clapboard houses, the kids playing in the road, the porches in the evening, and the sound of people laughing at each other from across a street.

When the federal contract ran out, nothing changed. He kept going back on his own time and his own film for the next five decades, with nobody paying him a dollar to do it.

Which brings us to an afternoon in 1983. He was walking the Fourth Ward with the camera the way he had walked it a thousand times, and there were people out on the sidewalk on an ordinary day on their own block.

And a boy decided to flip.

He went up off the pavement and turned over in the air, upside down, arms out, and Hudnall got him at the top of it.

Look at what is in that frame besides the child. There are neighbors watching from the walk, and there is the road under him, and rising up behind all of it, filling the whole top of the picture, is the skyline of downtown Houston.

Hudnall did not arrange that.

The boy went up and the city was already standing there.

In 1983 nobody official had yet decided the Fourth Ward was worth keeping. That took two more years.

On January 17, 1985, Freedmen's Town was added to the National Register of Historic Places, and the survey counted 530 historic structures standing on sixty-four acres. Fewer than thirty of them are standing today.

Roughly seventy-nine percent of the historic fabric of Freedmen's Town has come down since the day the federal government certified that it mattered. Of nineteen churches, eight remain.

The listing stopped federal money from paying for demolition. It did nothing whatsoever about private money, and private money never stopped coming.

So Hudnall was not photographing a neighborhood that afternoon. He was photographing the last of one, two years ahead of the paperwork and four decades ahead of the townhouses.

The picture is called Flipping Boy. The Smithsonian bought a print in 1994, a Houston Chronicle essay later called it the definitive photograph of the city, and it hangs today in Washington and in the Museum of Fine Arts Houston.

Nobody has ever printed the boy's name.

He is a man past fifty now, somewhere, and the label under his body says Flipping Boy, 1983, and not one word more. Which brings us back to Andrews Street, and to a woman who was watching all of this happen from inside her own house.

Gladys House-El is the fifth generation of the families who planned and developed Freedmen's Town. Her people were there for the mud and the petitions and the bricks.

"My family sold blocks of ice on the back of a horse-drawn buggy," she has said.

She was the fourth of fourteen children, four boys and ten girls, in a neighborhood where everybody's mother could correct anybody's child. She started fighting the city over this land when she was fourteen years old.

She still lives in the building her family's business ran out of. So on November 21, 2016, when the sound of heavy equipment came up Andrews Street, she did not need anybody to explain to her what was being torn out of the ground.

A resident named Rodney Jones saw it first, in the 1600 block, and got on the phone to the community. House-El heard the machine from inside her house and did not wait to get dressed properly.

She came out into the street in her housecoat with her phone already recording. Then she stood in front of a running excavator and told the operator he was in violation of federal as well as state law.

Think about what that takes. An older woman in a housecoat, alone in the road at first, filming a man on a machine and quoting statute at him until he shuts it off.

He shut it off.

By then roughly forty feet of the street was gone.

The mayor was in Mexico City for a football game and put out word that the work had never been authorized and that no one should have touched Andrews Street without him. The construction firm's general partner wrote him a letter conceding the company had made a serious mistake in removing pavers installed by the original residents of Freedmen's Town.

A month later a plumbing crew hit Andrews Street again, at the other end, also without permission. "To disrupt the sacred heritage of our brick streets is just overwhelming," House-El said.

She has also said, plainly, that her people have been on that ground since the beginning of time. By January 2018 she estimated seven thousand bricks were still out of the earth.

That March, city contractors began setting 3,610 of them back in, over a fresh leveling pad poured at Genesee and Andrews so the returned bricks would sit flush with the ones that had survived. The neighborhood held a celebration.

It lasted seven years.

On June 3, 2025, weeks before Juneteenth, a contractor working the corner of Andrews and Wilson damaged twenty-two more of them. Charonda Johnson, a fifth-generation resident and one of the two women the city designates to be notified before anyone touches that pavement, happened to be standing right there and stopped the work herself.

"I don't want to think about her not being there to stop it," the conservancy's director said afterward. In February of this year it happened again, a crew connecting water meters without telling either monitor, which is the exact thing the protocol exists to prevent.

Then on March 25 of this year, the Houston City Council voted unanimously to hand over the bricks the city had been keeping in a warehouse, so they can finally come home to the Fourth Ward. Dozens of pallets of them, cataloged over weeks by archaeologists working alongside neighborhood teenagers.

The conservancy and a museum are putting up $19,304 out of their own budgets to move them and build something to hold them. Under the agreement, the city does not have to pay for any of it.

So the community is paying to bring its own street home. That is the second time in a hundred and ten years that Black Houston has had to buy this road.

Here is the last thing, and it is the part that will not leave me alone. Jack Yates built his house on Andrews Street in 1870.

In 1994 that house was lifted off its lot and hauled a mile downtown to a heritage park, because moving it was the only way to keep a bulldozer off it. The house survived by leaving.

The street had to stay and take it.

And there are now two photographs of Andrews Street that matter, and they ought to be hung facing each other. In one of them, from 1983, a Black boy is upside down in the air over that road with the whole downtown skyline standing behind his head, and nobody has ever recorded his name.

In the other one, a Black woman is lying flat on her back in that same road, in a hole exactly forty-five bricks wide, because that was the only tool she had left.

One of them going up. One of them lying down.

Both of them on the same street, and both of them still waiting on the rest of us to finish what their great-grandparents started paying for in 1907.

Freedmen’s Town was built by people who had just walked out of slavery and decided they would build something of their own. I research forgotten stories like this because the communities that carried history deserve to have their names and places remembered. If you want to support this work:

text:
But the cough doesn't go away. A biopsy is performed and reveals pleural mesothelioma, a cancer caused by significant asbestos exposure.
This cancer was incurable at that time.
McQueen, who was 48 at the time, believes he was exposed to asbestos while in the Navy, where he had to remove asbestos linings from pipes on ships. He also admits to having come into contact with asbestos while racing, stating that there was something in the suits and helmets to protect against fire.
In early 1980, the cancer had metastasized, and although McQueen did his best to keep it a secret, the press revealed that he was suffering from terminal cancer.
￼
When his doctors were unable to offer him solutions, the star decided to go to Mexico to be treated by a doctor who promised him a revolutionary therapy.
The man in question was William Donald Kelley. He had basic training as an orthodontist (a profession he was no longer authorized to practice) but claimed to be an expert in cancer treatment...
￼
His miracle therapy to save Steve McQueen consisted of giving him coffee enemas, washing his body several times a day with shampoo, massaging him very frequently, injecting him daily with solutions of live cow and sheep cells and apricot seed powder...
Steve McQueen stayed at "Dr." Kelley's clinic for three months, paying the equivalent of 110,000 euros per month for "care."
Finally, the American media discovered that the star was being treated at this mysterious clinic, and the news spread widely. Everyone was talking about the miracle treatment that would save Steve McQueen.
In early October 1980, the latter returned to the U.S. William Donald Kelley then publicly announced that his treatment had worked and that Steve McQueen was cured.
￼
Immediately, his clinic was flooded with wealthy patients who wanted to undergo the same therapy...
But the American doctors who examined McQueen upon his return found that the cancer had not been defeated. On the contrary, it had progressed. A massive 2.3 kg tumor had developed in his liver...
Against the advice of his American doctors, who assured him that the tumor was inoperable and that his heart would not withstand the procedure, McQueen returned to Mexico to have it removed. The operation took place in a small clinic where the doctors were unaware of the star's true identity, as he used a pseudonym.
At 3:45 a.m. on November 7, 1980, Steve McQueen died of a heart attack in his sleep, twelve hours after having a tumor removed. He was 50 years old.
William Donald Kelley was not prosecuted for his questionable practices. He took advantage of the credulity of desperate patients for years until the ineffectiveness of his treatment was finally exposed.
He died of a heart attack in 2005, at the age of 79.
￼

Kimberly Guilfoyle was once married to California Governor Gavin Newsom, later became engaged to Donald Trump Jr., and is now the U.S. Ambassador to Greece.

According to an investigation by The Wall Street Journal, in the summer of 2025, just days before her Senate confirmation, Guilfoyle allegedly asked businessman Eric Deters for $100,000 to pay off credit card debt.

Deters, a Trump supporter and former congressional candidate from Kentucky, reportedly wanted Guilfoyle to help resolve his tax and legal problems. In exchange, he allegedly offered her up to $1 million.

Journalists reviewed correspondence in which Guilfoyle reportedly contacted the head of the Internal Revenue Service and reached out to the Department of Justice on Deters' behalf.

But Deters never paid her. He claims his wife would have objected and that Guilfoyle ultimately did nothing for him.

Guilfoyle's attorney has questioned the authenticity of the correspondence. He maintains that Deters simply owed her money for speaking engagements. Deters denies that explanation.

When Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked about Guilfoyle today, he dismissed the controversy as an attempt by reporters to manufacture a scandal.

The U.S. ambassador could now face serious legal and ethical questions.

Accepting money in exchange for improperly influencing government agencies can violate federal law, and nominees for senior government positions are required to disclose certain financial liabilities.

A former governor's wife. A president's son's former fiancée. Now an American ambassador facing allegations involving money, influence, and access to federal agencies.

And once again, the central question is whether political connections were being turned into a private business opportunity.

text:
France is on fire. An ISIS plotter just tried to turn the Mall of America into a killing floor. Yesterday, Abdul El-Sayed looked at both and offered the people Biden and Harris waved in a pathway to citizenship.

That is not compassion. That is recruitment.

On the debate stage he said America needs “a pathway to citizenship for folks who are stuck in limbo right now,” then called enforcement a “tough guy attitude” that “is not keeping us safe” and is “terrorizing folks in our streets.” He has wanted ICE abolished since 2018 and has said the vast majority here illegally should get a path to stay. 

Citizenship is the amnesty. The ballot is the weapon.

Christopher Wray, Biden’s own FBI director, refused to guarantee known or suspected terrorists were not among the gotaways. He called that unknown mass a source of “great concern,” warned of a “wide array of very dangerous threats” off the border, and put all 56 Joint Terrorism Task Forces on it. Watchlist hits set records while the flood did. 

El-Sayed’s answer is to naturalize the backlog and call the men who stop it the threat.

France is the trailer, and it is not a school protest. The pretext was leaky classrooms. The street delivered burned and ransacked schools, more than 6,000 arrests, hundreds of injured officers, and crowds chanting to Mohamed Merah, the terrorist who executed Jewish children, while Palestinian flags and far-left banners moved together. 

Pro-Palestinian groups declared October a month of revolt and fed the demonstrations. French observers already call it the red-green alliance: socialists and Islamists in the same column, aimed at the country. America ran the larger version in 2020, when one Democratic chamber and blue-city halls were enough to rename arson a summer of love.

Minnesota delivered the domestic proof this week. 

On October 6 the FBI arrested Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, a U.S. citizen of Somali descent, after he paid an undercover agent he thought was ISIS for an AK-47 and 200 rounds. He allegedly planned to murder dozens at the Mall of America on October 24 because, in his words, Jews owned it. Gangs and an ISIS pledge are not the same crime. They are the same crop: a population Democrats spent years treating as a client base, and a party that still brands the arrest the provocation.

The party is not hiding him. Barack Obama is flying to Detroit on October 24 to campaign for El-Sayed in person — the coalition’s high priest blessing the candidate who wants the limbo population made voters and ICE erased.

One Democratic gavel is enough. 

It was enough in 2020. It would be enough to stall removals, launder the pathway, and hand the street its alibi the next time police or the FBI arrest a Somali gang member or an ISIS plotter. 

France is what the alliance looks like after it wins. November decides whether it gets a chamber here.

#News James Talarico claimed he was in a Dallas urgent care the same night he was holding a fundraiser in New York, now Republicans in Texas are calling him a liar.
Talarico was supposed to be in Edinburg on September 30 for an in-person forum at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. He joined by video instead.
#newyork
On the video, he said
“Last night, it got so bad that I went to urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu.”
He said he had a fever and was in the “most contagious” stage and that he could not live with himself if he got someone’s grandmother or someone’s baby sick, and that the best thing was to put safety and health first.
He also said, “I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail.”
However, it appears as though his schedule doesn't match his excuse.
📷Monday, September 28, 7 p.m., downtown Manhattan fundraiser:
📷Tickets ran from $500 to $27,000. Talarico attended.
📷Tuesday, September 29, Greenwich Village, a second fundraiser, on his campaign’s invitation.
📷Tickets ran from $1,000 to $13,500. He held the reception.
📷A Tuesday night reception in Greenwich Village, New York and a Tuesday night urgent-care visit in Dallas is not the same thing.
The campaign hasn't given an explanation, proof of a flight, a timestamp, or even a clinic name.
While Talarico was in New York collecting out of state  money - his events in Texas were being cancelled.
📷The Edinburg forum on September 30 went virtual.
📷The Central Texas African American Civic Engagement Symposium was canceled.
📷An Austin fundraiser set for Tuesday was scrapped.
#Austin
Ken Paxton’s spokeswoman Madison Cercy said Talarico had time for a New York fundraiser but “can’t find time for Texans,” and that Paxton is working while Talarico “hides behind recycled rally footage and canceled events.”
📷On October 7 the campaign launched a “Where’s Jimmy?” count:
“It’s been 11 days since James Talarico was last seen campaigning in Texas.”
At President Trump’s San Antonio rally, Paxton led a “Where is Talarico?” chant.
Republicans say if he was in Dallas with the flu, the Greenwich Village fundraiser needs an explanation. If he was in Greenwich Village taking checks, the urgent-care story needs one. The campaign has offered neither.
Do you believe a man can be at a New York donor reception and a Dallas urgent care on the same night? Or are Republicans right in saying that Talarico is lying?

text:
ANALYSIS - The paper tiger of Riyadh

In November 2017, in a Riyadh hotel, some of the richest men in Saudi Arabia were held until they agreed to pay. The message was that a new kind of power had arrived: personal, total, unchallenged.

Then the story changed. Cinemas opened. Women drove. There were concerts. A kingdom founded in the eighteenth century on a pact between throne and clergy was told to become something else, a brand, a Vision. And the product on offer was a feeling: that here, at last, was a stable place in a region of fire. Safety.

This is the thing to understand about Mohammed bin Salman. His authority doesn't rest on oil alone. It rests on a story, told to foreigners and Saudis alike, that only he could modernise the country without losing control of it.
Stories have one weakness. A single image can break them.

Look at what the Houthis chose. Oil is abstract, hidden, Aramco's. They hit airports instead, at Abha and at King Khalid in Riyadh. Three dead, thirty-six injured, and about 15% of Riyadh's scheduled departures delayed the next day. A terminal is where the story is meant to be proven, where the investor lands and the tourist arrives and the family flies.

And there is a second wound, which comes from Washington. Axios reports that MBS called Trump twice on 10 September and asked for strikes. He was refused. In 2018 Trump said the old king would not last two weeks without American protection. In March he reportedly said of the son: "I didn't think he would kiss my ass."
I can't know what any of this feels like inside the palace. I can read what the man has built. A leader who staked everything on the image of command faces a dilemma with no clean exit. Hit back hard, and the war becomes unmistakably his. Hit back softly, and he confirms what his critics whisper. The Houthis fire cheap things at priceless targets. He answers with priceless things at cheap targets. Each exchange costs him even when he wins.

That is an escalation trap. It isn't a loss on the battlefield. It's a loss of narrative.

In 1979, armed men seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca and denounced the royal family as corrupt. It is a reminder that stories of control can fail from within. I see no public evidence of a repeat. But the structure is the same: everything depends on no one seeing the crack.

You don't need to defeat a story. You only need to land a drone in the middle of it.

Context over chaos.

On 17 September 2024 a Hunter and Central Coast brief set out the test and the risk. She signed it anyway. In her own hand she approved $15,000, calling continued care “special circumstances” under the Government Sector Finance Act. Documents tendered to parliament show this was the only time she ignored that advice. On 11 other occasions she took it. The carer is a trade union member with Labor links. Not just linked. Her father and brother are regarded as Labor royalty. She cannot be named. A Labor MP made the representations. Washington says she does not know her.
That $15,000 was the second cheque. CatholicCare Hunter Manning deauthorised the carer, then by its own clerical error kept paying the allowance for almost two years: $39,316.36. It sued. Washington had DCJ pay that sum so the agency would drop the case. The $15,000 was for three days a week between March 2023 and February 2024, after the allowance had stopped. Bureaucrats warned of significant reputational risk. She paid it anyway.
The diocese was stunned. Sean Scanlon took legal advice, refused the gag agreement, and the board considered ICAC. It did not, because of the funding. DCJ had already asked CatholicCare to take the Minister’s name off the paperwork.
At 5:43am on 22 September 2024 her acting chief of staff, Daniel Barakate, emailed DCJ, copied to the Office of the Secretary, to finalise the payments that week, including a staying-on allowance. Tidball’s electronic approval is on the file, dated 25 June 2024. At estimates on 25 August 2026 he said he was not sure he had authorised the money. He knows he signed it. The same Secretary wrote telling me to sue the department. Being the Minister’s lapdog does not keep children safe. He needs to be stood down.
She did not do that for me. Life Without Barriers and DCJ did not honour the THBC agreement for a high-needs child. The CAT score was cut from high to medium, and the THBC option was eliminated. Promised funding never came. She walked away. That cost a child his life, and left me self-funding him. Trauma at self-placement was valued at $380,000. After she allowed the breakdown, funding jumped to $780,000. A month before, the CAT score was put back to high. His needs had not changed. Washington and Tidball sacked the senior managers who had called me four times to offer condolences and ask if I needed support, and to conceal the death.
I left work. Savings gone. I sold my stake in a restaurant, assets and shares. The home was destroyed. Cards maxed. $30,000 in arrears. Car repossessed. She found $15,000 and $39,316 for a Labor unionist. Nothing to keep a suicidal child safe.
Once caught, she said carers were treated poorly in the past, but not on her watch, and no carer should be left out of pocket. That is false. Same minister. Same secretary. On 11 other occasions she took the advice and left them there. She did not turn her back on this one. Minns called it reasonable. He did not sack her. He did not sack Tidball. He condoned it.

text:
🚨 A Small Town Just Said "No Thanks" to a $45,000,000 Cash Drop From Amazon to Build a Data Center

Imagine getting a letter in the mail offering your family $10,000 in cash, completely tax-free, just to clear the path for a local construction project.

Now imagine your entire town collectively deciding to reject it.

That is exactly what just happened in Hazle Township, Pennsylvania.

💰 The Math
To force through a massive, controversial 1,283-acre AI data center facility known as "Project Hazelnut," the developer (with Jeff Bezos’s Amazon Web Services as the end user) tried a radical tactic:

$10,000 cash offered directly to every single household.

With 4,505 households in the township, that is over $45,000,000 in direct personal payouts.

It was all wrapped inside a staggering $165,000,000 "community benefits" package.

Activists and famed advocates like Erin Brockovich called it exactly what it looked like: an unabashed corporate bribe to bypass local zoning laws.

🛑 Why did residents stand firm?

Local homeowners realized that no one-time payout can fix the permanent, 24/7 realities of a hyperscale data center footprint:

1The 24/7 Hum: The infamous, non-stop industrial noise vibration that echoes through rural communities.

2Resource Strain: Enormous, unprecedented consumption of local water and grid energy required to keep AI servers cool.

3Plunging Property Values: As one resident put it, $10,000 doesn't mean much if the industrial complex tanks your home's total equity.

4The Wedge: Residents saw the cash as a deliberate attempt to pit neighbors against neighbors.

📉 The Bigger Picture
This isn't just a local dispute anymore. Amazon initially tried to hide its involvement in the project, which was only uncovered by activist public records requests.

Now, public pushback is exploding statewide. Recent polling shows 74% of Pennsylvanians oppose data center construction. 

Bipartisan lawmakers are pushing hard for a 3-year data center moratorium to freeze development and strip away 100% corporate tax exemptions.

⚠️ The Most Incredible Part
Hazle Township is not a wealthy, prosperous area. The local poverty rate sits near 17%, and median incomes are well below national averages. For many working-class families and retirees living here, $10,000 in cash is life-changing money—it's months of mortgage payments, a massive safety net, or a year of groceries.

Yet, they still stood together and refused to be bought out by Big Tech. They chose the long-term health and integrity of their community over a massive corporate check.

For now, Hazle Township has paused all data center applications. It turns out some things—like peace, quiet, and community—actually don't have a price tag.

#Amazon

text:
What does the Trump Organization consists of..?

For instance years back you could attend a Trump event that was part of Trump University (later renamed the Trump Entrepreneur Initiative), a for-profit business seminar operated under The Trump Organization. 

It was in fact dubious: the venture faced multiple high-profile fraud lawsuits and ultimately closed down, resulting in a $25 million settlement in 2016 to compensate former students. 

1. What The Trump Organization Consists Of

The Trump Organization is a massive, private international conglomerate that serves as the holding company for roughly 500 distinct business entities owned by Donald Trump. 
Its core operations generally fall into the following categories: 

* Core Real Estate: High-profile commercial, residential, and office skyscrapers—such as the headquarters at Trump Tower on Fifth Avenue in New York City. 

* Hospitality & Leisure: A global portfolio of luxury hotels, residential resorts, and 17+ golf courses located across the U.S., Scotland, Ireland, and Dubai. 

* Licensing & Branding: Deals where external developers pay millions to use the "Trump" brand name on luxury buildings, consumer goods, apparel, and a Virginia winery. 

* Media & Entertainment: Historically built on ventures like The Apprentice television show and beauty pageants. Today, it is closely tied to Trump Media & Technology Group (the parent company of Truth Social) and newer decentralized finance/crypto platforms. 

2. The 2005 Trump Entrepreneur Formula 

Trump University launched in May 2005. A process "to become rich" -you better walked away from- followed a highly specific, high-pressure sales funnel: 

* The Bait: Free introductory sessions marketed "insider real estate formulas" to get rich.

* The Upsell: Attendees at the free events were pressured to buy a three-day seminar for roughly $1,500.

* The Elite Package: During those three-day seminars, instructors pushed attendees to buy comprehensive "Gold Elite" mentorship programs costing up to $35,000. 

The Dubious Reality: Despite the heavy branding, it was not an accredited school, could not grant degrees, and did not offer college credits. Investigations by the New York Attorney General revealed that the "handpicked experts" teaching the courses were mostly independent sales contractors with little to no real estate background. State education officials ultimately forced the business to drop the word "University" from its name because it lacked a structural charter to operate as an educational institution...

The Trump name, a sales and marketing pitch, so many fall for..
