🌍 https://t.co/FMtlKoeGYk — What If the Next Travel Revolution Isn't About Where You Go, but How Freely You Get There?

The shortest route isn't always the smartest.

The fastest route isn't always the cheapest.

And the route recommended by an algorithm isn't necessarily the one a traveler would choose.

Consider this.

A delivery driver wants to avoid expensive toll roads.

An electric vehicle owner needs charging stops.

A road trip traveler wants spectacular scenery.

A truck operator needs vehicle-compatible roads.

A cyclist wants safer streets.

A family wants fewer stressful highway miles.

Yet most navigation experiences still begin with the same basic question:

Where do you want to go?

What if the better question were:

How do you want to get there?

Introducing https://t.co/FMtlKoeGYk.

A descriptive, globally relevant .com domain positioned at the intersection of intelligent navigation, route optimization, road travel, logistics technology, electric mobility, and AI-powered transportation.

https://t.co/FMtlKoeGYk — Your Journey. Your Rules.

🚀 THE COMPANY CONCEPT: FREE ROUTES

Imagine an intelligent routing platform that gives travelers and businesses more control over how journeys are planned.

Not another basic navigation application.

Not another generic map.

Not another route optimizer focused exclusively on distance.

An AI-powered route intelligence platform designed around personal preferences, operational constraints, and real-world travel priorities.

The mission?

Help people and businesses discover routes that better match their needs.

Avoid tolls.

Reduce unnecessary driving.

Find suitable EV charging.

Explore scenic roads.

Plan multiple destinations.

Respect commercial vehicle restrictions.

Compare alternative journeys.

The opportunity isn't simply finding a route.

It's finding the right route for the person or business taking it.

The proposed platform could combine seven interconnected capabilities.

⚡ RouteCore™ — The Intelligent Routing Engine

Every journey involves trade-offs.

Time.

Distance.

Cost.

Convenience.

Accessibility.

Vehicle limitations.

RouteCore would evaluate permitted mapping and transportation data to generate alternatives based on user-defined preferences.

Imagine a driver traveling between two cities.

Instead of receiving only the fastest route, the platform could compare:

A faster highway journey.

A toll-free alternative.

A route with suitable rest stops.

A scenic option.

A route optimized for a specific vehicle.

One destination. Multiple intelligent possibilities.

⚡ RouteFree™ — The Toll & Cost Optimization Network

For many drivers, the fastest route isn't necessarily the most economical.

Toll roads.

Fuel consumption.

Distance.

Vehicle-specific charges.

RouteFree would help compare estimated travel costs where reliable data is available.

Imagine a small delivery business operating dozens of vehicles.

Even modest route improvements could become commercially meaningful across repeated journeys.

The platform could compare time savings against estimated toll and fuel costs.

Because saving a few minutes isn't always worth paying more.

⚡ RouteEV™ — The Electric Mobility Planner

Electric vehicle routing introduces new variables.

Battery range.

Charging availability.

Connector compatibility.

Charging speed.

Terrain.

Weather.

text:
Happy birthday to former Booker T. Washington, Oklahoma State and NFL linebacker Jordan Brailford, born on this day in 1995 in Tulsa.

Brailford attended Tulsa's Booker T. Washington High School, where he was a first-team All-State selection as a senior in 2013 after making 105 tackles and nine sacks. He was also selected for the Semper Fidelis All-American Bowl, helping the West team win 31-24.

Brailford chose Oklahoma State over offers that included Baylor, Kansas State, Texas Tech, Tulsa and Washington State.

With the Cowboys, Brailford played in ten games as a redshirt freshman in 2015, making 23 tackles, 3.5 for loss and one sack.

A stress fracture in his leg suffered during the preseason caused him to miss the entire 2016 season. He bounced back in 2017, making 57 tackles, 11 for loss, five sacks and intercepting a pass, earning second-team All-Big 12 honors.

He followed it up by earning First-Team All-Big 12 a year later and was selected as a team captain. He made 54 tackles and had 16 tackles for loss and nine sacks, both of which led the Cowboys.

His play earned him the Cowboys' Leslie O'Neal Award, which goes to the team's outstanding defensive player.  In 2019, the Washington Redskins selected Brailford in the seventh round of the NFL Draft, but never played for Washington after being placed on injured reserve before the season's start.

In 2020, Brailford signed with the Minnesota Vikings and played in five games. In his first NFL game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, he had two tackles, forced and recovered a fumble as the Vikings won 27-24 in overtime.

He later signed with the Atlanta Falcons and the New Orleans Breakers and Memphis Showboats of the UFL.  Happy birthday Jordan! #tdfn #okpreps @BookerTFootball @CowboyFB

IDHS warns against disaster assistance fraud

INDIANAPOLIS - The Indiana Department of Homeland Security (IDHS) is warning survivors of the August 2026 disaster about attempts to fraudulently acquire state and federal disaster assistance.

State Disaster Relief Funds are intended for the survivors of disaster events to help those affected rebuild. The improper use and receipt of funds will be pursued by the State of Indiana to the maximum extent possible under Indiana law.

The State Disaster Relief Funds (SDRF) administered by IDHS are only intended for eligible applicants. Individual assistance is available for individuals and families to be spent on eligible categories.

For a period of up to three (3) years, in accordance with Indiana Code, IDHS has the authority to inspect and audit property that was the subject of financial assistance. If individuals are found to be in violation, IDHS may exercise all legal rights to recover funds and related costs of recovery for improperly received or spent assistance.

During the auditing of applications and funds received, IDHS will work with all local, state and federal entities to pursue SDRF funds that have been improperly or fraudulently obtained. This includes partnering with Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita to pursue civil actions in the recuperation of state funds, as well as with state and federal law enforcement to pursue applicable criminal charges.

Assistance in filing documents or filling out an application for federal or state assistance is available at no cost. Be careful of offers from those who say they will do it for a small fee. Spending state or federal assistance on ineligible expenses, such as taxes, repaying someone who completed your application, or any expense not listed in Indiana Code may be subjected to an audit and legal repercussions. IDHS is actively investigating cases of fraud and abuse of state disaster assistance. 

To report federal assistance fraud, email StopFEMAFraud@fema.dhs.gov. 

To report state assistance fraud, email IDHSSDRFfraud@dhs.in.gov.

647/648
A working sketch of Bobby Grow’s ((@ cum_granosalis)) books on Evangelical Calvinism vis-à-vis Christ’s vicarious humanity: two volumes co-edited with Myk Habets: 
•Evangelical Calvinism: Essays Resourcing the Continuing Reformation of the Church 
•Evangelical Calvinism, Volume 2: Dogmatics and Devotion 
→ 
The second volume is organized around the vicarious ministry of Christ. The same program is developed at length on his blog and in the fifteen theses that introduce the project.

The first move is methodological. Grow argues that many modern debates about salvation—classical Calvinism versus Arminianism, sovereignty versus free will, limited versus general atonement—begin in the wrong place. They start from soteriology, usually inside what he calls a Latin or Augustinian frame, and then try to fit Christ into that frame. He wants the order reversed. Thinking should begin with Christology, specifically with the hypostatic union: the place where Almighty God and humanity “kiss.” 

Jesus is not an instrument executing a prior decree. He is the electing God and the elected human in one person. Election, atonement, faith, and human agency are then read from that center rather than from an abstract mass of humanity standing before an abstract will of God.

That center is the vicarious humanity of Christ. 

The Son assumes real human nature, not a generic or partial humanity, and in that nature lives the whole human response to the Father: faith, repentance, obedience, worship, and intercession. The point is not only that Christ dies instead of us, but that Christ is human for us. Our humanity has its true ground in his recreated, resurrected humanity. Grow often puts this in Athanasian rather than Augustinian terms: salvation is ontological and participatory before it is merely juridical. God does not first set up a contract and then apply its benefits to selected individuals. God gives himself. Grace is “all the way down.” There is no independent natural platform from which a fallen person first decides to join God.

From this follow two claims that must be held together.

First, Christ’s work is for all humanity. Thesis 11 states that Christ lived, died, and rose again for all, so Evangelical Calvinism affirms universal atonement. Grow follows Torrance here: this is a finished work, not a mere possibility. By the incarnation there is a “carnal” or objective union of the Son with humanity as such. 

Election is christologically conditioned: humanity is elect in the Son’s assumption of human nature, not by an absolute decree that first splits the human race into two classes. The gospel can therefore be preached as already true of the hearer: Christ has bound himself to you before and apart from your believing.

Second, this is not universalism. Thesis 12 is explicit. Universal redemption does not entail that all will finally be saved. Grow distinguishes the objective inclusion of humanity in Christ from the subjective, Spirit-given realization of that inclusion. “Spiritual union” is a sharing in the one union already wrought in Jesus. Faith is not an independent human contribution that completes an incomplete work. It is the Spirit enabling a person to echo Christ’s own Yes to the Father—often with appeal to *pistis *Christou as the faith of Christ. Baptism and conversion, on this telling, are a living into a reality that is already true, not the first creation of that reality.

Rejection remains real. Grow can say that some “opt out,” refuse the grace given in Christ, and so condemn themselves. He cites Torrance to the effect that Christ has already made the person his own, and that even if someone refuses him and damns himself, that love does not cease. The refusal does not undo the incarnation or turn Christ’s Yes into a No. It is a contradiction of what God has done, and that contradiction becomes its own judgment.

What this is not, on Grow’s own terms, is a symmetric libertarian choice to “stay or leave,” as if the human will stood outside the work of Christ and then selected one of two equal options. He affirms something like total inability: fallen humanity is *incurvatus *in *se and cannot move toward God from an abstract free will. The initiative is Christ’s. Our Yes is participation in his Yes. Our No is possible, tragic, and self-condemning, but it is not the same kind of act as a first decision to join God. 

Grow thinks the usual dilemma—either God irresistibly saves the elect, or the human will is the decisive co-cause—still belongs to the older causal and contractual grammar. He wants agency relocated inside the vicarious humanity of the Son and the ministry of the Spirit, rather than treated as a rival sovereignty.
The resulting picture can be summarized without slogans:

•God has already said Yes to humanity in the incarnate Son.
•All humanity is objectively included in that Yes; redemption is not a limited offer waiting to be activated by the right kind of decision.
•No one is saved apart from personal faith, but that faith is a sharing in Christ’s own response, not a climb from outside into God’s favor.
•Final exclusion is possible as refusal of a gift already given, not as proof that Christ never represented that person.
•The “limit” of the atonement is not a restricted list of individuals chosen in a decree. It is the vicarious humanity of Jesus himself: the One for the many.

That is the framework Grow is gesturing toward when he tells interlocutors that starting from soteriology keeps Calvinists and non-Calvinists at loggerheads, and that the place to begin is the hypostatic union. As a description of what he is saying, this seems to be the shape.

Israeli Leaks: What Are They Hiding?
These leaks are not innocent.
Israel has a long-established practice of leaking such reports early to create anxiety in Washington, then building on that atmosphere to promote a narrative about what it describes as security concerns over Egypt. 

The objective is well known: to preserve Israel’s qualitative military edge and justify its continued monopoly on the most advanced weapons and systems the United States has to offer.

Simply put, today’s leak could be a prelude to demands for compensation or advanced arms deals tomorrow.
The issue concerns a U.S. study currently underway on the possible transfer of four KC-10 Extender aerial refueling aircraft, which have been retired from the U.S. Air Force, to a North African country.

Israeli sources were quick to assert that Egypt would be the recipient. Official U.S. reports, however, have yet to name the country, saying only that Egypt and Morocco are the leading candidates.

The fact that these aircraft have been retired means they were withdrawn from U.S. service by the end of 2024 and placed in the aircraft storage and retirement facility. But they are far from scrap. They can be refurbished and returned to operation at a high level of efficiency.

Egypt has no independent fleet of large aerial refueling aircraft. So far, it has relied on limited refueling capabilities between fighter jets, a system that falls well short of meeting the demands of long-range strategic operations.

If Egypt acquires these aircraft, it would mark a genuine leap in the capabilities of the Egyptian Air Force, enabling it to carry out strikes over greater distances, remain airborne for longer periods, and establish a broader air presence.

This would certainly be more than an ordinary addition to its fleet. It could change the rules of the game, particularly as Egypt is actively seeking an independent aerial refueling capability, whether through the Chinese option or other potential opportunities.

text:
Wyoming offered me a company that could keep a drilling debt from reaching our house. My investors pushed its papers back across the desk. Cheyenne, 1977: the state had passed its new LLC law, but no one could tell us how the IRS would tax one. The drilling rig was reserved until Friday.

We had money for one test well. Two men would put up most of it; I had found the lease and would run the work. If the hole came up dry, they wanted the losses treated as partnership losses on their tax returns. If a contractor went unpaid, I wanted our homes out of his reach.

Our lawyer set two folders beside the lease map. A corporation would put a company between us and its ordinary debts, but it did not give my investors the partnership tax treatment they had come for. In a limited partnership they could be passive investors. They wanted me to serve as general partner. In that role I would answer personally for its bills.

Then the lawyer showed us the new Wyoming limited liability company papers. The state would let all of us be members without making one of us the personally liable general partner. He had prepared the filing. The tax answer, he said, belonged to Washington, not Wyoming.

One investor asked for an IRS ruling. The lawyer opened his empty hands. The other investor said he would move his money to a different well if we were going to gamble on the tax treatment. I could hear the rig operator's terms in my head: sign by Friday or he would take another job.

I signed the limited partnership papers as general partner. I told my wife about the decision that night beside our pickup. I pointed toward the lease and said there was oil on the neighboring tract. She asked whether that would pay a bill on ours. I said we would find out.

We found no oil. The investors lost what they had put in. The rig operator sent the unpaid balance to me. I took the bill to our lawyer; his finger stopped at my name on the partnership agreement.

When the buyer came for our pickup, my wife handed him the keys. I stood beside her and watched the truck leave. In the lawyer's office, the LLC papers still lay in a folder without our signatures.

Company Law in Europe — a serialized story.

text:
$AMT: Closed at $166.73 on October 8 (+0.33%) and traded at approximately $175 (+5%) in after-hours. Market cap is around $77.8 billion; the dividend is approximately $7.16, yielding about 4.3%. The 52-week range is $160–$196, placing the stock near its yearly low. The forward P/E ratio is around 25x, the average analyst price target is approximately $216, and the consensus rating is "Buy." The next earnings report is scheduled for October 27. The investment thesis is straightforward: the tower company's cash flow continues to grow, yet the share price remains suppressed by interest rates; once U.S. Treasury yields retreat, high-dividend infrastructure stocks like this are likely to rally first.
Second-quarter property revenue was approximately $2.69 billion (up ~6% year-over-year), with adjusted EBITDA of around $1.81 billion. The company raised its full-year outlook for the second time this year, targeting a property revenue midpoint of $10.7–$10.8 billion and raising the AFFO per share (attributable to shareholders) guidance to approximately $11.00–$11.17. Excluding the one-time loss of Dish business and refinancing costs, AFFO growth is in the mid-single-digit range. Organic tenant billing growth remains weighed down by the loss of Dish business; management views 2026 as a trough, with a potential return to mid-to-high single-digit growth in 2027. CoreSite data center leasing hit record highs, serving as a growth driver alongside the tower business.

Mobile data usage continues to rise, and carriers need to densify existing sites and deploy new spectrum rather than decommissioning towers. Approximately 800 MHz of new spectrum is slated for deployment over the coming years, with 6G on the horizon. AI is altering the structure of backhaul and edge traffic, and towers serve as essential nodes in this infrastructure. A more direct pricing factor is interest rates: AMT operates with approximately 4.9x leverage and features long duration and high dividends; consequently, when U.S. Treasury yields fall, its valuation tends to recover faster than the underlying fundamentals might suggest. The post-market price movement observed recently appears driven more by interest rate trading than by new order activity.

The asset base comprises three segments: first, a global tower portfolio, where U.S. sites offer the highest margins while international sites contribute volume and currency-related upside; second, CoreSite, a U.S. multi-tenant data center business that benefits directly from cloud and interconnection demand; and third, a smaller segment covering services and equity-method investments. Revenue is fundamentally derived from long-term leases with annual escalation clauses and high renewal rates, while capital expenditure is primarily allocated to maintenance, selective new builds, and data center expansions.

Key Factors: Timeline and Impact
Past Events: Q2 earnings (reported July 28) exceeded expectations with raised guidance; CoreSite leasing hit record highs.
Past Events: In September, management reiterated that 2026 would mark the trough for organic growth, with momentum subsequently picking up via spectrum deployment, encryption services, and data center expansion.
Ongoing: Issuance of approximately $1.6 billion in senior unsecured notes to extend debt maturity and lock in liquidity.
October 27 (Q3 Earnings): The most critical event. The market will focus on whether organic tenant billings have stabilized, if the churn from Dish has played out as anticipated, whether CoreSite can maintain double-digit growth, and any commentary regarding 2027 guidance. Results exceeding expectations would reinforce the narrative that the "trough has passed," whereas underperformance could easily lead to a reversal of gains driven by the recent interest rate rally.
2027: New spectrum deployment and preparatory investments for 6G represent the drivers for upward revisions to mid-term lease revenue.

Once a tower is erected in an urban area or along a transportation corridor, relocation costs are high; consequently, operators prefer to add equipment or modify contracts at existing sites rather than switch landlords. AMT’s differentiation lies in its global diversification—which mitigates the impact of capital expenditure cycles specific to any single U.S. operator—combined with the growth trajectory provided by the CoreSite data center business. Compared to Crown Castle, it has greater international exposure and fewer U.S. fiber assets; while interest rates and exchange rates may amplify volatility, this also means its growth is not solely tied to the three major U.S. carriers.

Target Price: $172–$175

text:
America Couldn't Govern AI if it Wanted to

"Regulating AI isn’t a matter of programming it to perform a specific function — the way we program our alarm clocks to go off at a certain hour in the morning. It’s a matter of training it to make moral choices, to choose between good and bad in order to ensure AI’s 'alignment' with human goals.

To be sure, Washington can test models for bioweapon and cyberattack capabilities, restrict chip exports, and require companies to report incidents. These are worth doing.

But those measures don’t touch the problem at the heart of the regulation debate. For now, we can help stop a model from building a pathogen. But we can’t yet teach it right from wrong. And as these systems grow more capable than the people overseeing them, outside restrictions will only work as long as the AI itself has no desire to get around them. What’s really needed is moral formation...

Anthropic’s in-house philosopher, Amanda Askell, told the New York Times that she wants the models to be 'the best of us,' and to be able to discern what is in humanity’s best interest.

It’s a noble aim, but with a fatal flaw in its conception: Humanity itself lacks a consensus on what’s in its best interest. It offers many different interpretations on how to answer that question, and many, if not most of them, are mutually exclusive. In America alone, for instance, we can’t agree on when life begins, what marriage is, whether a man can become a woman, whether God exists, or on nearly any other important moral question.

So whose version of morality do we expect to instill in AI? And how could we possibly write it into law and enforce it?"

text:
Markets are getting more selective about what they’re willing to finance. AI demand remains strong, but investors are looking past headline revenue and promised capacity to actual cash flows. Meanwhile, energy costs, immigration policy and new competition are exposing vulnerabilities across established business models.

OpenAI’s $50B net versus $70B gross revenue distinction rattled AI stocks, not because compute demand suddenly disappeared, but because investors want to understand how much economic value is actually being generated.

The BIS found that 55% of investment value among the AI firms it studied came from other AI companies. That interconnectedness creates a problem for Nvidia and its ecosystem: weaker AI monetization could hit chip orders, cloud utilization, equity stakes and financing collateral simultaneously.

Firmus withdrawing its Australian IPO after pushback on a proposed A$44B valuation reinforces the shift. Investors are becoming less willing to pay today for infrastructure that may not generate revenue for years.

Washington adds another complication. The PERM suspension affecting Microsoft, Adobe and other technology employers creates uncertainty around skilled-worker retention and hiring, even though existing H-1B visas aren't automatically revoked.

Outside AI, Delta cut FY26 EPS guidance from $6.50–$7.50 to $5.10–$5.60 as a reported $6B fuel-cost increase overwhelmed resilient travel demand. Revenue growth offers little protection when energy inflation eats the margins.

Meanwhile, SpaceX's push into nationwide 800 MHz spectrum sent AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile sharply lower. Starlink's satellite-terrestrial ambitions threaten established wireless economics, although regulatory approval and commercial performance remain unproven.

The broader shift is worth watching: investors are moving from pricing future potential to demanding evidence of cash generation, capital efficiency and sustainable margins.

Growth stories still attract capital. The price investors are willing to pay for them is becoming much less forgiving.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran has submitted what it calls a "seven-day plan" and is reviewing the US position. A senior Iranian official had told Reuters on Wednesday that no talks were underway.

Earlier reporting said Washington has been negotiating a loosening of economic measures on Iran. In exchange, it seeks free traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and the shuttering of Iran's nuclear program.

Atomic Energy Organization head Mohammad Eslami said Iran will not give up enrichment and will not hand over its uranium. Vice President JD Vance had demanded a "meaningful" reduction in enrichment capacity.

Iran is reportedly not enriching at present. The IAEA estimates roughly 200 kg of enriched uranium may remain at Isfahan, the stock Eslami's refusal covers.

Having exhausted every contemporary pretext for Washington’s war of aggression against Iran, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood at the Acropolis and resorted to historical mythmaking.

By reaching back 2,500 years, Rubio attempted to drape modern military coercion in the mantle of ancient vengeance. In doing so, he offered a grotesque, weaponized caricature of classical Greece, reducing its vast humanistic legacy to a mere theater of raw power to make present-day aggression appear historically preordained. 

Framing a modern conflict as a timeless "clash of civilizations" is not merely lazy historiography; it is dangerous politics. Yet, to the Iranian people, a nation proud of its millennia-old history, such rhetoric sends an unmistakable signal: Washington’s war is an assault on Iranian identity itself. It seeks to malign a heritage that gave humanity foundational achievements in governance, science, and cultural pluralism, a rich legacy that has inspired generations across the globe.

Reaching back to antiquity to excuse modern war crimes is a pathetic diversion. Instead of digging through the ruins of ancient Athens for a moral shield, Washington must answer for the real-world devastation it is causing today.

text:
Trump’s Push for Data Center Expansion Puts Some G.O.P. Lawmakers in a Bind https://t.co/Q5HK3bzrB0 

Trump’s AI Dream Faces Growing Local Opposition; AI’s Moral Issue

(That dramatic success in AI evolution is facing opposition. Initially nobody understood which way the AI is heading. Two trillion dollars already spent has roundabout uses but no return on money spent. Now public is questioning its evolution and end point. Sooner than later Trump will be forced to bring some control over it.) 

President Trump’s ambitious push to make America the undisputed leader in artificial intelligence is beginning to encounter resistance on two fundamental fronts. The first is the enormous demand created by AI data centres, which can strain local electricity grids and water supplies. The second is the growing concern—even among some of AI’s own architects—that uncontrolled development without meaningful rules and guardrails could eventually create risks far beyond the technology’s intended benefits. It is a moral Issue at play.

Trump appears largely unmoved by either warning. His administration continues to encourage the rapid construction of data centres, often in clusters that place extraordinary demands on local infrastructure. AI companies argue that these problems can be managed through water recycling, private investment in additional power generation and long-term contracts for electricity. But for communities already facing pressure on water and power resources, the question is not simply who pays for expansion, but whether local infrastructure can sustain it.

The more profound issue is regulation. “Guardrails” could range from executive action to comprehensive congressional legislation establishing boundaries for the development and deployment of increasingly powerful AI systems. Trump, however, has shown little enthusiasm for regulations that might slow the industry. Trump, bringing AI executives together with congressional leaders and encouraging voluntary self-policing and periodic reviews may offer flexibility, but it leaves the industry largely responsible for policing itself.

That approach raises an obvious question: Can an industry moving at unprecedented speed realistically be expected to regulate itself when enormous commercial and strategic incentives are at stake?

Trump regards AI leadership as central to America’s economic and strategic future and is unlikely to support measures that significantly constrain its development. Unless political circumstances change, meaningful restraints may therefore remain difficult to impose.

China presents the other half of this emerging technological race. Beijing is investing heavily in its own AI capabilities and has demonstrated that it intends to compete with Washington rather than follow it. AI was reportedly among the subjects discussed by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at their recent Washington summit. With few public details released, the extent of any understanding remains unclear. Neither country appears prepared to surrender technological leadership.

The competition is therefore likely to continue. America possesses enormous financial markets and the ability to mobilize capital, even while adding to its already substantial debt burden. China has vast resources generated by decades of export-driven growth. 

Together, these two powers have the financial and technological capacity to dominate the next phase of AI development.
But the growing anxiety surrounding AI will not disappear through investment alone. The technology may need acceleration—but it also needs brakes. Trump’s AI ambitions may ultimately require a measure of restraint before enthusiasm outruns society’s ability to manage the consequences.

text:
Our minds aren’t equipped to handle AI | Benjamin Riley, The Verge

AI is junk food for the mind: easy, tempting and ultimately very bad for you.

Norbert Wiener, godfather of cybernetics, once said, “The thought of every age is reflected in its technique.” For the past century, our thought has been reflected in our computers, including by those in the AI industry. Google’s Demis Hassabis calls the brain “a biological approximation to a Turing machine.” Elon Musk puts it more bluntly, declaring that “people should just think of the brain as a biological computer.” (Musk’s brain often worries me.)

But humans are more complex than a straightforward comparison to computers gives us credit for — and far more than most of the AI industry seems to appreciate. And as their products push ever deeper into culture, this helps explain why they’re making such a mess. AI, it turns out, is something like a cognitive version of a hot dog: It appeals to us in the moment, but undermines the health and sustainability of cognitive systems we’ve evolved over several millennia.

To understand the problem, we’ll need a little neuroscience and the entirety of human evolutionary history.

The idea that brains are computers traces back to Alan Turing. It posits thought as a three-step process, functionally an algorithm: Our minds take in information from the world (input), manipulate it in some fashion (computation), and then enact behavior (output). Perception leads to cognition, which in turn leads to action. In slightly more elaborate terms, it looks something like this chart:

In many ways, this model has been productive. Imagining our brains as computers, technologists have pushed actual computing from simple adding machines to artificial neural networks and generative AI, seeking ever more detailed mirrors of our own minds.

But this mirror’s image, while not exactly wrong, is warped and limited. John von Neumann, a seminal figure in developing computers and computer science, doubted that the computational model could possibly capture the “exceptional complexity of the human nervous system.” That is, our nervous systems evolved to help us navigate the large ecological system that we call “the world.” And we act upon the world to exercise control over it (as best we can).

The computational approach looks at the end product of our minds and tries to “reverse engineer” how they function. But instead of working backward, we might instead examine the long arc of evolutionary history to build our model from the ground up. This is the approach favored by Paul Cisek, a neuroscientist at the University of Montreal, who’s patiently developed a biological model of brain and nervous system development spanning millions of years.

Cisek contends that rather than information processors, our brains are better understood as feedback-control systems. Our bodies don’t just receive input, they take action to adjust what that input is, contingent on what options are available. As Cisek himself is quick to note, this is not a new idea — writing at the turn of the 20th century, philosopher John Dewey described the mind as a circuit, “more truly termed organic than reflex, because the motor response determines the stimulus, just as truly as sensory stimulus determines movement.”

What exactly is the difference between the two approaches?

Here’s a classic example from baseball: catching a fly ball in the outfield. According to the computational model, solving this problem must involve some complicated and subconscious mental calculus wherein the outfielder estimates the ball’s velocity, calculates the effect of gravity, and undertakes untold other mathematical procedures to “compute” where the ball will go.

In contrast, the feedback-control approach suggests a simple heuristic — essentially, “keep the ball in the same position within your visual field, and then move to maintain that situation.” We take action to adjust the stimulus we receive.

This is not only more true to the experiences of anyone who’s played center field, it also avoids separating out the mental process from physical movement, and avoids invoking the use of complex calculations that the computational model requires. Humans are more dynamic than that. .

This approach also neatly maps to the biological architecture of brains as they’ve evolved over time. From ancient fish to amphibians to mammals to primates and eventually modern humans, what we observe is that new behaviors emerge in response to new environmental possibilities. When dinosaurs died off, for example, this meant some nocturnal creatures could move about the world in the daytime with less risk of being eaten, giving rise to a variety of new capacities. The history of our nervous system, Cisek observes, is one of “continuous extension of control further and further into the world.” (His forthcoming book will explore all this in greater detail, and yes, I’m hoping this essay puts subtle pressure on him to finish it.)

This leads to an alternative and very different diagram than the one above. We can both lay out a map of behaviors and abilities as they emerged over time and we can overlay the specific physical components of the brain to these capabilities, like so:

Instead of moving from left to right as in the computational model, this model should be seen as unfolding from top to bottom over evolutionary time. For example, a long time ago, as vertebrate animals developed more mobility, it became useful to have specialized systems for exploration — by using landmarks, say, or navigating at night. This led to the development of what we now call the hippocampus. Importantly, this also led our ancestors to remember important moments of scurrying from one spot to another, leading to the development of “episodic memory” of past experiences.

We can’t do anything remotely like this with the computational model of the mind; it simply does not sync up to observable neuroscientific structures. What’s more, it obscures that so much of what brains are doing involves controlling living organisms’ interactions within their environments. As such, Cisek suggests we need to dramatically shift the paradigm we’re using to understand the relationship between our brains and behavior, moving away from algorithmic input-outputs and toward more dynamic feedback systems.

Thus far, our story of human development has largely centered on feedback from the physical world. But one of humanity’s most important “feedback loops” arises from our profoundly social dispositions. The computational model, it turns out, doesn’t account for this well either — and neither does the AI industry. We’ve spent thousands of years building institutions and norms for learning from and communicating with each other, and over the course of less than a decade, Big Tech companies have systematically worked to dismantle them.

How? Again, we’ll need some historical context.

At some point around many hundreds of thousands of years ago, our distant ancestors did something incredible: They learned to imitate each other. Mimicking gestures and body movements allowed us to pass along successful practices — like chipping away at a stone tool — and coordinate more complex activities through shared ritualistic behaviors, which in turn shaped our cognition. It was the dawn of human culture.

We’ve spent thousands of years building institutions and norms for learning from and communicating with each other, and Big Tech companies are systematically working to dismantle them

Humans soon progressed to imitating sounds and, in turn, to oral language. As we’ve covered previously, language is not the same as thought, but it enables us to communicate our thoughts to each other. At some point, our wandering hunter-gatherer ancestors also started to settle down into non-transient communities, developing complex agricultural practices that allowed us to cultivate food rather than migrating to find it.

Finally, we started to use written marks to represent our spoken languages and other abstract ideas. We became capable of transmitting complex ideas across generations. Formal education, a process of ensuring knowledge is shared among a human group, emerged not long after. And so too in time did practices and institutions that collectivized human decision-making, such as “markets” and “law” and “democracy.”

Each claim I’ve just made is contestable, and cries out for far more detail than I can provide here. But this process is continuous with our biological evolution, in the sense that both foster an ever broader range of control over the world around us.

And sometimes this cultural change creates unintended consequences that hurt instead of help.

Human diets are perhaps the most obvious example. In our hunter-gatherer days, fatty foods were rare but precious to aid survival — just watch Alone if you doubt this — and we evolved to seek them out and store them in our bodies once found. But then we culturally developed the practice of farming and other agricultural techniques that, give or take 10,000 years, have made fatty foods plentiful today — if you want a hot dog, there’s plenty available.

AI clogs up our capacity to develop the knowledge we need to navigate the world

And that’s the problem. Hot dogs are a danger to our physical bodies, clogging our arteries with excessive fat we no longer need to store internally. AI poses a similar sort of danger to our cognitive capabilities, by clogging our capacity to develop the knowledge we need – in our heads – to navigate the world. It’s a cognitive hot dog.

The occasional hot dog won’t harm anyone, but it sure will if it becomes a regular meal at lunch or dinner. The same is true for AI — the harm is not from its occasional use, but making it part of our mental diet.

Yet that is exactly what Big Tech hyperscalers are trying to do.

In a July 2025 podcast about “how AI is transforming education,” OpenAI VP of education Leah Belsky boasted that “learners” made up more than half of the 900 million average monthly users of ChatGPT. The service was “the world’s largest learning platform,” she said. More recently, Anthropic announced a new initiative called “Claude for Teachers,” providing free access to premium models to practicing classroom educators.

These efforts will not benefit students, nor teachers. In fact, it’s the most obvious example of how AI weakens systems that we rely on to develop our cognition, for the benefit of convenience.

François Chollet, formerly a software engineer at Google, has memorably described AI as a tool of “cognitive automation,” which he defines as “encoding human abstractions in a piece of software, then using that software to automate tasks normally performed by humans.” Last year, an interdisciplinary group of scholars argued persuasively that we should view generative AI in the form of large language models not “primarily as intelligent agents, but as a new kind of cultural and social technology, allowing humans to take advantage of information other humans have accumulated” (emphasis added).

AI enthusiasts have made no shortage of predictions about the advantages of this, and they’ve largely dismissed the disadvantages as comparable to previous forms of automation, such as computers, calculators, and even the written word. (I’ve had citations to Plato’s alleged opposition to writing thrown at me so many times I’ve addressed them in a separate piece — he was a writer!)

Never before have we developed and broadly deployed something so explicitly intended to supplant human thinking

Whatever the effects of these earlier technologies, never before have we developed and broadly deployed something so explicitly intended to supplant human thinking — that’s what AI evangelists themselves argue.

Look at education. ChatGPT may be the world’s largest learning platform, but students are using it en masse to avoid the effortful thinking that’s necessary to build their durable knowledge. Evidence continues to mount demonstrating the negative impact of AI tools within education settings (and Gen Z generally hates it). A recent study from China revealed that thousands of students essentially stopped doing their homework once they started using AI (which substantially harmed their learning). There’s even evidence that when students use large language models for supposed learning purposes, they become habituated to relaxing their judgment and critical thinking in other contexts.

No other species’ brain and body develops over such an extended period as ours, and historically, we’ve complemented that with unique cultural institutions that transmit knowledge from one generation to the next. We should be zealously protective of this uniquely human endeavor, yet instead many university and school administrators, to say nothing of the Big Tech hyperscalers, are engaged in full-throated efforts to push AI as deep and as fast as they can into our education ecosystems.

If we only see the mind as a computer, AI might seem advantageous to learning — this is why many dream of building AI tutors. But already such efforts are failing, because our minds are more than just input-output devices. They exist, or rather we exist, within a broader cognitive ecosystem where we must make choices about how we choose to expend our cognitive energy. We do so to extend our agency, our control — however limited it may be — over our world.

If we only see the mind as a computer, AI might seem advantageous to learning — but this model is wrong

But this poses a challenge. Effortful thinking is hard, and if we’re offered technological off-ramps, we’ll take them — what some researchers recently called cognitive delegation. As cognitive delegation spreads, they warn, “the social environment that supports autonomous reasoning can weaken” — and as it does, such delegation “becomes still easier and more attractive.”

The researchers recommend a program of cognitive immunization from AI, one that preserves “the practices and institutions that keep human cognition active: unaided problem solving, verification, critical discussion, [and] periods of deliberate disengagement” from AI usage.

We call such institutions “schools.”

Policy levers will need to be pulled as well. I find it very interesting that Norway recently banned essentially all uses of AI in school for students under the age of 13. In the US, a major teachers’ union has likewise called for prohibiting chatbots in elementary schools, and major school districts such as Los Angeles and New York City have recently implemented bans as well. (Disclosure: I’ve provided informal advice to Schools Beyond Screens, an organization that pushed for these bans.) They won’t be the last to do so, or so I hope.

The good news, if it can be called that, is that resistance is growing — perhaps you’ve seen the many videos of college graduates booing commencement speakers praising AI? That’s no doubt in part due to job concerns, but I suspect many recognize the harm that AI has inflicted on their own cognitive development. Certainly, this is true for the students at the Oberlin Luddite Club, who wrote an open letter to their university president criticizing that institution’s embrace of AI: “As you embark on your year of AI, we’ll embark on our own year of self-actualization — of realizing the fruits of our labor, and of embracing human imperfection and raw inquiry.” Right on.

The control systems in our brains are the product of millions of years of biological evolution and several millennia of cultural evolution. We need to pull up from the computational model of the mind to see the full picture of what makes us human, and to appreciate our profoundly social nature, the driver of human culture. We have shown remarkable resiliency as a species, but gorging on cognitive hot dogs isn’t good for any of us.

Eat healthy, and think healthy.

📺 IS TODAY'S REBOUND A TRAP? MOMENTUM REMAINS FRAGILE + $SPY TESTS ITS 8-DAY & $QQQ FILLS ITS GAP + DON’T CHASE $SPCX + $MU, $SNDK & $WDC FLASH WARNING SIGNS

After yesterday's aggressive tech selloff, triggered by concerns surrounding OpenAI's revenue miss, stocks are bouncing back in today's premarket. 

But this is not an environment to aggressively chase strength. The major indices are holding up relatively well, while many individual momentum stocks continue to suffer significant technical damage.

*

The recent pullback in $SPY looks relatively normal after an extended advance toward $781. 

#SPY tested its 8-day moving average, shook out aggressive momentum traders, and held important support around $770. 

Now trading near $776.72 in the premarket, it faces immediate resistance at yesterday's $777 high and the $779 area. 

I doubt SPY can push decisively above that zone today. It could offer a tactical opportunity to reestablish some short exposure.

*

Similar story in $QQQ. After a strong multi-day rally that left the Nasdaq extended above its 8-day moving average, profit-taking was overdue. 

Yesterday's selloff brought #QQQ back toward that average, filled the previously identified gap near $743, and tested an important neckline. 

The action was sloppy, but the broader technical structure hasn't necessarily broken down. Still, a rebound doesn't automatically mean momentum has returned.

*

$SPCX  continues to be one of the few names that is still demonstrates relatively constructive momentum. 

After three consecutive down days into support, #SPCX is surging roughly $6 toward $166 in the premarket despite approximately 7% of its float becoming available for sale. 

I missed the entry near yesterday's close but I am not chasing the gap higher. 

Let the opening selling pressure play out, watch whether SPCX holds up during the first 30 minutes, and assess whether buyers can reclaim the previous topping-tail candle. 

Strong relative performance is encouraging, but entry price matters.

*

There is a growing divergence among semiconductors and memory-related stocks.

$MU is technically fine, but far from special. The stock continues to frustrate breakout traders with sideways action, failed momentum attempts, and limited follow-through. 

I would maintain disciplined positions around established support rather than repeatedly chasing rallies. A premarket bounce doesn't change the need for confirmation.

$SNDK technical picture is deteriorating. #SNDK is rolling below important moving averages, including the 50-day. I see little reason to chase until the stock stabilizes.

$WDC  is even weaker, with shares slipping below the 200-day moving average. This is not the kind of technical setup I would want to trade aggressively.

*

So, yesterday's selloff may have created a short-term rebound opportunity, but it hasn't repaired the damage beneath the surface. 

$SPY and $QQQ remain relatively resilient, yet failed breakouts, weak momentum, and deteriorating individual charts demand your caution.

Don't confuse a bounce with a sustainable breakout. Stay selective, respect resistance, avoid chasing opening gaps, and wait for the market to prove that buyers are genuinely back in control.

*

【Nvidia-Backed Data Center Abandons IPO】

(Nvidia-backed data center company Firmus has officially abandoned its IPO. The screenshots show how the company's shareholders and partners have been trading.

This reflects a market that is no longer willing to accept every AI company's promises. Investors are demanding stronger operating results and real profitability.

The stock performance of Firmus's shareholders and partners also highlights the potential risks for tech giants holding Anthropic shares. If Anthropic encounters unexpected problems when it goes public within the next two months, these companies could suffer significant declines as well.

Don't be misled by Bloomberg's clarification today that OpenAI's annualized revenue could reach $70 billion by year-end. This issue is not going away. The market now wants to see real revenue and actual cash coming in, not just projections.

Below is a report published in Australia today.)

On Monday, Firmus Technologies was expected to become one of the largest IPOs in Australian history. The company was pitching investors on a future powered by AI, built around liquid-cooled data centers packed with Nvidia chips.

By Friday, Firmus had dramatically withdrawn its plans to list on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX). The investor demand that had supposedly supported its heavily promoted IPO had failed to materialize.

The collapse raises serious questions about the claims made by Firmus's backers and the long-term viability of its business model.

Here is how the deal unraveled over the course of the week, according to people familiar with the process.

**Monday: Strong Demand on Paper**

Firmus was preparing to open its IPO order book, with Morgans, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, and Bank of America coordinating investor demand ahead of the listing.

Bankers circulated a message stating that, at the fixed offer price, demand indications significantly exceeded the number of shares available.

The IPO was initially priced at A$11 per share, targeting more than A$7 billion in proceeds and a valuation of approximately A$44 billion. That would have valued the company at roughly the same level as Woolworths, one of Australia's largest supermarket chains.

The valuation was striking for a company with only two small operating sites and a valuation of less than A$2 billion in 2025.

Bankers also indicated that 50% of the deal would be allocated to existing strategic investors, meaning the IPO needed to raise only about A$3.5 billion in new capital. At least five retail brokers were also involved.

The message was clear: demand was strong, and investors who hesitated risked missing out on a successful debut.

**Tuesday: Concerns About Insider Selling**

The order book opened as planned, with no obvious signs of trouble in public.

Behind the scenes, however, institutional investors became concerned after reviewing updated information. More than 50% of the shares on the register, including holdings controlled by Blackstone, Jane Street, and Coatue, could potentially be sold immediately after Firmus's planned October 23 listing.

Even Oliver Curtis, whose shares were reportedly subject to escrow arrangements, could use a financial instrument to monetize much of his stake immediately.

Rob Talevski, CEO of Webull Securities Australia, questioned whether retail investors were being positioned as an exit route for early investors.

The concerns were not without precedent. Shares in data center operator DigiCo Infrastructure have fallen by more than half since its late-2024 listing, despite a stronger broader market.

**Wednesday: Demand Falls Short**

Firmus's bankers failed to attract the expected demand from Australian institutions and U.S. investors seeking exposure to Asia's AI boom.

As pressure mounted, they turned to overseas hedge funds for US$150 million in bids. These investors, often described as liquidity providers, typically seek to make quick profits rather than hold shares for the long term.

Firmus was relying on the IPO to fund its planned data center expansion, including seven contracted facilities and four more in development. Almost all of its projected revenue depended on facilities that had yet to be built.

One fund manager following the process warned that the company would face serious problems if it could not raise capital, given its limited operating business.

The manager also noted that raising more private capital could leave existing investors without a clear exit route, since the IPO had been expected to provide that opportunity.

By Wednesday afternoon, bankers were attempting to cut the offer price from A$11 to A$9 per share, wiping billions of dollars off the proposed valuation. They also sought to reduce the fundraising target from around A$7 billion to just over A$4 billion.

Despite the reduced capital requirement, Australian superannuation funds showed little interest.

**Thursday: The Price Keeps Falling**

By Thursday, the proposed offer price had fallen further to A$5.50 per share, half the original A$11 price.

Each time the price changed, bankers had to return to potential investors to confirm whether they would still participate.

One fund manager told *Guardian Australia* that once a deal starts falling apart, the process can quickly become a downward spiral as negative momentum builds.

Firmus had expected to complete bookbuilding on Thursday, ahead of its ASX debut. Instead, company representatives abruptly withdrew from a scheduled parliamentary inquiry hearing on AI as they worked to salvage the IPO.

**Friday: IPO Abandoned**

On Friday, Firmus announced that it had withdrawn its ASX listing application, citing recent market volatility and current market conditions.

The timing is notable. Global technology indexes remain near record highs, arguably making this one of the most favorable environments for an AI infrastructure IPO.

A Firmus spokesperson said the company would now seek capital from private markets while considering other public and private financing options.

A third fund manager who had followed the bookbuilding process said retail investors had avoided a potential disaster.

“This is actually a good example of sanity prevailing and something that should never have happened being stopped in time.”

“If it had listed on the ASX, it would have ended in tears.” $nvda

On this day in 1942 – First three schools for enlisted WAVES open at Stillwater, OK (Yeoman), Bloomington, IN (Storekeepers), and Madison, WI (Radiomen).

-Stillwater, Oklahoma: Oklahoma A&M College (now Oklahoma State University) trained yeomen (secretaries and administrative staff).
-Bloomington, Indiana: Indiana University Bloomington trained storekeepers (supply and logistics personnel).
-Madison, Wisconsin: The University of Wisconsin trained radiomen (operators who sent and received coded messages).

Second Image: An original WWII Navy Recruitment poster, issued on January 13, 1943. The recruitment poster depicts a young woman in a U.S. Navy uniform, saluting. The top text reads, “Enlist in the Waves,” in white block text against a bold red background. Below, the text, “Release a Man to Fight at Sea,” appears in red block text. The poster urges women to “Apply to your nearest Navy Recruiting Station or Office of Naval Officer Procurement.”

Approved by Congress and signed into law by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in on July 30, 1942, the WAVES (Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service) program recruited women between 18 and 36 years old, and officers between 20 and 50, to serve onshore in the continental United States. Starting in 1944, many of these women also served in Alaska and Hawaii. The aim of the program was to enlist women to clerical jobs, in effort to free up male personnel for sea duty.

The WAVES program offered women who weren’t nurses the first chance to serve in the Navy. In addition to clerical and hospital jobs, the majority of WAVES were assigned to naval aviation units. Women maintained aircraft, tested parachutes, were domestic air traffic controllers and weather specialists, and trained men in navigation and gunnery. For a significant number of enlisted WAVES, the war provided the opportunity to work at jobs usually open only to men. During WWII, it is estimated that over 90,000 women served in the WAVES at enlisted and officer ranks.

"Release a Man to Fight at Sea" from the World War II WAVES (Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service) recruiting campaign means that women taking over non-combat, shore-based naval jobs allowed male sailors to leave those desk, clerical, and technical roles and deploy to active combat fleets in the Pacific and Atlantic

text:
Thus intellectually stimulating reading list brings together critical historiography, post-colonial critiques, geopolitical analyses, and foundational texts on Indian philosophy and civilization.

1. Deconstructing Western Paradigms & Indology

These texts critique how Western academic frameworks, colonial lenses, and secular models have shaped (and sometimes distorted) the understanding of Indian culture, religion, and society.

The Nay Science by Vishwa Adluri and Joydeep Bagchee (Critiques German Indological frameworks).
The Invention of World Religions by Tomoko Masuzawa (Examines how the modern concept of "religion" is a Western construct).
Western Foundations of the Caste System by Martin Farek et al. (Investigates how European ideas influenced the narrative on caste).
Europe, India, and the Limits of Secularism by Jakob De Roover (Explores the mismatch between Western secularism and Indian traditions).
Colonial Discourse and the Suffering of Indian American Children by K. Maheshwari & K. Singh (Looks at the real-world psychological impacts of these academic biases on the diaspora).

2. Indigenous Epistemology & Foundations of Indian Thought

This group focuses on understanding India through its own civilizational identity, philosophy, and foundational literature.

A History of Indian Philosophy by Surendranath Dasgupta (A monumental, authoritative survey of Indian philosophical schools).
The Vedas by Dr. Tulsi Ram (Direct access to primary spiritual and philosophical source texts).
Ramayana and Mahabharata by Bibek Debroy (Unabridged, rigorous translations of India's foundational epics).
India’s Contribution to World Thought and Culture (Showcases the global footprint of Indian ideas).
Indian Art and Architecture by P.C. Jain (Explores the aesthetic and material expressions of the culture).

3. History, Colonialism, & Institutional Disruptions

These books look at the historical timeline, the socio-economic impacts of colonialism, and the suppression of indigenous institutions.

India: The Definitive History by D. R. SarDesai (Provides a comprehensive chronological anchor for Indian studies).
The Beautiful Tree by Dharmapal (Crucial reading that uses British archives to prove India had a thriving, egalitarian indigenous education system before colonial rule).
Empire of Cotton by Sven Beckert (A global history that contextualizes how global capitalism and colonialism reshaped Indian industry).
The Indian Army in the Two World Wars by Kaushik Roy (Highlights India’s massive, often overlooked military contributions to global history).
Decline of Buddhism in India by KTS Sarao (A historical investigation into internal and external factors behind the shifting religious landscape).

4. Modern Geopolitics, Security, & Global Dynamics

A cluster focused on external security, civilizational conflicts, and global power structures that directly impact India's positioning today.

The Great Power Games by Vikram Sood (Insights into intelligence, statecraft, and global influence from India's perspective).
First Globalization by Geoffrey C. Gunn (Contextualizes the early modern Eurasian exchange).
The Party by Richard McGregor (Essential reading for understanding the internal machinery of China, India's primary geopolitical neighbor).
Sword and Scimitar by Raymond Ibrahim (Chronicles the historical, military confrontations between Western/Christian and Islamic civilizations).
The Darkening Age by Catherine Nixey (Details how early Christianity viewed classical Greco-Roman, offering a comparative look at civilizational transitions).
Aryan Idols by Stefan Arvidsson (Traces how Indo-European mythology was politicized in European science and ideology).

5. The Contemporary Civilizational Renaissance & Discourse

These texts represent the modern Indic intellectual movement, attempting to define India's contemporary identity and future trajectory outside of Westernized political frameworks.

India that is Bharat by J Sai Deepak (Deconstructs the constitutional, legal, and civilizational layers of decoloniality in India).
Breaking India & Snakes in the Ganga by Rajiv Malhotra et al. (Focuses on external and internal institutional threats to India's integrity, looking at fault lines and how they are exploited).
Hindutva Paradigm by Ram Madhav & Hindutva: Origin Evolution and Future by A. Neelakandan (Provide political and philosophical explorations of Hindu political thought of Integral Humanism).
A New Idea of India by H. Madhusudan & R. Mantri (Argues for a modern, progressive India that embraces both its cultural roots and economic liberty).
Sanatan Dharma: The Future of Civilization by H. B. Joshi (A forward-looking defense of traditional Indian ethics as a solution to global crises).
Feminism and World Religions by A. Sharma & K. K. Young (Offers a comparative critique of gender and spirituality across traditions).

list the major attacks IRGC has sponsored since 1979

Worked for 19s
The IRGC, especially its Quds Force, has directed or sponsored attacks since the early 1980s, usually through proxies such as Hezbollah, Saudi Hezbollah, Iraqi Shia militias, and later Hamas and the Houthis. The United States designated the entire IRGC a Foreign Terrorist Organization in April 2019. Attribution below rests on U.S. government findings, federal court rulings, Argentine judicial investigations, or Interpol notices—not on every claim Tehran denies.

Lebanon and the 1980s campaign
April 18, 1983 — U.S. Embassy, Beirut. A suicide car bomb killed 63 people, including 17 Americans. Claimed by Islamic Jihad, an early Hezbollah front that U.S. officials tied to Iranian direction.
October 23, 1983 — Beirut barracks bombings. Truck bombs killed 241 U.S. service members (220 Marines) and 58 French paratroopers. U.S. courts later held Iran liable; the operation is attributed to Hezbollah with IRGC involvement.
September 20, 1984 — U.S. Embassy annex, Beirut. A car bomb killed 24, including two Americans.
December 1983 — Kuwait bombings. Coordinated attacks on the U.S. and French embassies and other sites, linked to Iran-backed operatives (the “Kuwait 17,” including a relative of Imad Mughniyeh).
June 1985 — TWA Flight 847 hijacking. Hezbollah hijackers killed U.S. Navy diver Robert Stethem. Related kidnappings of Americans in Lebanon, including CIA station chief William Buckley (killed) and Marine Col. William Higgins (killed in 1989), are attributed to the same network.
Argentina
March 17, 1992 — Israeli embassy, Buenos Aires. A bomb killed 29 and wounded more than 240. Argentine and Israeli investigators attributed it to Hezbollah acting on Iranian orders.
July 18, 1994 — AMIA Jewish community center, Buenos Aires. A bomb killed 85 and injured more than 300, the deadliest antisemitic attack outside Israel since the Holocaust. Argentine courts and Interpol red notices named senior Iranian officials, including then-Quds Force commander Ahmad Vahidi, as organizers, with Hezbollah as the operational arm.
Saudi Arabia
June 25, 1996 — Khobar Towers, Dhahran. A truck bomb killed 19 U.S. Air Force personnel and wounded about 500. U.S. indictments and a 2006 federal court ruling found the attack was planned by IRGC officers (notably Brig. Gen. Ahmad Sharifi) and carried out by Saudi Hezbollah.
Iraq after 2003
2003–2011 — campaign against U.S. forces. The Pentagon has attributed at least 603 American deaths to Iranian-backed Shia militias armed, trained, and directed by the Quds Force under Qassem Soleimani, largely through explosively formed penetrators and rocket attacks.
January 20, 2007 — Karbala raid. Gunmen in U.S.-style uniforms attacked a coordination center, killing five American soldiers. The State Department later offered a reward for a Quds Force officer it said planned the raid. Asaib Ahl al-Haq has also claimed a role.
Plots and attacks outside the Middle East
October 2011 — Washington, D.C. (foiled). The Quds Force plotted to assassinate the Saudi ambassador, using Manssor Arbabsiar and a purported Mexican cartel hitman who was a U.S. informant. Gholam Shakuri, a Quds Force officer, was indicted.
February 2012 — New Delhi, Tbilisi, and Bangkok. Near-simultaneous attacks and a botched plot targeted Israeli diplomats. India, Thailand, and U.S. officials attributed them to IRGC operatives.
July 18, 2012 — Burgas, Bulgaria. A suicide bombing of a bus of Israeli tourists killed six (five Israelis and the Bulgarian driver). Bulgaria and the EU attributed it to Hezbollah.
2018 — Paris (foiled). An Iranian diplomat, Assadollah Assadi, was convicted in Belgium for directing a bomb plot against an opposition rally.
Later proxy campaigns
Gaza and Lebanon wars. The IRGC has long funded, trained, and armed Hezbollah, Hamas, and Palestinian Islamic Jihad. Hezbollah’s 2006 war with Israel and Hamas’s rocket campaigns, including the October 7, 2023 attack and the war that followed, used Iranian-supplied weapons and training. Direct Quds Force command of the October 7 operation itself is not established in public evidence; material support is.
January 28, 2024 — Tower 22, Jordan. A drone strike by Iran-aligned Iraqi militias killed three U.S. soldiers. The State Department later tied groups in that network to Iranian funding and direction.
Red Sea and Gulf shipping, 2019 onward. IRGC naval forces and the Houthis (armed and advised by the Quds Force) attacked tankers and commercial ships; Houthi strikes intensified after October 2023.
Dissident assassinations. From the 1980 killing of Ali Akbar Tabatabaei in Maryland through dozens of murders of exiles in Europe in the 1980s–90s, and more recent plots against journalists and activists in the U.S. and Europe, the IRGC and Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence have run a parallel campaign of targeted killings. Open-source trackers count on the order of 200 Iranian external plots since 1979.
The pattern is consistent: the Quds Force supplies money, training, weapons, and often operational direction, while a proxy or cutout claims or obscures responsibility. U.S. courts have entered large default judgments against Iran and the IRGC for Beirut, Khobar Towers, and related cases.

🚨Missing Missouri Couple Update After Our Interview 🚨

The link below, is an update from Tara the host of Citizen MC on Facebook.

We may have been remote, with internet issues, a streaming restart, while both of Glen and I were 🤧🤦🏻‍♀️, and the hotel we had just checked into that evening - only had 1 chair, so I (Jen) was sitting on a hardtop suitcase for over 2 hours 😩, but we got through the interview to bring the information to our audience. 😅And all of you were amazing in your support! So, thank you!!! 🙏🏼 

Tara, our guest, had great information, and was very patient with restarting our livestream, and our crazy situation, and for that we’re very grateful!

However, there is something I want to address in her latest update . 

Tara voiced to her audience in this clip, that she felt we asked questions that put her in the position of defending the sheriffs department of her hometown. 

We in no way meant to make her feel uncomfortable or defensive.

Two elderly people, from the same family, with their dog had been reported missing after they had been gone for over a week. A search warrant for THE COUPLE’S property was needed to search for them ON THE COUPLE’S own property, and it  took several days before the warrant was issued.  We asked 2 sets of neighbors of the Lindeman’s if they knew the reason, and they too seemed concerned at the turn around time.

We’ve  since heard from an inside source that there’s another warrant that was needed for another property, and that was also supposedly taking several days as well.

We feel it’s appropriate to ask, “why”?

We tried to reach out to the detective in charge of the case 3 separate times, over several days, in the first two weeks this was reported, and were told each time that we’d get a call back. We understood he must be busy, and we were patiently waiting. We did however continue to reach out, in an effort to make sure that what we were reporting was accurate and true!

However, those calls have yet to be returned. 

We called a 4th time, before our trip,  to inquire as to the status of our requests for an interview, and we were told there were many requests from others as well, and it could be awhile, before we hear back.

 With no response, no press conferences scheduled, and no PIO to speak to, we were very excited to get Tara on our show for an interview. 

Tara has said publicly, that she being a long time and generational McDonald County resident, has a close relationship with the sheriff.  Therefore, she has been fortunate enough to have been granted multiple interviews, and updates in the case. Which is invaluable, in a case such as the Lindeman’s.

We asked questions that we and our audience had been asking about the warrants and searches, since we first reported on the case from our visit to the neighborhood. We hoped she might have the answers. We in no way meant to make Tara feel uncomfortable. 

We appreciate Tara’s willingness to share her information, and patience with our remote and rough working conditions for the interview . 

We also want to thank our audience for their patience in restarting the livestream, the outpouring of support when we tried to organize a search team, and the amazing offers from everyone willing to search with us!
