text:
A Chicago packing house refused to hire Black women, so the Negro Labor Relations League waited for chitterling season and took the company apart in the one month it could not afford to lose a customer. Agar did not just start hiring Black women on the packing floor. It hired them into the front office. You are looking at the same outfit that handed the man in this photograph his sign.

The man in the photograph has no name.

He is standing on a Chicago sidewalk in July of 1941, shirt white, collar buttoned, tie knotted at the throat in summer heat. On his shoulder he carries a plank of wood the way a soldier carries a rifle at rest.

The sign is hand-lettered. It reads: If Negro men can carry guns for Uncle Sam surely they can drive milk wagons for Bowman Dairy.

A federal photographer named John Vachon made the picture that month, and the print is in a New York museum now, catalogued and credited and measured to the eighth of an inch. Nobody wrote down who the man was.

But he did not make that board by himself, and he was not out there on a feeling.

The people who put him on that sidewalk had a name, an office, a newspaper, and a method. And a few months before this, that same method had broken a packing house in half.

Start there, because it tells you exactly who you are looking at.
The Agar Packing Company in Chicago had a hiring rule, and it was not written in code.

No Black women wanted.

That was the whole policy. A Black woman could walk into Agar with twenty years of packing experience and she would not be hired to sweep the floor, and everybody on the South Side knew it, and for years nothing happened about it.

The Negro Labor Relations League did not go pound on Agar's door in July.
They waited for chitterling season.

Understand what that means, because if you did not grow up with it you will miss the whole blade of this. Chitterlings were a cold weather food, a winter food, the thing that came out of the pot when the money was thin and the family was large and the house needed to smell like somebody loved it.

Which means a Chicago packing house that sold chitterlings made a serious share of its year in a few cold months. And it made that money almost entirely out of Black kitchens.

Agar had built a business on Black women's grocery dollars while refusing to let a Black woman touch a paycheck, so the League let the calendar come around.

When the cold hit and the demand rose and the orders started stacking up, the Crusader went to press against Agar, hard, and it kept printing. And Black Chicago quit buying.

Not for a week. Through the season, through the one window a chitterling packer cannot afford to lose, in a city with a Black population big enough to make that decision felt in an accountant's ledger by the second week.

Agar broke.

And it did not break halfway, which is the part that should raise the hair on your arms. The company did not just start hiring Black women onto the packing floor, it hired them into the front office.

Front office. Desks, telephones, payroll, the rooms where Black women had never been allowed to sit down in that building.

That was not luck and it was not a moral awakening at Agar. That was a group of people who had studied a company's calendar until they found the exact week it could be hurt.

Now you know what kind of outfit handed a man a plank of wood outside a dairy.
The Negro Labor Relations League was organized in Chicago in 1937 to break the color line in hiring, and it ran on two men who could not have looked less alike on paper.

Joseph H. Jefferson was a South Side native who owned a wrecking company. He knew how to take a building down, which is a useful cast of mind.

Jefferson never ran for office in his life, and he was arrested again and again for the demonstrations he organized.

Sit with that sentence a second. Not arrested once, as a young man, in a burst of nerve.

Arrested repeatedly, across years, as a business owner with something to lose, and then out on the sidewalk again the next time. A man who has been booked once and quits is ordinary and forgivable.

A Chicago packing house refused to hire Black women, so the Negro Labor Relations League waited for chitterling season and took the company apart in the one month it could not afford to lose a customer. Agar did not just start hiring Black women on the packing floor. It hired them into the front office. You are looking at the same outfit that handed the man in this photograph his sign.

A man who has been booked five times and shows up for the sixth is a different animal.

Balm L. Leavell Jr. was born in Louisville, Kentucky, went to Fisk, and intended to be a doctor. He came to Chicago in 1930 instead, about twenty years old, and went to work in the liquor and beverage trade.

By 1938 he was organizing the Dining Car Waiters Union. He spent his days with men who fed white passengers across the country and came home to a city that would not hire them to drive a truck.

That is the year the two of them met.

Together they went after the motion picture operators' unions and the local theaters. They went after the Milk Wagon Drivers union, the city's dairies, and several of the major daily newspapers.

That list is not my summary of their work. It is Jefferson's own accounting, written in a column he published the week after Leavell died.

They pushed the Pabst Brewing Company until Black men were driving its trucks on the South Side. They got Black men onto beer trucks and bread trucks and buses.

They went after the pawnbrokers who had been quietly bleeding people who could not read a contract closely. They walked out of that negotiation with an agreement that changed how the whole trade dealt with Black customers.

Both men were threatened for it, and neither one of them stopped.

And in June of 1940, a year before that photograph, the two of them started a newspaper because nobody else was going to write any of this down.
It was one page.

They ran it out of an apartment in the Ida B. Wells Homes on the South Side, and Jefferson said plainly what they wanted it for. They wanted a house organ that would cover the League's work completely and sincerely.

There was a hole where that coverage should have been. The Chicago Defender's founder, Robert S. Abbott, had died four months earlier, and his paper was locked in a succession fight that would end in court.

So two men with a job to do put out one sheet of paper about Black people getting hired.
And they gave it away free for seventeen years.

Do that math with a business eye. Seventeen years of paper, ink, and labor, handed out on street corners for nothing, because the point was never the paper.

The point was that when the League leaned on a company, twenty thousand people had to know why by Saturday.
That single sheet became the Chicago Crusader, which is still publishing today, and it is the reason we can say with certainty that the man outside Bowman Dairy was not a lone soul with a grievance.

Now the job he was standing there for, because it was a real job and he knew exactly what it paid.

Bowman was the biggest prize in the city. It was the largest fluid-milk distributor in Chicago, employing more than three thousand people in the Chicago area by the middle of the 1930s.

And it had built its big bottling plants on the South Side.

The plants stood in and beside the Black Belt. The bottles came out of those plants, rode to Black kitchens, went up Black front steps, and were paid for out of Black pockets, carried by a white man in a Bowman uniform.

A Chicago milkman's day started at four forty-five in the morning, the earliest hour the union contract would allow, which tells you men had once been made to start earlier than that.
He loaded at the plant door and rolled out after five fifteen.

Then a hundred and fifty stops, twenty-two miles out and back, in the dark for the first hours of it. He solicited the trade, sold the product, billed the customer, collected the money, and settled every argument about a short quart personally, at the door, before six in the morning.

At the end of it he came back, wrote his tickets for the empties, handed his cash to the cashier, and ordered tomorrow. Then he either filled his gasoline tank or unhitched his horse, because in Chicago in 1941 it could still be a horse.

Nine-hour day on paper, and fifty-six in the actual telling of the men who did it.

And the basic union wage for that work was forty-eight dollars a week, guaranteed, before commissions, in a trade where drivers were averaging around fifty-two.
Put that number in a kitchen and see what it buys.

Forty-eight dollars a week is a family that pays rent on the first without a conversation about it. It is shoes that fit, coal in February, a doctor when the baby's chest rattles, and a Sunday where nobody counts.

For a household that had come north on a train to get out from under Mississippi wages, that job was not a job. It was the whole reason for the train.

Which brings us to the wall.

Federal investigators surveyed Chicago drivers that same winter and found the typical man on a milk route was about forty-two years old. He had been driving milk for nearly fifteen years and had been with the same dairy more than eleven.

The government's own analysts explained why. The industry had barely hired anybody in a decade.

So this was not a wide field with a color bar at the gate. It was a nearly frozen field with a color bar at the gate, and the rare opening that did come went to a white man who then held it for fifteen years.

Meanwhile the men locked out of it took what Chicago handed them. The killing floors of the stockyards, the heat of the mills, red caps, porters, elevator work, and other people's kitchens.

Now hold that forty-eight dollars a week against what the country was offering him that same month.

The first peacetime draft in American history had been signed the previous September, and Black men across Chicago went down and registered like everybody else. The Army took them, into segregated units, under white officers, and it sorted the overwhelming majority into labor and service battalions rather than combat arms.

Which means the Army had already decided what a Black man was for. It decided he was for loading, hauling, digging, cooking, and driving trucks.

Read that last one twice.

The Army would put him behind a wheel and point him at a war. Bowman would not put him behind a wheel and point him at Sixty-Third Street.

And an Army private in July of 1941 started at twenty-one dollars a month.

Twenty-one a month with a rifle. Forty-eight a week with a milk bottle, and he could not have the milk bottle.

That is the arithmetic he was carrying on his shoulder, and he had every legal right to carry it, which is its own buried story.

On March 28, 1938, the Supreme Court decided New Negro Alliance against Sanitary Grocery. The facts were almost absurdly small.

A Black civic group asked a grocery chain to hire Black clerks in stores whose customers were Black. The company ignored them, so the group put one person in front of one store on one day with a placard.

One person, one sign, one day.

The placard said the company employed no Negroes, and a lower court ruled that this was not a labor dispute at all and shut the picketing down.
Two Black lawyers, Belford V. Lawson Jr. and Thurman L. Dodson, took it to the Supreme Court of the United States and won it six to two.

Justice Roberts wrote that this was a labor dispute, that the Norris-LaGuardia Act reached it, and that the information on the placard was true. That ruling is the reason a man could stand outside a Chicago dairy three years later with a homemade board and not be dragged off for it.

Now look at the union he was asking to join.

The Milk Wagon Drivers' Union of Chicago, Local 753, had carried its own picketing fight all the way to the Supreme Court and lost it on February 10, 1941. Five months before this photograph, the milk drivers of Chicago were in Washington arguing that their right to walk a line was close to sacred.

Five months later a Black man was walking a line for permission to become one of them.

And the union and the dairy were not strangers to each other: in November of 1938 a federal grand jury indicted the whole Chicago milk market for restraint of trade. Bowman Dairy and Local 753 both sat on that defendant list, and they settled together in September of 1940.

The company and the union could find each other in a courtroom. Neither one could find him on the sidewalk.

One more thing had happened, one month before Vachon lifted his camera, and it is the reason this photograph should sting.

A. Philip Randolph told the White House that a hundred thousand Black people would march on the capital on July 1, 1941, demanding an end to discrimination in defense hiring and in the armed forces. Roosevelt met him and Walter White on June 18 and tried to talk him out of it.

The President said he could not issue an order for one group, because then there would be "no end to other groups coming in here" asking for theirs.
Randolph did not move.

On June 25, 1941, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 8802, declaring there would be no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries and in government because of race, creed, color, or national origin. It was the first presidential directive on race since Reconstruction, and Randolph called off the march.

And then, in July, a man walked out onto a Chicago sidewalk with a plank of wood, because a dairy is not a defense plant.

That is the buried thing inside this picture. The order reached federal agencies and companies doing war work, and milk carried up a back staircase on the South Side was neither.

He was standing in the gap the order left behind, days after the most celebrated civil rights document in seventy years had been signed without reaching him. He knew that, and he went out anyway.

We never learn how it ended for him. Nobody recorded whether Bowman gave in, or whether he ever drove one of those wagons.

But we know what it cost the men who sent him, because that part is written down.
Jefferson kept getting arrested and kept going back out, all the way through, and he lived until 1984 and died at seventy-six.

Balm Leavell did not get that long.

Sometime around 1959, a teenage girl from Pine Bluff, Arkansas went to see Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun. Afterward a man offered her and her friend a ride home.

In the car she talked the whole way about the newspaper job she was going to get and everything she meant to do once she had it. She had no idea she was talking to the publisher.

When her friend told her afterward who had been driving, Dorothy said she almost died. She went to the interview anyway, which is the sentence that explains the rest of her life.

Two people had called in sick at the Crusader that day and Balm Leavell needed hands. He hired her at thirty-five dollars a week to keep the books.

Two people out sick. That is how thin the thread was.

They married in 1963. They had five years.

In July of 1968 Balm went into Michael Reese Hospital for exploratory surgery, and the surgeons found stage four pancreatic cancer.

He was awake on October 23 for his wife's twenty-fourth birthday. The next day he slipped into a coma, and on Friday, October 25, 1968, he died with her beside him.

She was twenty-four years old. She had a three-year-old, a two-year-old, and two newspapers.

According to the Crusader's own account of that week, Balm's children from an earlier marriage tried to keep her from his bedside while he was dying. They made threats to her at the funeral and in the days after.

Twenty-four, widowed, two babies, and threatened over the body.

There was a twenty-four-hour wake at First Deliverance Church in Bronzeville, and nearly a hundred floral arrangements around the casket. She wore black with a veil and led the mourners out to Lincoln Cemetery, where her husband was laid in a mausoleum a short distance from Robert Abbott.

Then the children went to court for the estate.

And Joseph Jefferson, made executor by Judge Richard Gumbel, held a majority interest in the company and could have taken the whole thing. Instead he put his weight behind the twenty-four-year-old widow and made her publisher.

He had spent thirty years fighting people who kept Black folks out of rooms. He was not about to start doing it himself at the end.

Dorothy R. Leavell has run those papers ever since, from 1968 to right now, and in all that time the Crusader has never missed an issue.

Not one, through the assassinations, the riots, the collapse of American newspapers, a pandemic. Fifty-eight years of getting a paper out on time for a readership that other publishers decided was not worth the postage.

In October of 2016 the city of Chicago finally did something for the two men who started it.

There was a small ceremony in a parking lot half a block from the Crusader office on King Drive. Alderman, historian, former alderman, family, a few dozen people standing around in the fall.

Then somebody pulled a cover off a street sign.

It is brown, rectangular, and sixteen inches long. It hangs on the pole underneath the sign that says Martin Luther King Jr. Drive.

Sixteen inches of painted metal for the men who put Black women in Agar's front office, Black drivers on Pabst's trucks, and a man in a pressed white shirt outside the largest dairy in Chicago.
Dorothy Leavell stood there and said she was excited and very pleased, and that the men being honored were legends.

She was seventy-one. She had been waiting since she was twenty-four.

Now go back to the photograph one last time, and look at what got kept and what got thrown away.

Bowman Dairy was bought out in 1966, and its old bottles turn up on collector sites now, the glass with the arrow through the B, and people pay real money for them. The company's name is preserved in a business encyclopedia, on shelves in antique shops, and, more permanently than either, on a picket sign hanging in a museum.

John Vachon's name is preserved. It is under the photograph, in the surveys of Depression-era photographers, in the credit line every time the image runs.

Every word on that board is preserved, down to the punctuation, in two archives and a Smithsonian exhibit.
The month is preserved, the city, the dimensions of the print in inches, and the year a museum bought it.

The man is not.

He is the only person in the frame and the only thing in it without a name, and he stood there in July heat asking for a job that started at four forty-five in the morning. Somebody with a camera was standing directly in front of him and never asked him who he was.

So here is the smallest honest repair available to us, eighty-five years late.

Stop calling him a man with a sign. He was a member of an organization, carrying an argument worked out in meetings by men who went to jail for it and got up and went back.

And when you tell somebody about this picture, do not stop at the picture. Tell them about the packing house that got broken in the middle of chitterling season, and the one-page paper handed out free for seventeen years, and the twenty-four-year-old in the veil who never missed an issue.

That crowd made him. He is what they looked like on an ordinary Tuesday.

And he asked for a milk route, and he said surely.

The man in this photograph never left us his name, but the movement around him changed Chicago forever. I research forgotten stories like his because the people who fought quietly for progress deserve to be remembered.
If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/Vm6JEQzdIW
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
Some professions have absolutely brutal expiration dates.

Athletes probably being the worst.

Father Time is undefeated. If you’re hitting a ball, throwing one, or tossing one in a round cylinder… Father Time is the 1996 Bulls crossed with the 1927 Yankees.

I know some guys who got a taste of the big time. Maybe had a cup of coffee in the majors. Maybe had a great college career.

Let’s just say the years following their “expiration date” were not always the easiest.

Or worse yet, the peaked in high-school Rob Lowe guy still posting his old sports highlights on Instagram reels.

Ouch.

I spent basically my entire childhood convinced I was going to be Ken Griffey Jr.

I was a really good baseball player. I also was not going to be Ken Griffey Jr.

And the more I think about it, I’m kind of glad. And I'm glad I knew it by high school.

Because what I do now doesn’t have much of an expiration date.

I can be a better writer at 45 than I am today. Better businessman at 50. Better husband and friend at 60.

Of course, that doesn’t mean I don’t invent expiration dates for myself.

I read Andrew Ross Sorkin’s 1929 earlier this year. For some reason this stands out.

Unbelievable book. No notes. Not that I could offer Sorkin any.

Then I heard him on like four podcasts and CNBC. He's written bestsellers and produced TV shows. Interviews everyone who matters. 

Seems to have a great family life and be a genuinely nice dude.

You look at someone like that and start thinking: “What the hell have I accomplished?”

Then I looked him up.

He’s 49. I’m 36.

Naturally my brain went, "Still time I suppose?"

Which is honestly kind of  ridiculous.

Athletes have real expiration dates. The rest of us mostly make them up in our heads.

A little anxiety is probably useful. A little comparison is probably useful too.

Without any pressure, we’d all be deadbeats playing COD in our parents’ basements.

But if the scoreboard is all that matters, you’re probably going to be miserable no matter how much you accomplish.

I’m happy with where I am today. And also a bit anxious to accomplish more.

Both can be true. I think.

That’s what this week’s blog is about.

Ken Griffey Jr. Chris Rock. Andrew Ross Sorkin. Expiration dates. And the completely made-up timelines we use to judge our lives.

Full blog here: https://t.co/loGnJ8ofBs

text:
For years, women in South Florida knew her as "the Duchess." She offered cosmetic injections to give women fuller hips and curvier figures. She charged far less than a real doctor. There was a reason for that. She wasn't one. Oneal Ron Morris had no medical license. And according to investigators, what she was injecting into her patients wasn't medical-grade anything.

They said her mixture included silicone, mineral oil, cement, and Fix-a-Flat tire sealant. Witnesses said that after each injection, she sealed the wound by super gluing a cotton ball over it. One of her patients was Shatarka Nuby, a 31-year-old mother. Between 2007 and 2010, she received around 10 injections from Morris, paying about $2,000. Over time, the injection sites turned hard. Then they turned black.

Nuby wrote to Florida's health department, warning that something terrible had been put into her body. In 2012, she died. The medical examiner said the substance had spread throughout her body. Morris denied ever using anything from a hardware store. Her lawyers argued her patients knew she wasn't a real doctor.

In 2017, she pleaded no contest to manslaughter and practicing medicine without a license. The judge sentenced her to 10 years in prison. "Putting her in jail won't bring her back," Nuby's aunt said in court.

text:
Francis Smith Mogambi is a Kenyan man who had been living as an immigrant in Lincoln, Nebraska.

Mogambi was recently charged with second-degree forgery, a Class 2A felony, following a cross-border federal student loan identity theft investigation. 

According to police records, his sudden access to thousands of dollars in disposable cash allowed him to freely wire large sums of money across international borders back to Kenya while living comfortably on the proceeds of federal funding.

Mogambi’s operation relied on a sophisticated, multi-step pipeline combining cyber-theft, educational fraud, and forgery. His relatives back in Kenya would illegally harvest, purchase, or steal the Personal Identifiable Information (PII)—including names, dates of birth, and Social Security Numbers (SSNs)—of legitimate U.S. citizens. 

Mogambi would then use these stolen identities to register the victims into online distance-learning programs at major US institutions. Once the "ghost students" were accepted, he would apply for maximum federal student financial aid loans in their names. 

 When the universities disbursed the excess financial aid via paper checks, the letters were intercepted or routed to addresses Mogambi controlled. He would then forge the victims' signatures, endorse the checks to himself, and deposit them into his personal bank accounts.

Investigators linked Mogambi to student aid profiles and financial aid checks originating from multiple online degree institutions, explicitly including Grand Canyon University, Colorado Technical University, and American Public University.

 In April 2026, Mogambi grew overconfident and attempted to expand his local operations by recruiting an acquaintance. He offered this witness a massive payout of $2,000 per week to assist him in managing, signing, or cashing the fraudulent checks.

Shocked by the blatant illegality of the operation, the witness refused the offer and called the Lincoln Police Department (LPD). They arranged to meet investigators directly at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Student Union to file a formal belated fraud report, providing the police with their first major breakthrough.

Once the tip was received, the Lincoln Police Department launched a meticulous forensic investigation on Mogambi's activities. 

Detectives subpoenaed bank records and retrieved physical financial aid refund checks cashed by Mogambi. Forensic signature analysis revealed that multiple different checks, allegedly signed by completely different "students," all shared the exact same handwriting traits and signatures, with several being directly endorsed over to Mogambi’s name.

According to investigator's report, one victim of this fraud, a resident of Wisconsin, had absolutely no knowledge of the scheme until they checked their credit score and discovered an active, mounting federal student loan debt for an online college they had never applied to or attended.

Detectives tracked Mogambi's bank accounts and mapped out a clear paper trail showing thousands of dollars in student loan payouts entering his account and immediately being wired out to recipient bank accounts in Kenya.

Armed with an arrest affidavit, police searched his residence and uncovered physical photos of checks and a cache of academic loan documents from Grand Canyon University.

With irrefutable physical and forensic evidence in hand, police officially arrested Mogambi and charged him with second-degree forgery, a serious Class 2A felony under Nebraska law.

If convicted of a Class 2A felony in Nebraska, he faces a maximum penalty of up to 20 years in prison.

Because he is a non-US citizen, Kenyan national, a felony conviction of this magnitude will result in the permanent forfeiture of his legal residency status in the United States, followed by mandatory deportation back to Kenya upon completion of any prison term.

text:
In 1633 Rembrandt painted Christ asleep in a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee while a storm breaks over it. It is his only painted seascape.

Mark tells the story. The waves fill the boat while Jesus sleeps on a pillow in the stern, and the disciples wake him: "Master, carest thou not that we perish?"

In the painting a wave breaks over the bow and tears the sail. The disciples fight to keep the boat under control, and one is sick over the side. Only Christ, at the right, is calm. One man steadies himself on a rope, holds his cap and looks straight at us. The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum says his face "seems familiar from Rembrandt's self-portraits."

In the early hours of 18 March 1990, thieves stole the painting and twelve other works from the Gardner Museum in Boston, cutting the canvas from its frame. The works have never been found, and the FBI offers a reward of up to $10 million. The museum keeps the empty frames as placeholders for their return.

In Mark, Jesus "arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm."

text:
SPOT 🎯N WITH JOHNNY

🔥 IF THE DEVIL WANTED TO DESTROY AMERICA, WOULD HE REALLY NEED TO CHANGE HIS STRATEGY? 🔥

🎙️ In 1965, legendary broadcaster Paul Harvey delivered a remarkable commentary titled “If I Were the Devil.”

He imagined how Satan might gradually corrupt a nation, not through an obvious invasion, but by quietly undermining its faith, families, morality, and foundational values.

More than six decades later, his warning still deserves our attention!

WHAT IF THE DEVIL'S GREATEST WEAPON ISN'T GETTING PEOPLE TO WORSHIP HIM, BUT GETTING THEM TO LIVE AS THOUGH GOD DOESN'T EXIST?

Think about it!

If I were the devil, I wouldn't begin by closing every church. I'd encourage Christians to attend on Sunday while ignoring God's Word the rest of the week.

I wouldn't immediately destroy marriages. I'd introduce temptation, pornography, selfishness, and resentment until husbands and wives became strangers beneath the same roof.

I wouldn't openly declare war on children. I'd persuade parents that everything else deserves their attention before teaching their children about Jesus Christ.

I wouldn't necessarily convince people that evil is good overnight. I'd slowly blur the distinction until standing for biblical truth became more offensive than celebrating sin.

I wouldn't need to remove every Bible. I'd simply convince people they were too busy to read one.

And perhaps most dangerously...

I'D MAKE CHRISTIANS SO BUSY FIGHTING ONE ANOTHER THAT THEY FORGOT WHO THEIR REAL ENEMY IS!

📖 EPHESIANS 6:12 (KJV)

"For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."

Beloved, Paul Harvey's commentary wasn't Scripture or a prophecy. It was a warning about moral and spiritual compromise.

But the Bible warned us about Satan's schemes long before Paul Harvey ever approached a microphone!

📖 1 PETER 5:8 (KJV)

"Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:"

🔥 HERE'S WHAT SHOULD WAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN UP!

Satan doesn't have to convince everyone to hate Jesus.

Sometimes all he needs is for believers to become indifferent toward Him.

A neglected Bible.

A prayerless home.

A compromised conscience.

A marriage without forgiveness.

Children growing up without knowing the Gospel.

SPIRITUAL DECLINE DOESN'T ALWAYS ARRIVE WITH A ROAR. SOMETIMES IT ENTERS THROUGH THE QUIET DOOR OF COMPROMISE!

But here's the glorious news!

THE DEVIL DOES NOT GET THE FINAL WORD! JESUS CHRIST DOES!

📖 JAMES 4:7 (KJV)

"Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."

America's greatest need isn't merely better behavior, stronger institutions, or another political victory.

OUR GREATEST NEED IS GENUINE REPENTANCE, BIBLICAL TRUTH, AND HEARTS TRANSFORMED BY JESUS CHRIST!

✝️ MY FINAL THOUGHT:

Paul Harvey challenged Americans to recognize the dangers of moral decay.

But Scripture gives Christians something greater than a warning.

IT GIVES US THE ANSWER!

Open your Bible. Get on your knees. Love your family. Teach your children. Stand for truth. Share the Gospel.

And remember:

🔥 SATAN MAY BE WORKING TO DECEIVE THE WORLD, BUT HE CANNOT OVERTHROW THE KING OF KINGS!

❤️ Thank you for taking the time to read this far. Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Salvation is God's gift through faith, not works (Ephesians 2:8–9). If you've wandered far from God, turn to Jesus Christ today!

THE DEVIL WANTS YOUR DESTRUCTION. JESUS CHRIST OFFERS YOU ETERNAL LIFE!

Stay SPOT 🎯N the Word of God and Walking on the Narrow Road! 🙌
